abstract: We demonstrate the ability of a two-layer network of thresholded summation units to support representation of 3D objects in which several distinct 2D views are stored for ea.ch object. Using unsupervised Hebbian relaxation, the network learned to recognize ten objects from different viewpoints. The training process led to the emergence of compact representations of the specific input views. When tested on novel views of the same objects, the network exhibited a substantial generalization capability. In simulated psychophysical experiments, the network's behavior was qualitatively similar to that of human subjects.

paragraphs: The paper explores recognizing three-dimensional objects by storing several two-dimensional views of each object. Its network has two layers of units that sum their inputs and apply a threshold. This gives the system a way to represent an object through distinct appearances associated with different viewpoints.

Using unsupervised Hebbian relaxation, the network learns to recognize ten objects across viewpoints. Training produces compact representations of the particular views it encounters. The important connection is between organizing individual views and recognizing the objects they depict: the learned representation must accommodate changes in appearance while supporting object recognition.

When shown previously unseen views of the same objects, the network exhibits substantial generalization. Its recognition ability therefore extends beyond the specific views presented during training. In simulated psychophysical experiments, its behavior also resembles human behavior qualitatively. That resemblance concerns the pattern of behavior rather than a stated numerical match. Together, the findings support multiple stored views as a useful basis for recognition across changes in viewpoint.
summary.tldr: A two-layer network learns compact representations of object views and generalizes to unseen viewpoints of the same objects.

title: A self-organizing multiple-view representation of 3D objects

abstract: A simple architecture and algorithm for analytically guaranteed associa(cid:173) tive memory storage of analog patterns, continuous sequences, and chaotic attractors in the same network is described. A matrix inversion determines network weights, given prototype patterns to be stored. There are N units of capacity in an N node network with 3N 2 weights. It costs one unit per static attractor, two per Fourier component of each sequence, and four per chaotic attractor. There are no spurious attractors, and there is a Lia(cid:173) punov function in a special coordinate system which governs the approach of transient states to stored trajectories. Unsupervised or supervised incre(cid:173) mental learning algorithms for pattern classification, such as competitive learning or bootstrap Widrow-Hoff can easily be implemented. The archi(cid:173) tecture can be "folded" into a recurrent network with higher order weights that can be used as a model of cortex that stores oscillatory and chaotic attractors by a Hebb rule. Hierarchical sensory-motor control networks may be constructed of interconnected "cortical patches" of these network modules. Network performance is being investigated by application to the problem of real time handwritten digit recognition.

paragraphs: The paper describes an associative memory that can store static analog patterns, continuous sequences, and chaotic attractors in one network. Given prototype patterns, a matrix inversion determines the connection weights. The storage construction comes with analytical guarantees, including the absence of spurious attractors: the network does not introduce additional attracting behaviors outside those specified.

Capacity is expressed through an explicit accounting system. A network with N nodes and 3N² weights has N capacity units. A static attractor uses one unit, each Fourier component of a sequence uses two, and a chaotic attractor uses four. Thus, different kinds of stored behavior consume different portions of the same capacity.

A Lyapunov function in a special coordinate system describes how transient states approach stored trajectories. The authors also discuss incremental learning and a recurrent reformulation with higher-order weights that supports Hebbian storage of oscillatory and chaotic behavior. Interconnected modules are proposed for hierarchical sensory-motor control, while handwritten-digit recognition is described as an application under investigation.
summary.tldr: A mathematically specified associative memory stores static patterns and dynamic attractors with explicit capacity costs and no spurious attractors.

title: CAM Storage of Analog Patterns and Continuous Sequences with 3N2 Weights

abstract: In visual processing the ability to deal with missing and noisy informa(cid:173) tion is crucial. Occlusions and unreliable feature detectors often lead to situations where little or no direct information about features is availa(cid:173) ble. However the available information is usually sufficient to highly constrain the outputs. We discuss Bayesian techniques for extracting class probabilities given partial data. The optimal solution involves inte(cid:173) grating over the missing dimensions weighted by the local probability densities. We show how to obtain closed-form approximations to the Bayesian solution using Gaussian basis function networks. The frame(cid:173) work extends naturally to the case of noisy features. Simulations on a complex task (3D hand gesture recognition) validate the theory. When both integration and weighting by input densities are used, performance decreases gracefully with the number of missing or noisy features. Per(cid:173) formance is substantially degraded if either step is omitted.

paragraphs: This paper studies visual classification when features are missing or unreliable because of occlusion or imperfect detection. Even partial observations can strongly constrain the correct class. The authors use a Bayesian framework to extract class probabilities from the information that remains, rather than requiring every feature to be observed directly.

The optimal calculation integrates over possible values of the missing features and weights those possibilities by their local probability densities. Both operations matter: integration accounts for multiple possible completions, while density weighting gives more plausible completions greater influence. The authors derive closed-form approximations using Gaussian basis function networks and extend the framework to noisy features.

Simulations on three-dimensional hand gesture recognition support the approach. When both integration and density weighting are included, performance deteriorates gradually as more features become missing or noisy. Omitting either operation substantially worsens performance. The finding identifies a concrete source of robustness: uncertainty must be considered across possible feature values, with their probabilities incorporated into the classification calculation.
summary.tldr: Bayesian integration weighted by input densities makes visual classification degrade gracefully as features become missing or noisy.

title: Some Solutions to the Missing Feature Problem in Vision

abstract: A simple but powerful modification of the standard Gaussian dis(cid:173) tribution is studied. The variables of the rectified Gaussian are constrained to be nonnegative, enabling the use of nonconvex en(cid:173) ergy functions. Two multimodal examples, the competitive and cooperative distributions, illustrate the representational power of the rectified Gaussian. Since the cooperative distribution can rep(cid:173) resent the translations of a pattern, it demonstrates the potential of the rectified Gaussian for modeling pattern manifolds.

Since the cooperative distribution can rep(cid:173) resent the translations of a pattern, it demonstrates the potential of the rectified Gaussian for modeling pattern manifolds.

paragraphs: This paper studies a modification of the Gaussian distribution in which all variables are constrained to be nonnegative. That restriction changes the kinds of energy functions the distribution can use, allowing nonconvex forms. The energy function shapes which configurations receive greater probability, so this change expands the structures that the model can represent.

The authors illustrate the distribution's expressive capacity through two multimodal examples, called competitive and cooperative distributions. Multimodality means that probability can concentrate around several distinct configurations. These examples demonstrate how the nonnegative formulation supports richer arrangements of likely states within the proposed distribution family.

The cooperative example can represent translations of a pattern, connecting the distribution to the modeling of pattern manifolds. A translated pattern belongs to a related family of configurations, and representing that family is a step toward describing continuous pattern variation. The paper's contribution is thus both a distributional construction and an illustration of its potential for representing structured families of patterns.
summary.tldr: Constraining Gaussian variables to be nonnegative enables nonconvex, multimodal models, including one that represents translations of a pattern.

title: The Rectified Gaussian Distribution

abstract: Prioritized sweeping is a model-based reinforcement learning method that attempts to focus an agent's limited computational resources to achieve a good estimate of the value of environment states. To choose ef(cid:173) fectively where to spend a costly planning step, classic prioritized sweep(cid:173) ing uses a simple heuristic to focus computation on the states that are likely to have the largest errors. In this paper, we introduce generalized prioritized sweeping, a principled method for generating such estimates in a representation-specific manner. This allows us to extend prioritized sweeping beyond an explicit, state-based representation to deal with com(cid:173) pact representations that are necessary for dealing with large state spaces. We apply this method for generalized model approximators (such as Bayesian networks), and describe preliminary experiments that compare our approach with classical prioritized sweeping.

paragraphs: Prioritized sweeping is a reinforcement-learning method that decides where an agent should spend its planning effort. Because computation is limited, it tries to update estimates of state value where errors are likely to be largest. Classical prioritized sweeping makes that choice using a simple heuristic tied to an explicit representation of individual states.

The paper introduces a principled way to generate priorities that depends on the representation being used. This matters when an environment has too many states for an explicit state-based description to be practical. Compact representations can capture the environment more economically, but the mechanism for deciding which planning operation is valuable must work with that representation.

The authors apply generalized prioritized sweeping to model approximators such as Bayesian networks and describe preliminary comparisons with the classical method. The central advance is extending the allocation of planning effort beyond individually represented states. It makes prioritization part of the representation's design, allowing the same overall objective to be pursued with more compact environment models.
summary.tldr: Generalized prioritized sweeping adapts planning priorities to compact model representations for large state spaces.

title: Generalized Prioritized Sweeping

abstract: We present an analog VLSI cellular architecture implementing a simpli(cid:173) . fied version of the Boundary Contour System (BCS) for real-time image processing. Inspired by neuromorphic models across several layers of visual cortex, the design integrates in each pixel the functions of sim(cid:173) ple cells, complex cells, hyper-complex cells, and bipole cells, in three orientations interconnected on a hexagonal grid. Analog current-mode CMOS circuits are used throughout to perform edge detection, local inhi(cid:173) bition, directionally selective long-range diffusive kernels, and renormal(cid:173) izing global gain control. Experimental results from a fabricated 12 x 10 pixel prototype in 1.2 J-tm CMOS technology demonstrate the robustness of the architecture in selecting image contours in a cluttered and noisy background.

paragraphs: This paper translates a simplified Boundary Contour System into an analog chip architecture for real-time image processing. The design draws on models of several visual cortical cell types. Its purpose is to select image contours even when background clutter and noise make individual edge signals difficult to interpret.

Each pixel combines functions associated with simple, complex, hyper-complex, and bipole cells. These functions operate in three orientations, with pixels connected on a hexagonal grid. Analog current-mode CMOS circuits implement edge detection, local inhibition, direction-sensitive interactions over longer distances, and global gain control. The architecture therefore brings several stages of contour processing together within the pixel array.

The authors fabricated a prototype containing 12 by 10 pixels in 1.2-micrometer CMOS technology. Experiments with that prototype demonstrate robust contour selection against cluttered and noisy backgrounds. This provides hardware evidence for the proposed architecture: the coordinated processing is implemented in physical circuitry, and its contour-selection behavior is demonstrated on the fabricated device.
summary.tldr: A fabricated analog chip implements cortical-inspired contour processing and demonstrates robustness to background clutter and noise.

title: Analog VLSI Cellular Implementation of the Boundary Contour System

abstract: When a visual image consists of a figure against a background, V1 cells are physiologically observed to give higher responses to image regions corresponding to the figure relative to their responses to the background. The medial axis of the figure also induces rela(cid:173) tively higher responses compared to responses to other locations in the figure (except for the boundary between the figure and the background). Since the receptive fields of V1 cells are very smal(cid:173) l compared with the global scale of the figure-ground and medial axis effects, it has been suggested that these effects may be caused by feedback from higher visual areas. I show how these effects can be accounted for by V1 mechanisms when the size of the figure is small or is of a certain scale. They are a manifestation of the processes of pre-attentive segmentation which detect and highlight the boundaries between homogeneous image regions.

paragraphs: This paper examines why neurons in primary visual cortex, V1, can respond more strongly to a figure than to its background. Responses can also be elevated along the figure's medial axis, its central internal structure, compared with other interior locations. These effects extend across image regions much larger than an individual V1 cell's receptive field.

That mismatch in spatial scale has motivated explanations involving feedback from higher visual areas. The paper shows how mechanisms within V1 can account for the effects when the figure is small or lies within a certain scale. The scale condition is central: the claim is that local visual processing can explain these observations under those circumstances.

The proposed explanation connects the response patterns to segmentation before attention is directed to the image. These processes detect and emphasize boundaries between regions with relatively uniform visual properties. Figure-ground and medial-axis responses thus become manifestations of the same segmentation processes, providing a V1-based explanation for effects that might otherwise be attributed to higher-area feedback.
summary.tldr: V1 segmentation mechanisms can explain figure-ground and medial-axis response enhancements for figures within particular size conditions.

title: Can VI Mechanisms Account for Figure-Ground and Medial Axis Effects?

abstract: A standard view of memory consolidation is that episodes are stored tem- porarily in the hippocampus, and are transferred to the neocortex through replay. Various recent experimental challenges to the idea of transfer, particularly for human memory, are forcing its re-evaluation. However, although there is independent neurophysiological evidence for replay, short of transfer, there are few theoretical ideas for what it might be doing. We suggest and demonstrate two important computational roles associated with neocortical indices.

paragraphs: The paper reconsiders what replay might contribute to memory consolidation. A standard account holds that episodes are stored temporarily in the hippocampus and transferred to the neocortex through replay. The authors note experimental challenges to this transfer account, particularly for human memory, that motivate reconsidering its interpretation.

A key distinction is between evidence that replay occurs and an explanation of its purpose. The abstract points to independent neurophysiological evidence for replay even as the transfer hypothesis faces challenges. This leaves a computational question: what useful role could replay serve if its function is not adequately explained by moving episodic memories between brain systems?

The authors suggest and demonstrate two computational roles associated with neocortical indices. Their contribution is to offer additional functional accounts of replay in a setting where theoretical alternatives to transfer were scarce. The significance lies in separating a supported neural phenomenon from one particular explanation of it, and in investigating computational roles that preserve a place for replay while the standard consolidation account is being reevaluated.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes and demonstrates two computational roles for replay associated with neocortical indices as alternatives to a transfer-centered account.

title: Replay, Repair and Consolidation

abstract: Signiﬁcant plasticity in sensory cortical representations can be driven in mature animals either by behavioural tasks that pair sensory stimuli with reinforcement, or by electrophysiological experiments that pair sensory input with direct stimulation of neuromodulatory nuclei, but usually not by sensory stimuli presented alone. Biologically motivated theories of representational learning, however, have tended to focus on unsupervised mechanisms, which may play a signiﬁcant role on evolutionary or devel- opmental timescales, but which neglect this essential role of reinforce- ment in adult plasticity. By contrast, theoretical reinforcement learning has generally dealt with the acquisition of optimal policies for action in an uncertain world, rather than with the concurrent shaping of sensory representations. This paper develops a framework for representational learning which builds on the relative success of unsupervised generative- modelling accounts of cortical encodings to incorporate the effects of reinforcement in a biologically plausible way.

paragraphs: The paper asks how reinforcement can change the way sensory cortex represents incoming information. Its motivation comes from adult animals: substantial changes in sensory representations can follow tasks that pair stimuli with reinforcement, or experiments that pair sensory input with stimulation of neuromodulatory nuclei. Presenting sensory stimuli alone usually does not produce the same effect.

This creates a gap between two traditions of learning theory. Unsupervised accounts explain how representations can develop from sensory experience, but tend to leave reinforcement out of adult plasticity. Reinforcement learning, meanwhile, has generally concentrated on choosing actions in uncertain environments, rather than explaining how sensory representations change alongside action learning.

The authors develop a framework that adds reinforcement effects to generative-model accounts of cortical encoding in a biologically plausible way. Its contribution is to connect learning what sensory inputs represent with learning what is behaviorally consequential. The abstract presents this framework as an extension of existing representational accounts, without claiming that unsupervised learning has no role in development or evolution.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a biologically plausible framework for incorporating reinforcement into the learning of sensory representations.

title: A Biologically Plausible Algorithm for Reinforcement-shaped Representational Learning

abstract: In applying Hidden Markov Models to the analysis of massive data streams, it is often necessary to use an arti(cid:12)cially reduced set of states; this is due in large part to the fact that the basic HMM estimation algorithms have a quadratic dependence on the size of the state set. We present algorithms that reduce this computational bottleneck to linear or near-linear time, when the states can be embedded in an underlying grid of parameters. This type of state representation arises in many domains; in particular, we show an application to tra(cid:14)c analysis at a high-volume Web site.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models can become expensive to estimate when their state sets are large. The basic estimation algorithms have a quadratic dependence on the number of states, creating a bottleneck for massive data streams. The abstract identifies a practical consequence: applications often use an artificially reduced state set to keep the computation manageable.

The authors present algorithms that reduce this bottleneck to linear or nearly linear time when the states can be embedded in an underlying grid of parameters. That structural condition is central to the result. The computational improvement uses an organized representation of the state space, and the stated guarantee applies when that representation is available.

The paper demonstrates an application to traffic analysis at a high-volume website and notes that parameter-grid representations arise in multiple domains. Its contribution is a route to more efficient estimation for suitably structured HMMs. By reducing the dependence on state count, the algorithms address a computational reason for shrinking models in large-stream applications.
summary.tldr: For HMM states embedded in a parameter grid, the proposed algorithms reduce a quadratic estimation bottleneck to linear or near-linear time.

title: Fast Algorithms for Large-State-Space HMMs with Applications to Web Usage Analysis

abstract: We consider the scaling of the number of examples necessary to achieve good performance in distributed, cooperative, multi-agent reinforcement learning, as a function of the the number of agents n. We prove a worstcase lower bound showing that algorithms that rely solely on a global reward signal to learn policies confront a fundamental limit: They require a number of real-world examples that scales roughly linearly in the number of agents. For settings of interest with a very large number of agents, this is impractical. We demonstrate, however, that there is a class of algorithms that, by taking advantage of local reward signals in large distributed Markov Decision Processes, are able to ensure good performance with a number of samples that scales as O(log n). This makes them applicable even in settings with a very large number of agents n.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much experience cooperative reinforcement learning requires as the number of agents grows. Its focus is the number of real-world examples needed for good performance. In a large distributed system, that requirement can determine whether learning is practical even when agents share a common objective.

The authors prove a worst-case lower bound for algorithms that learn policies solely from a global reward signal. For those algorithms, the required number of examples scales roughly linearly with the number of agents. This establishes a fundamental limitation of relying only on that shared feedback in the worst case.

They also identify a class of algorithms that uses local reward signals in large distributed Markov decision processes and guarantees good performance with sample requirements scaling as O(log n). This result shows how the form of feedback can change the scaling of learning. The logarithmic guarantee applies to the described algorithm class and setting, giving a route to learning with very many agents.
summary.tldr: Global-reward-only learning has a roughly linear worst-case sample requirement, while a class using local rewards achieves logarithmic scaling.

title: On Local Rewards and Scaling Distributed Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Diffusion Tensor Magnetic Resonance Imaging (DT-MRI) is a non inva- sive method for brain neuronal ﬁbers delineation. Here we show a mod- iﬁcation for DT-MRI that allows delineation of neuronal ﬁbers which are inﬁltrated by edema. We use the Muliple Tensor Variational (MTV) framework which replaces the diffusion model of DT-MRI with a mul- tiple component model and ﬁts it to the signal attenuation with a vari- ational regularization mechanism. In order to reduce free water con- tamination we estimate the free water compartment volume fraction in each voxel, remove it, and then calculate the anisotropy of the remaining compartment. The variational framework was applied on data collected with conventional clinical parameters, containing only six diffusion di- rections. By using the variational framework we were able to overcome the highly ill posed ﬁtting. The results show that we were able to ﬁnd ﬁbers that were not found by DT-MRI.

paragraphs: The paper modifies diffusion tensor MRI to delineate neuronal fibers in brain regions infiltrated by edema. The central issue addressed is contamination from free water, which affects the diffusion signal used to identify fibers. The method aims to separate that contribution before assessing the directional properties associated with the remaining tissue compartment.

The authors use a Multiple Tensor Variational framework, replacing the usual diffusion model with a model containing multiple components. They estimate the free-water volume fraction in each voxel, remove its contribution, and calculate the anisotropy of the remaining compartment. Variational regularization supports fitting this more complex model to the measured signal attenuation.

The framework is applied to data acquired with conventional clinical parameters and only six diffusion directions. The authors report that regularization enables them to overcome the highly ill-posed fitting problem in this setting. Their results identify fibers that conventional diffusion tensor MRI did not find, supporting the usefulness of explicitly modeling free-water contamination in the studied edema data.
summary.tldr: A regularized multicomponent diffusion model removes estimated free-water contamination and reveals fibers missed by conventional diffusion tensor MRI.

title: Neuronal Fiber Delineation in Area of Edema from Diffusion Weighted MRI

abstract: Schizophrenia is a complex psychiatric disorder that has eluded a characterization in terms of local abnormalities of brain activity, and is hypothesized to affect the collective, ``emergent working of the brain. We propose a novel data-driven approach to capture emergent features using functional brain networks [Eguiluzet al] extracted from fMRI data, and demonstrate its advantage over traditional region-of-interest (ROI) and local, task-specific linear activation analyzes. Our results suggest that schizophrenia is indeed associated with disruption of global, emergent brain properties related to its functioning as a network, which cannot be explained by alteration of local activation patterns. Moreover, further exploitation of interactions by sparse Markov Random Field classifiers shows clear gain over linear methods, such as Gaussian Naive Bayes and SVM, allowing to reach 86% accuracy (over 50% baseline - random guess), which is quite remarkable given that it is based on a single fMRI experiment using a simple auditory task.

paragraphs: The paper investigates schizophrenia through patterns of interaction across the brain. Its motivation is that abnormalities in individual locations may not adequately characterize a disorder involving collective brain function. The authors extract functional brain networks from fMRI data and use them to represent properties that emerge from the network as a whole.

They report advantages over traditional region-of-interest analysis and local, task-specific linear activation analysis. Their results suggest that schizophrenia is associated with disrupted global network properties that local activation changes cannot explain in their analysis. This supports the proposed network perspective, while remaining an association rather than an established causal account of the disorder.

The authors also use sparse Markov random field classifiers to capture interactions, reporting gains over Gaussian Naive Bayes and SVM methods. Classification reaches 86% accuracy against a 50% random-guess baseline. These results come from a single fMRI experiment involving a simple auditory task. The stated finding is that interaction-sensitive representations and classifiers can extract useful discriminatory information from that experimental setting.
summary.tldr: Functional brain networks and interaction-based classifiers distinguish schizophrenia in an fMRI experiment better than the compared local and linear approaches.

title: Discriminative Network Models of Schizophrenia

abstract: We propose a new approach to the analysis of Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP) by establishing a formula that connects the Hessian of the Bethe free energy with the edge zeta function. The formula has a number of theoretical implications on LBP. It is applied to give a sufficient condition that the Hessian of the Bethe free energy is positive definite, which shows non-convexity for graphs with multiple cycles. The formula clarifies the relation between the local stability of a fixed point of LBP and local minima of the Bethe free energy. We also propose a new approach to the uniqueness of LBP fixed point, and show various conditions of uniqueness.

title: Graph Zeta Function in the Bethe Free Energy and Loopy Belief Propagation

abstract: Sodium entry during an action potential determines the energy efficiency of a neuron. The classic Hodgkin-Huxley model of action potential generation is notoriously inefficient in that regard with about 4 times more charges flowing through the membrane than the theoretical minimum required to achieve the observed depolarization. Yet, recent experimental results show that mammalian neurons are close to the optimal metabolic efficiency and that the dynamics of their voltage-gated channels is significantly different than the one exhibited by the classic Hodgkin-Huxley model during the action potential. Nevertheless, the original Hodgkin-Huxley model is still widely used and rarely to model the squid giant axon from which it was extracted. Here, we introduce a novel family of Hodgkin-Huxley models that correctly account for sodium entry, action potential width and whose voltage-gated channels display a dynamics very similar to the most recent experimental observations in mammalian neurons. We speak here about a family of models because the model is parameterized by a unique parameter the variations of which allow to reproduce the entire range of experimental observations from cortical pyramidal neurons to Purkinje cells, yielding a very economical framework to model a wide range of different central neurons. The present paper demonstrates the performances and discuss the properties of this new family of models.

paragraphs: The paper revisits how Hodgkin–Huxley models represent the energy cost of neuronal action potentials. Sodium entry determines that efficiency, and the classic model admits about four times the minimum charge required for its depolarization. The motivating experimental observations indicate that mammalian neurons can operate much closer to the metabolic optimum.

The authors introduce a family of models intended to capture sodium entry and action-potential width while reproducing voltage-gated channel dynamics similar to those observed in mammalian neurons. This addresses a mismatch between the classic model's behavior and the more efficient action potentials described in the experimental evidence.

A single parameter varies the model across the reported range of observations, from cortical pyramidal neurons to Purkinje cells. The family therefore offers a compact way to represent differences among these central neurons while attending to both waveform properties and sodium use. The paper demonstrates the models' performance and discusses their properties, presenting the single-parameter construction as an economical framework for this range of neuronal behavior.
summary.tldr: A single-parameter Hodgkin–Huxley model family captures observed sodium efficiency, spike width, and channel dynamics across several mammalian neuron types.

title: Sodium entry efficiency during action potentials: A novel single-parameter family of Hodgkin-Huxley models

abstract: Undirected graphical models, or Markov networks, such as Gaussian graphical models and Ising models enjoy popularity in a variety of applications. In many settings, however, data may not follow a Gaussian or binomial distribution assumed by these models. We introduce a new class of graphical models based on generalized linear models (GLM) by assuming that node-wise conditional distributions arise from exponential families. Our models allow one to estimate networks for a wide class of exponential distributions, such as the Poisson, negative binomial, and exponential, by fitting penalized GLMs to select the neighborhood for each node. A major contribution of this paper is the rigorous statistical analysis showing that with high probability, the neighborhood of our graphical models can be recovered exactly. We provide examples of high-throughput genomic networks learned via our GLM graphical models for multinomial and Poisson distributed data.

paragraphs: Graphical models describe relationships among variables, but familiar Gaussian and Ising models impose distributional assumptions that may not suit the data. This paper introduces a class of undirected graphical models based on generalized linear models. Its starting assumption is that each node's distribution, conditional on the other nodes, belongs to an exponential family.

The approach estimates the network by fitting penalized generalized linear models to select each node's neighborhood. This connects network estimation to a familiar regression framework while accommodating distributions such as Poisson, negative binomial, and exponential. The model family therefore offers ways to match network estimation to data that do not follow the usual Gaussian or binomial assumptions.

A central theoretical contribution is an analysis showing that exact neighborhood recovery can hold with high probability. This is a probabilistic recovery result, rather than certainty for every observed dataset. The paper also presents genomic network examples using multinomial and Poisson data, illustrating how the modeling framework applies to high-throughput biological measurements.
summary.tldr: Penalized generalized linear models enable network estimation for diverse exponential-family data, supported by high-probability neighborhood-recovery analysis.

title: Graphical Models via Generalized Linear Models

abstract: The Shape Boltzmann Machine (SBM) has recently been introduced as a state-of-the-art model of foreground/background object shape. We extend the SBM to account for the foreground object's parts. Our model, the Multinomial SBM (MSBM), can capture both local and global statistics of part shapes accurately. We combine the MSBM with an appearance model to form a fully generative model of images of objects. Parts-based image segmentations are obtained simply by performing probabilistic inference in the model. We apply the model to two challenging datasets which exhibit significant shape and appearance variability, and find that it obtains results that are comparable to the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Separating an object from its background does not explain how the object is divided into parts. This paper extends the Shape Boltzmann Machine, a model of foreground and background shape, to represent those internal divisions. The resulting Multinomial Shape Boltzmann Machine models the shapes of an object's parts rather than treating its foreground as a single undifferentiated region.

The model captures both local and global statistics of part shapes. This allows its representation to account for small-scale shape patterns as well as broader organization across the object. The authors combine that shape representation with an appearance model, producing a generative model of object images. Segmentation then becomes a probabilistic inference problem: the model is used to infer how an observed image should be divided into parts.

The authors evaluate the approach on two challenging datasets with substantial variation in shape and appearance. They report performance comparable to the state of the art. The contribution is therefore a unified probabilistic approach to part segmentation, with reported results showing that its combined shape and appearance representation can handle considerable visual variability.
summary.tldr: A generative model combines object-part shapes and appearance to infer segmentations with results comparable to the state of the art.

title: A Generative Model for Parts-based Object Segmentation

abstract: We propose a novel class of algorithms for low rank matrix completion. Our approach builds on novel penalty functions on the singular values of the low rank matrix. By exploiting a mixture model representation of this penalty, we show that a suitably chosen set of latent variables enables to derive an Expectation-Maximization algorithm to obtain a Maximum A Posteriori estimate of the completed low rank matrix. The resulting algorithm is an iterative soft-thresholded algorithm which iteratively adapts the shrinkage coefficients associated to the singular values. The algorithm is simple to implement and can scale to large matrices. We provide numerical comparisons between our approach and recent alternatives showing the interest of the proposed approach for low rank matrix completion.

The resulting algorithm is an iterative soft-thresholded algorithm which iteratively adapts the shrinkage coefficients associated to the singular values. The algorithm is simple to implement and can scale to large matrices. We provide numerical comparisons between our approach and recent alternatives showing the interest of the proposed approach for low rank matrix completion.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix completion fills in missing matrix entries while favoring a compact underlying structure. This paper introduces a class of algorithms built around penalties on the matrix's singular values. These penalties control the spectral representation of the completed matrix, making the treatment of singular values central to how low rank is encouraged.

The authors express the penalty through a mixture model and introduce suitable latent variables. This probabilistic construction yields an Expectation-Maximization algorithm for obtaining a maximum a posteriori estimate of the completed matrix. The resulting procedure repeatedly applies soft thresholding, adapting the shrinkage coefficients associated with the singular values as optimization proceeds.

The adaptive coefficients allow the regularization applied to the singular values to evolve during estimation. The authors describe the algorithm as simple to implement and scalable to large matrices. Numerical comparisons with recent alternatives support the usefulness of the approach for matrix completion. The contribution links a probabilistic penalty representation to a practical iterative algorithm with adaptive spectral regularization.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic matrix-completion method adaptively shrinks singular values through an Expectation-Maximization algorithm.

title: Probabilistic Low-Rank Matrix Completion with Adaptive Spectral Regularization Algorithms

abstract: The prediction of time-changing variances is an important task in the modeling of financial data. Standard econometric models are often limited as they assume rigid functional relationships for the evolution of the variance. Moreover, functional parameters are usually learned by maximum likelihood, which can lead to overfitting. To address these problems we introduce GP-Vol, a novel non-parametric model for time-changing variances based on Gaussian Processes. This new model can capture highly flexible functional relationships for the variances. Furthermore, we introduce a new online algorithm for fast inference in GP-Vol. This method is much faster than current offline inference procedures and it avoids overfitting problems by following a fully Bayesian approach. Experiments with financial data show that GP-Vol performs significantly better than current standard alternatives.

paragraphs: Financial time series often have variances that change over time, making variance prediction an important modeling task. Standard econometric approaches can impose rigid relationships on that evolution. Their parameters are also commonly fitted by maximum likelihood, which the authors identify as a possible source of overfitting.

The paper introduces GP-Vol, a nonparametric volatility model based on Gaussian processes. It can represent highly flexible functional relationships governing changing variances. The authors pair this model with a new online inference algorithm that is much faster than the offline inference procedures used for comparison. A fully Bayesian treatment is presented as the mechanism for avoiding the overfitting problems motivating the work.

Experiments on financial data show significantly better performance than standard alternatives in the reported comparisons. The contribution combines flexibility in how variance evolves with a faster way to perform Bayesian inference. These two aspects address separate modeling concerns: restrictive assumptions about volatility dynamics and the computational cost of learning a richer probabilistic model.
summary.tldr: GP-Vol combines flexible Gaussian-process volatility modeling with fast online Bayesian inference and improves on standard alternatives in financial-data experiments.

title: Gaussian Process Volatility Model

abstract: We propose RoBiRank, a ranking algorithm that is motivated by observing a close connection between evaluation metrics for learning to rank and loss functions for robust classification. The algorithm shows a very competitive performance on standard benchmark datasets against other representative algorithms in the literature. Further, in large scale problems where explicit feature vectors and scores are not given, our algorithm can be efficiently parallelized across a large number of machines; for a task that requires 386,133 x 49,824,519 pairwise interactions between items to be ranked, our algorithm finds solutions that are of dramatically higher quality than that can be found by a state-of-the-art competitor algorithm, given the same amount of wall-clock time for computation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces RoBiRank, a ranking algorithm motivated by a connection between ranking evaluation metrics and robust classification losses. The key idea is to use that relationship when designing a method for ordering items. This links the objective used in learning to quantities relevant to evaluating the resulting ranking.

On standard benchmark datasets, RoBiRank performs very competitively against representative ranking algorithms. The paper also addresses a large-scale setting in which explicit feature vectors and scores are unavailable. In that setting, the algorithm can be efficiently distributed across many machines, making parallel computation a substantial part of its practical contribution.

The large-scale evaluation involves a task with 386,133 by 49,824,519 pairwise interactions between the items to be ranked. Given the same wall-clock computation time, RoBiRank obtains solutions of dramatically higher quality than the state-of-the-art competitor used in that comparison. The result supports the usefulness of the robust-classification connection together with parallel execution for this demanding ranking task, rather than establishing a universal advantage on every ranking problem.
summary.tldr: RoBiRank connects ranking metrics with robust classification losses and achieves strong benchmark results, including substantially better large-scale rankings at equal computation time.

title: Ranking via Robust Binary Classification

abstract: In this paper we present a definition for visual saliency grounded in information theory. This proposal is shown to relate to a variety of classic research contributions in scale-space theory, interest point detection, bilateral filtering, and to existing models of visual saliency. Based on the proposed definition of visual saliency, we demonstrate results competitive with the state-of-the art for both prediction of human fixations, and segmentation of salient objects. We also characterize different properties of this model including robustness to image transformations, and extension to a wide range of other data types with 3D mesh models serving as an example. Finally, we relate this proposal more generally to the role of saliency computation in visual information processing and draw connections to putative mechanisms for saliency computation in human vision.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an information-theoretic definition of visual saliency, seeking a shared account of what makes parts of visual data stand out. The definition connects with established work on scale space, interest-point detection, bilateral filtering, and previous saliency models. Its aim is therefore both explanatory and computational.

Using the proposed definition, the authors obtain results competitive with leading methods on two distinct tasks: predicting human eye fixations and segmenting salient objects. These tasks test different uses of saliency, one concerned with where people look and the other with identifying prominent objects. The reported results support the usefulness of the definition across both applications.

The paper also examines robustness to image transformations and extensions beyond images, using three-dimensional meshes as an example. More broadly, it relates saliency to visual information processing and discusses possible mechanisms in human vision. These connections provide a wider interpretation of the model, while the proposed links to human mechanisms remain suggestive rather than an established account of how biological vision computes saliency.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic definition connects several saliency-related methods and delivers competitive fixation-prediction and salient-object segmentation results.

title: Saliency, Scale and Information: Towards a Unifying Theory

abstract: An active learner is given a hypothesis class, a large set of unlabeled examples and the ability to interactively query labels to an oracle of a subset of these examples; the goal of the learner is to learn a hypothesis in the class that fits the data well by making as few label queries as possible.This work addresses active learning with labels obtained from strong and weak labelers, where in addition to the standard active learning setting, we have an extra weak labeler which may occasionally provide incorrect labels. An example is learning to classify medical images where either expensive labels may be obtained from a physician (oracle or strong labeler), or cheaper but occasionally incorrect labels may be obtained from a medical resident (weak labeler). Our goal is to learn a classifier with low error on data labeled by the oracle, while using the weak labeler to reduce the number of label queries made to this labeler. We provide an active learning algorithm for this setting, establish its statistical consistency, and analyze its label complexity to characterize when it can provide label savings over using the strong labeler alone.

paragraphs: Active learning tries to build an accurate classifier while asking for relatively few labels. This paper considers a setting with two sources of labels: a strong labeler that serves as the reference oracle, and a weaker labeler that is cheaper but sometimes wrong. The practical question is whether the cheaper source can reduce reliance on the expensive one.

The authors propose an active learning algorithm that uses both labelers while targeting low error relative to the strong labeler. Their medical-image example makes the distinction concrete: a physician supplies expensive reference labels, while a resident supplies less expensive, potentially incorrect labels. The objective is to save strong-labeler queries without losing the connection to that reference standard.

The paper establishes statistical consistency and analyzes label complexity, meaning how many labeling requests the algorithm needs. That analysis characterizes when the weak labeler can provide savings compared with using the strong labeler alone. The result is therefore conditional: access to a cheaper labeler creates an opportunity for savings, whose availability the theory seeks to explain.
summary.tldr: An active learning algorithm combines strong and weak labelers, with consistency guarantees and an analysis of when weaker labels save expensive queries.

title: Active Learning from Weak and Strong Labelers

abstract: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) is a very popular model for topic modeling as well as many other problems with latent groups. It is both simple and effective. When the number of topics (or latent groups) is unknown, the Hierarchical Dirichlet Process (HDP) provides an elegant non-parametric extension; however, it is a complex model and it is difficult to incorporate prior knowledge since the distribution over topics is implicit. We propose two new models that extend LDA in a simple and intuitive fashion by directly expressing a distribution over the number of topics. We also propose a new online Bayesian moment matching technique to learn the parameters and the number of topics of those models based on streaming data. The approach achieves higher log-likelihood than batch and online HDP with fixed hyperparameters on several corpora.

We propose two new models that extend LDA in a simple and intuitive fashion by directly expressing a distribution over the number of topics. We also propose a new online Bayesian moment matching technique to learn the parameters and the number of topics of those models based on streaming data. The approach achieves higher log-likelihood than batch and online HDP with fixed hyperparameters on several corpora.

paragraphs: Latent Dirichlet Allocation is a useful model for topics and other hidden groups, but choosing the number of groups can be difficult. Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes address an unknown topic count through a nonparametric extension. This paper seeks a simpler alternative that makes the distribution over the number of topics explicit.

The authors introduce two extensions of LDA that directly represent uncertainty about topic count. That choice addresses a difficulty they identify in HDP: its implicit distribution over topics makes prior knowledge difficult to incorporate. They also develop online Bayesian moment matching to learn both model parameters and the number of topics as data arrives in a stream.

Across several corpora, the approach achieves higher log-likelihood than the compared batch and online HDP methods with fixed hyperparameters. This is a comparison under that stated configuration. The contribution combines an explicit treatment of topic-count uncertainty with streaming inference, offering a more direct modeling formulation and reported gains in how well the learned models explain the data.
summary.tldr: Two LDA extensions explicitly model topic-count uncertainty and use online Bayesian moment matching to learn from streaming data.

title: Online Bayesian Moment Matching for Topic Modeling with Unknown Number of Topics

abstract: We develop a general duality between neural networks and compositional kernel Hilbert spaces. We introduce the notion of a computation skeleton, an acyclic graph that succinctly describes both a family of neural networks and a kernel space. Random neural networks are generated from a skeleton through node replication followed by sampling from a normal distribution to assign weights. The kernel space consists of functions that arise by compositions, averaging, and non-linear transformations governed by the skeleton's graph topology and activation functions. We prove that random networks induce representations which approximate the kernel space. In particular, it follows that random weight initialization often yields a favorable starting point for optimization despite the worst-case intractability of training neural networks.

The kernel space consists of functions that arise by compositions, averaging, and non-linear transformations governed by the skeleton's graph topology and activation functions. We prove that random networks induce representations which approximate the kernel space. In particular, it follows that random weight initialization often yields a favorable starting point for optimization despite the worst-case intractability of training neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper connects neural networks with compositional kernel Hilbert spaces, providing two mathematical views of related function families. The organizing device is a computation skeleton: an acyclic graph that describes both a family of networks and a corresponding kernel space. This shared structure makes the relationship between architecture and representational capacity explicit.

To construct a random network, the authors replicate nodes in the skeleton and assign weights sampled from a normal distribution. The associated kernel space is built through composition, averaging, and nonlinear transformations determined by the same graph and activation functions. The authors prove that representations induced by random networks approximate that kernel space.

The result gives a theoretical reason that random initialization can often provide a favorable starting point for optimization. Useful representational structure can already be present before training changes the weights. This does not remove the stated worst-case intractability of neural network training; it explains how favorable starting representations can coexist with that general difficulty through the connection to kernel spaces.
summary.tldr: A duality with compositional kernel spaces explains why random neural network initialization can often produce useful starting representations.

title: Toward Deeper Understanding of Neural Networks: The Power of Initialization and a Dual View on Expressivity

abstract: The move from hand-designed features to learned features in machine learning has been wildly successful. In spite of this, optimization algorithms are still designed by hand. In this paper we show how the design of an optimization algorithm can be cast as a learning problem, allowing the algorithm to learn to exploit structure in the problems of interest in an automatic way. Our learned algorithms, implemented by LSTMs, outperform generic, hand-designed competitors on the tasks for which they are trained, and also generalize well to new tasks with similar structure. We demonstrate this on a number of tasks, including simple convex problems, training neural networks, and styling images with neural art.
originalAbstract: The move from hand-designed features to learned features in machine learning has been wildly successful. In spite of this, optimization algorithms are still designed by hand. In this paper we show how the design of an optimization algorithm can be cast as a learning problem, allowing the algorithm to learn to exploit structure in the problems of interest in an automatic way. Our learned algorithms, implemented by LSTMs, outperform generic, hand-designed competitors on the tasks for which they are trained, and also generalize well to new tasks with similar structure. We demonstrate this on a number of tasks, including simple convex problems, training neural networks, and styling images with neural art.

paragraphs: Machine learning routinely learns useful features from data, yet the optimization procedures used to train models are often designed by hand. This paper treats the optimizer itself as something that can be learned. The objective is to discover an optimization strategy that takes advantage of recurring structure in the problems it encounters.

The learned optimization algorithms are implemented using long short-term memory networks, or LSTMs. This makes optimizer design a learning problem: training shapes the procedure used to solve other optimization tasks. The approach therefore introduces a second level of learning, where experience with problems influences how future problems are optimized.

The authors demonstrate the idea on simple convex problems, neural-network training, and image styling through neural art. Their learned optimizers outperform generic hand-designed competitors on the tasks for which they were trained and generalize well to new tasks with similar structure. That qualification defines the scope of the result: the evidence supports specialization and transfer among related problems, rather than an optimizer established to be best for every possible task.
summary.tldr: LSTM-based learned optimizers outperform generic hand-designed methods on their training tasks and transfer well to structurally similar tasks.

title: Learning to learn by gradient descent by gradient descent

abstract: We study the online learning problem of a bidder who participates in repeated auctions. With the goal of maximizing his T-period payoff, the bidder determines the optimal allocation of his budget among his bids for $K$ goods at each period. As a bidding strategy, we propose a polynomial-time algorithm, inspired by the dynamic programming approach to the knapsack problem. The proposed algorithm, referred to as dynamic programming on discrete set (DPDS), achieves a regret order of $O(\sqrt{T\log{T}})$. By showing that the regret is lower bounded by $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ for any strategy, we conclude that DPDS is order optimal up to a $\sqrt{\log{T}}$ term. We evaluate the performance of DPDS empirically in the context of virtual trading in wholesale electricity markets by using historical data from the New York market. Empirical results show that DPDS consistently outperforms benchmark heuristic methods that are derived from machine learning and online learning approaches.

With the goal of maximizing his T-period payoff, the bidder determines the optimal allocation of his budget among his bids for $K$ goods at each period. As a bidding strategy, we propose a polynomial-time algorithm, inspired by the dynamic programming approach to the knapsack problem. The proposed algorithm, referred to as dynamic programming on discrete set (DPDS), achieves a regret order of $O(\sqrt{T\log{T}})$. By showing that the regret is lower bounded by $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ for any strategy, we conclude that DPDS is order optimal up to a $\sqrt{\log{T}}$ term. We evaluate the performance of DPDS empirically in the context of virtual trading in wholesale electricity markets by using historical data from the New York market. Empirical results show that DPDS consistently outperforms benchmark heuristic methods that are derived from machine learning and online learning approaches.

paragraphs: This paper studies a bidder who repeatedly allocates a budget among bids for multiple goods. The aim is to maximize total payoff over T periods, so each allocation is part of an ongoing learning problem. The authors seek a strategy that is computationally practical and has a provable bound on the payoff lost through learning.

Their algorithm, dynamic programming on discrete set, or DPDS, draws inspiration from dynamic programming for the knapsack problem. It runs in polynomial time and achieves regret of order O(sqrt(T log T)). The authors also prove an Omega(sqrt(T)) regret lower bound for any strategy. Together, these results place DPDS within a factor of sqrt(log T) of the optimal regret order.

The empirical evaluation uses historical New York wholesale electricity market data for virtual trading. DPDS consistently outperforms the benchmark heuristics derived from machine learning and online learning approaches. Thus, the paper combines a near-order-optimal theoretical result with evidence of effective bidding in the evaluated market setting, while retaining the logarithmic gap in its regret guarantee.
summary.tldr: DPDS learns budget allocations for repeated auctions in polynomial time with regret within a square-root-logarithmic factor of the optimal order.

title: Online Learning of Optimal Bidding Strategy in Repeated Multi-Commodity Auctions

abstract: Policy gradient methods are among the best Reinforcement Learning (RL) techniques to solve complex control problems. In real-world RL applications, it is common to have a good initial policy whose performance needs to be improved and it may not be acceptable to try bad policies during the learning process. Although several methods for choosing the step size exist, research paid less attention to determine the batch size, that is the number of samples used to estimate the gradient direction for each update of the policy parameters. In this paper, we propose a set of methods to jointly optimize the step and the batch sizes that guarantee (with high probability) to improve the policy performance after each update. Besides providing theoretical guarantees, we show numerical simulations to analyse the behaviour of our methods.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods improve a control policy using an estimated direction of improvement. In some applications, learning begins with a policy that already works well, and trying a worse policy may be unacceptable. This paper studies how to choose updates with that concern in mind, focusing on both the amount of data collected and the size of the policy change.

The batch size determines how many samples are used to estimate the gradient direction. The step size determines how far the policy parameters move along that direction. The authors propose methods that optimize these two choices jointly, addressing a decision that receives less attention when the focus is only on selecting a step size.

The methods provide high-probability guarantees of improved policy performance after each update. That qualification matters: the stated safety property is probabilistic, rather than an unconditional promise about every update. Numerical simulations examine the methods' behavior, complementing the theory and illustrating the role of jointly selecting sampling effort and update size.
summary.tldr: Jointly choosing batch size and step size gives policy gradient updates with high-probability guarantees of performance improvement.

title: Adaptive Batch Size for Safe Policy Gradients

abstract: Most large-scale network models use neurons with static nonlinearities that produce analog output, despite the fact that information processing in the brain is predominantly carried out by dynamic neurons that produce discrete pulses called spikes. Research in spike-based computation has been impeded by the lack of efficient supervised learning algorithm for spiking neural networks. Here, we present a gradient descent method for optimizing spiking network models by introducing a differentiable formulation of spiking dynamics and deriving the exact gradient calculation. For demonstration, we trained recurrent spiking networks on two dynamic tasks: one that requires optimizing fast (~ millisecond) spike-based interactions for efficient encoding of information, and a delayed-memory task over extended duration (~ second). The results show that the gradient descent approach indeed optimizes networks dynamics on the time scale of individual spikes as well as on behavioral time scales. In conclusion, our method yields a general purpose supervised learning algorithm for spiking neural networks, which can facilitate further investigations on spike-based computations.

This differs from the analog outputs of the static nonlinearities used in many large neural network models. The paper addresses a training obstacle for spike-based computation: the lack of an efficient supervised learning procedure for optimizing these dynamic networks.

The authors introduce a differentiable formulation of spiking dynamics and derive an exact gradient calculation for that formulation. This makes gradient descent available for adjusting the network’s behavior over time. The methodological contribution is a way to connect supervised optimization directly to the dynamics responsible for producing and coordinating spikes.

Two recurrent-network demonstrations examine different timescales. One requires fast interactions around the millisecond scale for information encoding; the other requires retaining information over roughly a second. The results show successful optimization at both individual-spike and behavioral timescales. These demonstrations support the method as a general-purpose supervised learning approach and a tool for further investigation of spike-based computation.
summary.tldr: A differentiable formulation of spiking dynamics enables exact gradient calculation and supervised training across fast spike interactions and longer memory tasks.

title: Gradient Descent for Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) remains the method of choice for deep learning, despite the limitations arising for ill-behaved objective functions. In cases where it could be estimated, the natural gradient has proven very effective at mitigating the catastrophic effects of pathological curvature in the objective function, but little is known theoretically about its convergence properties, and it has yet to find a practical implementation that would scale to very deep and large networks. Here, we derive an exact expression for the natural gradient in deep linear networks, which exhibit pathological curvature similar to the nonlinear case. We provide for the first time an analytical solution for its convergence rate, showing that the loss decreases exponentially to the global minimum in parameter space. Our expression for the natural gradient is surprisingly simple, computationally tractable, and explains why some approximations proposed previously work well in practice. This opens new avenues for approximating the natural gradient in the nonlinear case, and we show in preliminary experiments that our online natural gradient descent outperforms SGD on MNIST autoencoding while sharing its computational simplicity.

paragraphs: The paper investigates natural-gradient optimization as a way to address difficult curvature in neural-network training objectives. Such curvature can make ordinary stochastic gradient descent struggle. Natural gradients have shown promise where they can be estimated, but their convergence behavior and practical use in very large, deep networks have remained difficult to establish.

The authors derive an exact natural-gradient expression for deep linear networks, which retain pathological curvature resembling that of nonlinear networks. They obtain an analytical convergence rate showing exponential loss reduction toward the global minimum in parameter space. The expression is computationally tractable and also helps explain why some previously proposed approximations perform well in practice.

The linear-network result supplies a basis for developing natural-gradient approximations for nonlinear models. The authors explore this direction with an online natural-gradient method and report preliminary MNIST autoencoding experiments in which it outperforms SGD while retaining computational simplicity. The theoretical guarantee concerns the linear setting; the nonlinear application is supported here by preliminary experimental evidence.
summary.tldr: An exact natural gradient for deep linear networks yields exponential convergence and motivates a promising preliminary optimizer for nonlinear networks.

title: Exact natural gradient in deep linear networks and its application to the nonlinear case

abstract: Recent methods for learning a linear subspace from data corrupted by outliers are based on convex L1 and nuclear norm optimization and require the dimension of the subspace and the number of outliers to be sufficiently small [27]. In sharp contrast, the recently proposed Dual Principal Component Pursuit (DPCP) method [22] can provably handle subspaces of high dimension by solving a non-convex L1 optimization problem on the sphere. However, its geometric analysis is based on quantities that are difficult to interpret and are not amenable to statistical analysis. In this paper we provide a refined geometric analysis and a new statistical analysis that show that DPCP can tolerate as many outliers as the square of the number of inliers, thus improving upon other provably correct robust PCA methods. We also propose a scalable Projected Sub-Gradient Descent method (DPCP-PSGD) for solving the DPCP problem and show it admits linear convergence even though the underlying optimization problem is non-convex and non-smooth. Experiments on road plane detection from 3D point cloud data demonstrate that DPCP-PSGD can be more efficient than the traditional RANSAC algorithm, which is one of the most popular methods for such computer vision applications.

paragraphs: Learning a linear subspace becomes difficult when many observations are outliers. Dual Principal Component Pursuit, or DPCP, addresses this through a nonconvex optimization problem on a sphere and can handle high-dimensional subspaces. However, its earlier geometric guarantees involved quantities that were difficult to interpret or connect to statistical analysis.

This paper refines that geometric analysis and adds a statistical treatment. The results show that DPCP can tolerate an outlier count scaling as the square of the inlier count within the analyzed setting. This improves the stated guarantees over other provably correct robust principal-component methods and gives a clearer account of DPCP’s ability to operate amid substantial contamination.

The authors also introduce DPCP-PSGD, a scalable projected subgradient algorithm for solving the problem. They establish linear convergence despite the objective being both nonconvex and nonsmooth. Experiments detecting road planes in three-dimensional point clouds show that the method can be more efficient than RANSAC. The paper thus advances both the explanation of DPCP’s robustness and its practical optimization.
summary.tldr: Sharper analysis strengthens DPCP’s outlier-tolerance guarantees, while a projected subgradient solver offers linear convergence and promising practical efficiency.

title: Dual Principal Component Pursuit: Improved Analysis and Efficient Algorithms

abstract: Both resources in the natural environment and concepts in a semantic space are distributed "patchily", with large gaps in between the patches. To describe people's internal and external foraging behavior, various random walk models have been proposed. In particular, internal foraging has been modeled as sampling: in order to gather relevant information for making a decision, people draw samples from a mental representation using random-walk algorithms such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). However, two common empirical observations argue against people using simple sampling algorithms such as MCMC for internal foraging. First, the distance between samples is often best described by a Levy flight distribution: the probability of the distance between two successive locations follows a power-law on the distances. Second, humans and other animals produce long-range, slowly decaying autocorrelations characterized as 1/f-like fluctuations, instead of the 1/f^2 fluctuations produced by random walks. We propose that mental sampling is not done by simple MCMC, but is instead adapted to multimodal representations and is implemented by Metropolis-coupled Markov chain Monte Carlo (MC3), one of the first algorithms developed for sampling from multimodal distributions. MC3 involves running multiple Markov chains in parallel but with target distributions of different temperatures, and it swaps the states of the chains whenever a better location is found. Heated chains more readily traverse valleys in the probability landscape to propose moves to far-away peaks, while the colder chains make the local steps that explore the current peak or patch. We show that MC3 generates distances between successive samples that follow a Levy flight distribution and produce 1/f-like autocorrelations, providing a single mechanistic account of these two puzzling empirical phenomena of internal foraging.

paragraphs: The paper examines mental information gathering as sampling from a representation with separated clusters of concepts. Simple random-walk sampling has difficulty explaining two observed patterns: movement distances that follow a Lévy-flight distribution and slowly decaying, 1/f-like correlations over time. The authors seek one mechanism that can account for both patterns.

Their proposal uses Metropolis-coupled Markov chain Monte Carlo, or MC3, which runs multiple chains at different temperatures and exchanges their states. Heated chains move more readily between distant high-probability regions, while colder chains explore the current region locally. This combination fits the idea of a patchy mental representation containing multiple separated peaks.

The authors show that MC3 generates both Lévy-flight-like distances between consecutive samples and 1/f-like autocorrelations. This makes it a unified mechanistic account of the two phenomena that challenge simpler sampling models. The finding supports the proposed explanation through the patterns the algorithm produces; the abstract presents MC3 as a model of mental sampling rather than establishing that people literally implement this algorithm.
summary.tldr: A coupled sampling model reproduces both long jumps and persistent temporal correlations observed in mental information gathering.

title: Mental Sampling in Multimodal Representations

abstract: Zero-shot learning extends the conventional object classification to the unseen class recognition by introducing semantic representations of classes. Existing approaches predominantly focus on learning the proper mapping function for visual-semantic embedding, while neglecting the effect of learning discriminative visual features. In this paper, we study the significance of the discriminative region localization. We propose a semantic-guided multi-attention localization model, which automatically discovers the most discriminative parts of objects for zero-shot learning without any human annotations. Our model jointly learns cooperative global and local features from the whole object as well as the detected parts to categorize objects based on semantic descriptions. Moreover, with the joint supervision of embedding softmax loss and class-center triplet loss, the model is encouraged to learn features with high inter-class dispersion and intra-class compactness. Through comprehensive experiments on three widely used zero-shot learning benchmarks, we show the efficacy of the multi-attention localization and our proposed approach improves the state-of-the-art results by a considerable margin.

paragraphs: Zero-shot learning recognizes previously unseen classes through semantic descriptions. This paper argues that the visual features used for that recognition deserve attention alongside the mapping between visual and semantic representations. It focuses on finding object regions that distinguish classes, so the model can use informative details as well as the overall object.

The proposed semantic-guided multi-attention model automatically discovers discriminative object parts without human annotations for that localization. It jointly learns global features from the whole object and local features from the detected parts. Semantic descriptions guide categorization, while embedding softmax and class-center triplet losses encourage different classes to spread apart and examples within a class to cluster together.

Experiments on three widely used zero-shot learning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the localization component and report a considerable improvement over state-of-the-art results. The findings support combining semantic guidance with learned part discovery. The contribution connects where a model looks with how it organizes class representations, making visual feature learning an explicit part of recognizing unseen categories.
summary.tldr: Semantic-guided attention discovers informative object parts and combines local and global features to improve zero-shot recognition.

title: Semantic-Guided Multi-Attention Localization for Zero-Shot Learning

abstract: Modeling real-world multidimensional time series can be particularly challenging when these are sporadically observed (i.e., sampling is irregular both in time and across dimensions)—such as in the case of clinical patient data. To address these challenges, we propose (1) a continuous-time version of the Gated Recurrent Unit, building upon the recent Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Chen et al., 2018), and (2) a Bayesian update network that processes the sporadic observations. We bring these two ideas together in our GRU-ODE-Bayes method. We then demonstrate that the proposed method encodes a continuity prior for the latent process and that it can exactly represent the Fokker-Planck dynamics of complex processes driven by a multidimensional stochastic differential equation. Additionally, empirical evaluation shows that our method outperforms the state of the art on both synthetic data and real-world data with applications in healthcare and climate forecast. What is more, the continuity prior is shown to be well suited for low number of samples settings.
