paragraphs: Many multidimensional time series are incomplete in two ways: observations arrive at irregular times, and different variables are measured on different occasions. Clinical patient records are one motivating example. GRU-ODE-Bayes addresses this pattern by combining continuous evolution of a hidden state with updates that incorporate measurements whenever they become available.

The method joins a continuous-time version of the Gated Recurrent Unit with a Bayesian update network for sporadic observations. Its continuous dynamics encode a continuity prior for the latent process. The authors also show that the model can exactly represent Fokker-Planck dynamics for complex processes driven by a multidimensional stochastic differential equation, connecting the architecture to the evolution of probability distributions.

Empirical evaluations report improvements over the state of the art on synthetic and real-world data, including healthcare and climate forecasting applications. The continuity prior is also shown to be useful when few samples are available. The findings connect the model's explicit treatment of time and incoming observations with strong performance in the evaluated irregular-data settings.
summary.tldr: GRU-ODE-Bayes combines continuous hidden dynamics with Bayesian observation updates to model irregularly measured multidimensional time series.

title: GRU-ODE-Bayes: Continuous Modeling of Sporadically-Observed Time Series

abstract: This paper studies statistical characteristics of multivariate observations with irregular changes in their covariance structures across input space. We propose a unified nonstationary modeling framework to jointly encode the observation correlations to generate a piece-wise representation with a hyper-level Gaussian process (GP) governing the overall contour of the pieces. In particular, we couple the encoding process with automatic relevance determination (ARD) to promote sparsity to account for the inherent redundancy. The hyper GP enables us to share statistical strength among the observation variables over a collection of GPs defined within the observation pieces to characterize the variables' respective local smoothness. Experiments conducted across domains show superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: This paper models observations with several variables whose covariance structure changes irregularly across the input space. The challenge is to represent how variables relate to one another when those relationships do not remain constant. The proposed framework jointly encodes these correlations while allowing different parts of the input space to exhibit different statistical behavior.

The model builds a piecewise representation governed by a higher-level Gaussian process. Within the pieces, a collection of Gaussian processes describes the local smoothness of individual observation variables. The higher-level process coordinates their overall structure and allows information to be shared across variables. This combines locally varying behavior with a common statistical organization.

Automatic relevance determination is coupled to the encoding process to encourage sparsity and account for redundancy. That component helps the representation emphasize relevant structure while the Gaussian-process hierarchy connects the pieces. Experiments across multiple domains report better performance than state-of-the-art methods. The stated contribution is a unified way to handle changing correlations, local smoothness, shared information, and redundant structure within one model.
summary.tldr: A sparse hierarchical Gaussian-process framework models irregularly changing correlations while sharing information across observation variables.

title: Multivariate Sparse Coding of Nonstationary Covariances with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Machine Learning (ML) models trained on data from multiple demographic groups can inherit representation disparity (Hashimoto et al., 2018) that may exist in the data: the model may be less favorable to groups contributing less to the training process; this in turn can degrade population retention in these groups over time, and exacerbate representation disparity in the long run. In this study, we seek to understand the interplay between ML decisions and the underlying group representation, how they evolve in a sequential framework, and how the use of fairness criteria plays a role in this process. We show that the representation disparity can easily worsen over time under a natural user dynamics (arrival and departure) model when decisions are made based on a commonly used objective and fairness criteria, resulting in some groups diminishing entirely from the sample pool in the long run. It highlights the fact that fairness criteria have to be defined while taking into consideration the impact of decisions on user dynamics. Toward this end, we explain how a proper fairness criterion can be selected based on a general user dynamics model.

paragraphs: A demographic group that contributes less training data may receive less favorable model decisions. Those decisions can then influence whether its members remain in the population supplying future data. This paper studies that feedback process, asking how repeated machine-learning decisions, group representation, and fairness criteria interact as users arrive and leave.

Under a natural model of user dynamics, the authors show that representation disparity can worsen over time even when decisions use a commonly employed objective and fairness criteria. Some groups can eventually disappear from the sample pool. This is a result about the modeled sequential process: evaluating fairness at individual decision stages may fail to account for how those decisions change future participation.

The paper also explains how an appropriate fairness criterion can be selected using a general model of user dynamics. Its contribution is to connect fairness requirements to retention behavior, rather than treating the composition of the training population as fixed. The findings make the consequences for future group representation part of the fairness question itself.
summary.tldr: Sequential decision models show that fairness criteria can coexist with worsening group retention unless user dynamics inform their design.

title: Group Retention when Using Machine Learning in Sequential Decision Making: the Interplay between User Dynamics and Fairness

abstract: Program synthesis of general-purpose source code from natural language specifications is challenging due to the need to reason about high-level patterns in the target program and low-level implementation details at the same time. In this work, we present Patois, a system that allows a neural program synthesizer to explicitly interleave high-level and low-level reasoning at every generation step. It accomplishes this by automatically mining common code idioms from a given corpus, incorporating them into the underlying language for neural synthesis, and training a tree-based neural synthesizer to use these idioms during code generation. We evaluate Patois on two complex semantic parsing datasets and show that using learned code idioms improves the synthesizer's accuracy.

paragraphs: Generating source code from natural-language specifications requires decisions at different levels. A system must capture the program’s overall patterns while also supplying implementation details. Patois addresses this combination by allowing a neural program synthesizer to interleave high-level and low-level reasoning throughout generation.

The system automatically extracts recurring code idioms from a supplied corpus. It adds those idioms to the language available to the synthesizer, then trains a tree-based neural model to use them when producing programs. Common patterns become explicit generation options, alongside the choices needed to express lower-level details. The idioms are learned from code rather than supplied solely as manually defined patterns.

The authors evaluate Patois on two complex semantic parsing datasets and find that learned idioms improve synthesis accuracy. This supports making recurring program structure available directly to the generator. The contribution is the combination of corpus-based idiom discovery and a synthesizer trained to mix those higher-level constructs with detailed program generation.
summary.tldr: Patois learns recurring code idioms and lets a neural synthesizer combine them with low-level generation, improving accuracy on two datasets.

title: Program Synthesis and Semantic Parsing with Learned Code Idioms

abstract: For multi-valued functions---such as when the conditional distribution on targets given the inputs is multi-modal---standard regression approaches are not always desirable because they provide the conditional mean. Modal regression algorithms address this issue by instead finding the conditional mode(s). Most, however, are nonparametric approaches and so can be difficult to scale. Further, parametric approximators, like neural networks, facilitate learning complex relationships between inputs and targets. In this work, we propose a parametric modal regression algorithm. We use the implicit function theorem to develop an objective, for learning a joint function over inputs and targets. We empirically demonstrate on several synthetic problems that our method (i) can learn multi-valued functions and produce the conditional modes, (ii) scales well to high-dimensional inputs, and (iii) can even be more effective for certain uni-modal problems, particularly for high-frequency functions. We demonstrate that our method is competitive in a real-world modal regression problem and two regular regression datasets.

paragraphs: A prediction problem can have several plausible outputs for the same input. In that situation, predicting the conditional average can obscure the distinct outcomes that the data actually favors. Modal regression instead seeks the peaks of the conditional output distribution. The paper develops a parametric approach to this problem, motivated by the scaling difficulties of many existing nonparametric methods.

The method learns a joint function of inputs and candidate outputs. Its training objective is developed using the implicit function theorem, allowing the model to represent relationships with multiple output values. This formulation also makes it possible to use parametric approximators such as neural networks to capture complex relationships between the inputs and targets.

On synthetic problems, the authors show that the approach can recover conditional modes, learn multivalued functions, and handle high-dimensional inputs effectively. It can also outperform alternatives on certain single-mode problems, particularly those involving high-frequency functions. Results on a real-world modal regression task and two ordinary regression datasets are competitive, suggesting that the formulation has uses beyond explicitly multimodal prediction.
summary.tldr: An implicit-function-based regression objective learns conditional modes, enabling parametric models to represent multiple plausible outputs for one input.

title: An implicit function learning approach for parametric modal regression

abstract: The k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) classifier is a fundamental non-parametric machine learning algorithm. However, it is well known that it suffers from the curse of dimensionality, which is why in practice one often applies a kNN classifier on top of a (pre-trained) feature transformation. From a theoretical perspective, most, if not all theoretical results aimed at understanding the kNN classifier are derived for the raw feature space. This leads to an emerging gap between our theoretical understanding of kNN and its practical applications. In this paper, we take a first step towards bridging this gap. We provide a novel analysis on the convergence rates of a kNN classifier over transformed features. This analysis requires in-depth understanding of the properties that connect both the transformed space and the raw feature space. More precisely, we build our convergence bound upon two key properties of the transformed space: (1) safety -- how well can one recover the raw posterior from the transformed space, and (2) smoothness -- how complex this recovery function is. Based on our result, we are able to explain why some (pre-trained) feature transformations are better suited for a kNN classifier than other. We empirically validate that both properties have an impact on the kNN convergence on 30 feature transformations with 6 benchmark datasets spanning from the vision to the text domain.
originalAbstract: The k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) classifier is a fundamental non-parametric machine learning algorithm. However, it is well known that it suffers from the curse of dimensionality, which is why in practice one often applies a kNN classifier on top of a (pre-trained) feature transformation. From a theoretical perspective, most, if not all theoretical results aimed at understanding the kNN classifier are derived for the raw feature space. This leads to an emerging gap between our theoretical understanding of kNN and its practical applications. In this paper, we take a first step towards bridging this gap. We provide a novel analysis on the convergence rates of a kNN classifier over transformed features. This analysis requires in-depth understanding of the properties that connect both the transformed space and the raw feature space. More precisely, we build our convergence bound upon two key properties of the transformed space: (1) safety -- how well can one recover the raw posterior from the transformed space, and (2) smoothness -- how complex this recovery function is. Based on our result, we are able to explain why some (pre-trained) feature transformations are better suited for a kNN classifier than other. We empirically validate that both properties have an impact on the kNN convergence on 30 feature transformations with 6 benchmark datasets spanning from the vision to the text domain.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification often works on transformed features because applying it directly to high-dimensional inputs is difficult. However, much of its theoretical analysis concerns the original feature space. This paper analyzes convergence after a feature transformation, bringing the theory closer to the common practice of placing a nearest-neighbor classifier on top of a pretrained representation.

The convergence bound depends on two properties linking the transformed and original spaces. Safety measures how well the original class posterior can be recovered from the transformed representation. Smoothness measures the complexity of that recovery function. Together, these distinguish whether useful class information remains available and how difficult it is to recover that information.

This analysis provides an explanation for why some transformations are better suited to nearest-neighbor classification than others. A useful representation must be assessed through its relationship to the classification problem, including both retained information and recovery complexity. Experiments with 30 feature transformations across six vision and text datasets validate that both properties affect convergence, supporting the relevance of the theoretical distinction.
summary.tldr: A convergence analysis explains transformed-feature kNN through information preservation and the smoothness of recovering class probabilities.

title: On Convergence of Nearest Neighbor Classifiers over Feature Transformations

abstract: This paper proposes a human parsing based texture transfer model via cross-view consistency learning to generate the texture of 3D human body from a single image. We use the semantic parsing of human body as input for providing both the shape and pose information to reduce the appearance variation of human image and preserve the spatial distribution of semantic parts. Meanwhile, in order to improve the prediction for textures of invisible parts, we explicitly enforce the consistency across different views of the same subject by exchanging the textures predicted by two views to render images during training. The perceptual loss and total variation regularization are optimized to maximize the similarity between rendered and input images, which does not necessitate extra 3D texture supervision. Experimental results on pedestrian images and fashion photos demonstrate that our method can produce higher quality textures with convincing details than other texture generation methods.

paragraphs: Generating a textured 3D person from one image requires handling both visible appearance and body regions hidden from view. This paper proposes a texture transfer model that uses semantic human parsing: a representation identifying the person’s body parts. That input supplies shape and pose information while preserving where the semantic parts lie.

The model learns to improve predictions for unseen regions through consistency across views of the same person. During training, textures predicted from two views are exchanged and used to render images. This makes the relationship between views part of the learning signal. Perceptual loss and total variation regularization guide the rendered images toward the inputs without requiring additional 3D texture supervision.

Experiments use pedestrian images and fashion photographs. The authors report higher-quality textures with convincing details compared with other texture generation methods. The approach matters because it combines a structured description of the body with a training signal that connects viewpoints. Although prediction uses one image, training across views helps address appearance that the single input cannot directly show.
summary.tldr: Body-part parsing and cross-view training help generate detailed 3D human textures from one image without additional 3D texture supervision.

title: Human Parsing Based Texture Transfer from Single Image to 3D Human via Cross-View Consistency

abstract: While Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has emerged as a promising approach to many complex tasks, it remains challenging to train a single DRL agent that is capable of undertaking multiple different continuous control tasks. In this paper, we present a Knowledge Transfer based Multi-task Deep Reinforcement Learning framework (KTM-DRL) for continuous control, which enables a single DRL agent to achieve expert-level performance in multiple different tasks by learning from task-specific teachers. In KTM-DRL, the multi-task agent first leverages an offline knowledge transfer algorithm designed particularly for the actor-critic architecture to quickly learn a control policy from the experience of task-specific teachers, and then it employs an online learning algorithm to further improve itself by learning from new online transition samples under the guidance of those teachers. We perform a comprehensive empirical study with two commonly-used benchmarks in the MuJoCo continuous control task suite. The experimental results well justify the effectiveness of KTM-DRL and its knowledge transfer and online learning algorithms, as well as its superiority over the state-of-the-art by a large margin.

paragraphs: Training one reinforcement-learning agent to handle several continuous-control tasks is difficult even when specialized agents can solve the tasks individually. This paper introduces KTM-DRL, a framework that transfers knowledge from task-specific teachers into one multitask agent. Its objective is to combine expert-level abilities across different tasks within a single learner.

Learning proceeds in two stages. An offline transfer algorithm first uses the teachers’ experience to quickly establish a control policy. That algorithm is designed specifically for an actor-critic architecture. The agent then continues learning online from newly collected transitions, with the teachers still providing guidance. This second stage lets it improve through fresh interaction after the initial transfer.

The authors evaluate the framework on two commonly used benchmarks from the MuJoCo continuous-control suite. They report evidence supporting both the knowledge-transfer and online-learning components, together with a large performance advantage over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The findings support teacher-guided transfer as an effective way to build a capable multitask controller in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: KTM-DRL combines offline teacher transfer with guided online learning to train one agent for multiple continuous-control tasks.

title: Knowledge Transfer in Multi-Task Deep Reinforcement Learning for Continuous Control

abstract: As power management has become a primary concern in modern data centers, computing resources are being scaled dynamically to minimize energy consumption. We initiate the study of a variant of the classic online speed scaling problem, in which machine learning predictions about the future can be integrated naturally. Inspired by recent work on learning-augmented online algorithms, we propose an algorithm which incorporates predictions in a black-box manner and outperforms any online algorithm if the accuracy is high, yet maintains provable guarantees if the prediction is very inaccurate. We provide both theoretical and experimental evidence to support our claims.

paragraphs: Dynamic speed scaling adjusts computing resources to reduce energy use as work arrives. The difficulty is that an online decision must be made before the future is fully known. This paper studies a version of the classic problem in which machine-learning predictions about the future can inform those decisions.

The proposed algorithm accepts predictions through a black-box interface. Its design therefore incorporates predictive information without tying the scheduling method to the internal workings of a particular predictor. The central objective is to benefit from useful forecasts while retaining a mathematical performance guarantee when those forecasts are very inaccurate.

The authors establish that sufficiently accurate predictions allow their method to outperform any online algorithm in the comparison described by the abstract. They also prove guarantees for the inaccurate-prediction case and provide experimental evidence supporting their claims. The advantage is conditional on prediction quality, while the fallback guarantee addresses poor forecasts. Together, these results show how future-oriented learning can be integrated into an online energy-management algorithm without making its guarantees depend entirely on accurate predictions.
summary.tldr: A prediction-assisted speed-scaling algorithm saves energy with accurate forecasts while retaining provable guarantees when forecasts are poor.

title: Learning Augmented Energy Minimization via Speed Scaling

abstract: Transplant-organs are a scarce medical resource. The uniqueness of each organ and the patients' heterogeneous responses to the organs present a unique and challenging machine learning problem. In this problem there are two key challenges: (i) assigning each organ "optimally" to a patient in the queue; (ii) accurately estimating the potential outcomes associated with each patient and each possible organ. In this paper, we introduce OrganITE, an organ-to-patient assignment methodology that assigns organs based not only on its own estimates of the potential outcomes but also on organ scarcity. By modelling and accounting for organ scarcity we significantly increase total life years across the population, compared to the existing greedy approaches that simply optimise life years for the current organ available. Moreover, we propose an individualised treatment effect model capable of addressing the high dimensionality of the organ space. We test our method on real and simulated data, resulting in as much as an additional year of life expectancy as compared to existing organ-to-patient policies.

paragraphs: Allocating donor organs involves both predicting patient outcomes and deciding how to use a scarce resource. Each organ is different, and patients can respond differently to the same organ. A policy that chooses the best immediate match may therefore overlook how scarcity affects the total benefit available across the waiting population.

OrganITE combines estimates of potential patient-organ outcomes with an explicit model of organ scarcity. Its assignment decisions account for both, extending beyond greedy policies that optimize life years for the organ currently available. The authors also introduce an individualized treatment-effect model designed to handle the high-dimensional space of organ characteristics, addressing the prediction problem underlying those decisions.

Tests on real and simulated data show increased total population life years compared with the greedy approaches considered. The reported improvement reaches as much as an additional year of life expectancy relative to existing assignment policies. This is a result from the evaluated settings, not a promised benefit for every recipient. The paper’s central contribution is linking individualized outcome estimates to scarcity-aware allocation.
summary.tldr: OrganITE combines patient-specific outcome estimates with organ scarcity to improve population life-year outcomes in real and simulated evaluations.

title: OrganITE: Optimal transplant donor organ offering using an individual treatment effect

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the input and hidden variables of a stochastic multi-layer neural network from an observation of the output. The hidden variables in each layer are represented as matrices with statistical interactions along both rows as well as columns. This problem applies to matrix imputation, signal recovery via deep generative prior models, multi-task and mixed regression, and learning certain classes of two-layer neural networks. We extend a recently-developed algorithm -- Multi-Layer Vector Approximate Message Passing (ML-VAMP), for this matrix-valued inference problem. It is shown that the performance of the proposed Multi-Layer Matrix VAMP (ML-Mat-VAMP) algorithm can be exactly predicted in a certain random large-system limit, where the dimensions $N\times d$ of the unknown quantities grow as $N\rightarrow\infty$ with $d$ fixed. In the two-layer neural-network learning problem, this scaling corresponds to the case where the number of input features, as well as training samples, grow to infinity but the number of hidden nodes stays fixed. The analysis enables a precise prediction of the parameter and test error of the learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover the inputs and hidden variables of a stochastic multilayer neural network from its observed output. The unknown quantities are matrices, with statistical relationships along both rows and columns. That structure makes the problem relevant to matrix imputation, signal recovery with deep generative priors, mixed and multitask regression, and certain two-layer network-learning problems.

The authors extend Multi-Layer Vector Approximate Message Passing into a matrix-valued algorithm called ML-Mat-VAMP. The theoretical contribution is an exact prediction of its performance in a particular random large-system limit. For unknown matrices of size N by d, N grows without bound while d remains fixed, so the guarantee concerns a specific asymptotic regime.

For the two-layer learning application, that regime means that input features and training samples increase together while the number of hidden nodes stays fixed. Within this setting, the analysis precisely predicts parameter-estimation error and test error. The result links an inference procedure to a detailed account of its learning performance, with the fixed-width asymptotic scaling defining the scope of the prediction.
summary.tldr: ML-Mat-VAMP extends multilayer message passing to matrix-valued inference and admits exact performance predictions in a specified large-system limit.

title: Matrix Inference and Estimation in Multi-Layer Models

abstract: Existing analyses of optimization in deep learning are either continuous, focusing on (variants of) gradient flow, or discrete, directly treating (variants of) gradient descent. Gradient flow is amenable to theoretical analysis, but is stylized and disregards computational efficiency. The extent to which it represents gradient descent is an open question in the theory of deep learning. The current paper studies this question. Viewing gradient descent as an approximate numerical solution to the initial value problem of gradient flow, we find that the degree of approximation depends on the curvature around the gradient flow trajectory. We then show that over deep neural networks with homogeneous activations, gradient flow trajectories enjoy favorable curvature, suggesting they are well approximated by gradient descent. This finding allows us to translate an analysis of gradient flow over deep linear neural networks into a guarantee that gradient descent efficiently converges to global minimum almost surely under random initialization. Experiments suggest that over simple deep neural networks, gradient descent with conventional step size is indeed close to gradient flow. We hypothesize that the theory of gradient flows will unravel mysteries behind deep learning.

paragraphs: Gradient flow describes learning as continuous motion, while gradient descent updates parameters in discrete steps. Continuous dynamics are often easier to analyze, but practical training uses discrete computation. This paper asks when conclusions about gradient flow can meaningfully describe gradient descent, treating the latter as an approximate numerical solution of the former.

The authors find that approximation quality depends on curvature around the gradient-flow trajectory. They then show favorable curvature properties for deep networks with homogeneous activations. These properties suggest that gradient descent can closely approximate the continuous trajectory, giving a mathematical route for connecting the two kinds of optimization analysis.

For deep linear networks, the authors use this connection to turn a gradient-flow analysis into a guarantee of efficient gradient-descent convergence to a global minimum, almost surely under random initialization. Experiments on simple deep networks also suggest closeness with conventional step sizes. The broader promise of gradient-flow theory is presented as a hypothesis, beyond this specific convergence result.
summary.tldr: Curvature analysis connects gradient flow to gradient descent and yields an efficient convergence guarantee for deep linear networks.

title: Continuous vs. Discrete Optimization of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We study the gradient flow for a relaxed approximation to the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergencebetween a moving source and a fixed target distribution.This approximation, termed theKALE (KL approximate lower-bound estimator), solves a regularized version ofthe Fenchel dual problem defining the KL over a restricted class of functions.When using a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) to define the functionclass, we show that the KALE continuously interpolates between the KL and theMaximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). Like the MMD and other Integral ProbabilityMetrics, the KALE remains well defined for mutually singulardistributions. Nonetheless, the KALE inherits from the limiting KL a greater sensitivity to mismatch in the support of the distributions, compared with the MMD. These two properties make theKALE gradient flow particularly well suited when the target distribution is supported on a low-dimensional manifold. Under an assumption of sufficient smoothness of the trajectories, we show the global convergence of the KALE flow. We propose a particle implementation of the flow given initial samples from the source and the target distribution, which we use to empirically confirm the KALE's properties.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to move a source probability distribution toward a fixed target using a relaxed version of KL divergence. This relaxation, KALE, comes from a regularized dual formulation restricted to a chosen function class. With a reproducing kernel Hilbert space as that class, KALE continuously interpolates between KL divergence and maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD.

KALE combines two properties relevant to distributions with different supports. Like MMD, it remains well defined even for mutually singular distributions. At the same time, it retains greater sensitivity than MMD to mismatches in where the distributions place their mass. The authors argue that this combination makes its gradient flow particularly suitable for targets concentrated on low-dimensional manifolds.

The paper proves global convergence of the flow under an assumption that its trajectories are sufficiently smooth. It also develops a particle implementation using initial samples from both source and target distributions. Experiments with that implementation support the stated properties of KALE. The contribution connects a distribution discrepancy, a conditional convergence result, and a sample-based procedure for realizing the flow.
summary.tldr: KALE blends KL and MMD properties to define distribution flows across disjoint supports, with convergence under a smoothness assumption.

title: KALE Flow: A Relaxed KL Gradient Flow for Probabilities with Disjoint Support

abstract: Accurately backpropagating the gradient through categorical variables is a challenging task that arises in various domains, such as training discrete latent variable models. To this end, we propose CARMS, an unbiased estimator for categorical random variables based on multiple mutually negatively correlated (jointly antithetic) samples. CARMS combines REINFORCE with copula based sampling to avoid duplicate samples and reduce its variance, while keeping the estimator unbiased using importance sampling. It generalizes both the ARMS antithetic estimator for binary variables, which is CARMS for two categories, as well as LOORF/VarGrad, the leave-one-out REINFORCE estimator, which is CARMS with independent samples. We evaluate CARMS on several benchmark datasets on a generative modeling task, as well as a structured output prediction task, and find it to outperform competing methods including a strong self-control baseline. The code is publicly available.

To this end, we propose CARMS, an unbiased estimator for categorical random variables based on multiple mutually negatively correlated (jointly antithetic) samples. CARMS combines REINFORCE with copula based sampling to avoid duplicate samples and reduce its variance, while keeping the estimator unbiased using importance sampling. It generalizes both the ARMS antithetic estimator for binary variables, which is CARMS for two categories, as well as LOORF/VarGrad, the leave-one-out REINFORCE estimator, which is CARMS with independent samples. We evaluate CARMS on several benchmark datasets on a generative modeling task, as well as a structured output prediction task, and find it to outperform competing methods including a strong self-control baseline. The code is publicly available.

paragraphs: Learning through categorical random choices requires estimating how model parameters affect an objective despite the choices being discrete. Such gradient estimates can be noisy. CARMS addresses this problem by coordinating multiple samples so that they are negatively correlated, making repeated selections less common and reducing estimation variance.

The method combines REINFORCE with copula-based sampling to construct these jointly antithetic samples. Because changing the sampling relationships could otherwise distort the estimate, importance sampling keeps the gradient estimator unbiased. This means its expected value remains the intended gradient while its sampling variability can be reduced.

CARMS also connects existing estimators within one framework. With two categories it recovers the binary ARMS estimator, and with independent samples it recovers the leave-one-out REINFORCE estimator known as LOORF or VarGrad. Experiments on generative modeling and structured-output prediction find that CARMS outperforms competing methods, including a strong self-control baseline. The results support coordinated sampling as a useful way to improve discrete-variable learning without introducing gradient-estimation bias.
summary.tldr: CARMS uses negatively correlated categorical samples to reduce gradient-estimation variance while preserving unbiasedness.

title: CARMS: Categorical-Antithetic-REINFORCE Multi-Sample Gradient Estimator

abstract: Bilevel optimization has been widely applied in many important machine learning applications such as hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning. Recently, several momentum-based algorithms have been proposed to solve bilevel optimization problems faster. However, those momentum-based algorithms do not achieve provably better computational complexity than $\mathcal{\widetilde O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ of the SGD-based algorithm. In this paper, we propose two new algorithms for bilevel optimization, where the first algorithm adopts momentum-based recursive iterations, and the second algorithm adopts recursive gradient estimations in nested loops to decrease the variance. We show that both algorithms achieve the complexity of $\mathcal{\widetilde O}(\epsilon^{-1.5})$, which outperforms all existing algorithms by the order of magnitude. Our experiments validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the superior empirical performance of our algorithms in hyperparameter applications.

We show that both algorithms achieve the complexity of $\mathcal{\widetilde O}(\epsilon^{-1.5})$, which outperforms all existing algorithms by the order of magnitude. Our experiments validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the superior empirical performance of our algorithms in hyperparameter applications.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves one optimization problem whose outcome affects another, as in hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning. Faster algorithms are valuable because solving these coupled problems can be computationally demanding. This paper targets a gap between momentum methods proposed for speed and the computational improvements that had actually been proved.

The authors introduce two algorithms. One uses recursive iterations with momentum. The other uses recursive gradient estimates within nested loops to reduce variance. Both achieve a stated computational complexity proportional to the target accuracy raised to minus 1.5, ignoring logarithmic factors. The previous SGD-based bound scales with accuracy raised to minus 2, and the earlier momentum methods had not provably improved it.

The smaller exponent means that the theoretical cost grows more slowly as the requested error tolerance becomes tighter. Experiments in hyperparameter optimization support the theoretical findings and show improved empirical performance. The contribution therefore combines new recursive optimization procedures with a stronger complexity guarantee and practical evidence in an application of bilevel learning.
summary.tldr: Two recursive bilevel optimization algorithms improve the stated complexity exponent from 2 to 1.5, with supporting hyperparameter-optimization experiments.

title: Provably Faster Algorithms for Bilevel Optimization

abstract: Object detection has achieved substantial progress in the last decade. However, detecting novel classes with only few samples remains challenging, since deep learning under low data regime usually leads to a degraded feature space. Existing works employ a holistic fine-tuning paradigm to tackle this problem, where the model is first pre-trained on all base classes with abundant samples, and then it is used to carve the novel class feature space. Nonetheless, this paradigm is still imperfect. Durning fine-tuning, a novel class may implicitly leverage the knowledge of multiple base classes to construct its feature space, which induces a scattered feature space, hence violating the inter-class separability. To overcome these obstacles, we propose a two-step fine-tuning framework, Few-shot object detection via Association and DIscrimination (FADI), which builds up a discriminative feature space for each novel class with two integral steps. 1) In the association step, in contrast to implicitly leveraging multiple base classes, we construct a compact novel class feature space via explicitly imitating a specific base class feature space. Specifically, we associate each novel class with a base class according to their semantic similarity. After that, the feature space of a novel class can readily imitate the well-trained feature space of the associated base class. 2) In the discrimination step, to ensure the separability between the novel classes and associated base classes, we disentangle the classification branches for base and novel classes. To further enlarge the inter-class separability between all classes, a set-specialized margin loss is imposed. Extensive experiments on standard Pascal VOC and MS-COCO datasets demonstrate that FADI achieves new state-of-the-art performance, significantly improving the baseline in any shot/split by +18.7. Notably, the advantage of FADI is most announced on extremely few-shot scenarios (e.g. 1- and 3- shot).

paragraphs: Learning to detect a new object category from very few examples can produce poorly organized internal representations. The paper argues that conventional fine-tuning may implicitly borrow from several previously learned categories, scattering the new category’s features and making classes harder to distinguish. FADI addresses this through two explicit stages of knowledge transfer and separation.

First, the association stage matches each new category to a familiar category using semantic similarity. The new category then imitates that particular category’s established feature space, encouraging a compact representation. This gives the transfer process a specific reference instead of allowing the new representation to draw implicitly from multiple base categories.

Next, the discrimination stage separates classification branches for base and novel categories so that imitation does not leave the paired classes indistinguishable. A specialized margin loss further encourages separation across classes. Experiments on Pascal VOC and MS-COCO report state-of-the-art performance and substantial baseline improvements. The advantage is especially pronounced when only one or three examples are available, supporting the usefulness of organizing transfer carefully under severe data scarcity.
summary.tldr: FADI improves few-shot detection by first associating novel categories with familiar ones and then explicitly separating their representations.

title: Few-Shot Object Detection via Association and DIscrimination

abstract: In this paper, we present non-asymptotic optimization guarantees of gradient descent methods for estimating structured transition matrices in high-dimensional vector autoregressive (VAR) models. We adopt the projected gradient descent (PGD) for single-structured transition matrices and the alternating projected gradient descent (AltPGD) for superposition-structured ones. Our analysis demonstrates that both gradient algorithms converge linearly to the statistical error even though the strong convexity of the objective function is absent under the high-dimensional settings. Moreover our result is sharp (up to a constant factor) in the sense of matching the phase transition theory of the corresponding model with independent samples. To the best of our knowledge, this analysis constitutes first non-asymptotic optimization guarantees of the linear rate for regularized estimation in high-dimensional VAR models. Numerical results are provided to support our theoretical analysis.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we present non-asymptotic optimization guarantees of gradient descent methods for estimating structured transition matrices in high-dimensional vector autoregressive (VAR) models. We adopt the projected gradient descent (PGD) for single-structured transition matrices and the alternating projected gradient descent (AltPGD) for superposition-structured ones. Our analysis demonstrates that both gradient algorithms converge linearly to the statistical error even though the strong convexity of the objective function is absent under the high-dimensional settings. Moreover our result is sharp (up to a constant factor) in the sense of matching the phase transition theory of the corresponding model with independent samples. To the best of our knowledge, this analysis constitutes first non-asymptotic optimization guarantees of the linear rate for regularized estimation in high-dimensional VAR models. Numerical results are provided to support our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: Vector autoregressive models describe how several time-varying quantities depend on earlier values through a transition matrix. Estimating that matrix becomes challenging in high dimensions, where structural restrictions help make the problem manageable. This paper studies how quickly gradient-based optimization can estimate such structured matrices from temporally dependent observations.

The authors analyze projected gradient descent for a matrix with a single structure and alternating projected gradient descent for a superposition of structures. They prove that both algorithms converge at a linear rate until reaching the statistical error level. Here, linear convergence describes geometric reduction of optimization error, while the statistical error marks the estimation accuracy supported by the data.

The guarantees hold despite the absence of strong convexity in the high-dimensional objective. They are non-asymptotic, addressing finite settings rather than only limiting behavior. The results also match the corresponding independent-sample model’s phase-transition theory up to a constant factor. Numerical experiments support the analysis, linking practical gradient methods to sharp optimization guarantees for structured time-series estimation.
summary.tldr: The paper proves linear convergence to statistical accuracy for projected gradient methods estimating structured high-dimensional autoregressive models.

title: Linear Convergence of Gradient Methods for Estimating Structured Transition Matrices in High-dimensional Vector Autoregressive Models

abstract: Communication cost is one major bottleneck for the scalability for distributed learning. One approach to reduce the communication cost is to compress the gradient during communication. However, directly compressing the gradient decelerates the convergence speed, and the resulting algorithm may diverge for biased compression. Recent work addressed this problem for stochastic gradient descent by adding back the compression error from the previous step. This idea was further extended to one class of variance reduced algorithms, where the variance of the stochastic gradient is reduced by taking a moving average over all history gradients. However, our analysis shows that just adding the previous step's compression error, as done in existing work, does not fully compensate the compression error. So, we propose ErrorCompensateX, which uses the compression error from the previous two steps. We show that ErrorCompensateX can achieve the same asymptotic convergence rate with the training without compression. Moreover, we provide a unified theoretical analysis framework for this class of variance reduced algorithms, with or without error compensation.

paragraphs: Communicating gradients can limit the scalability of distributed training. Compressing them reduces communication, but it also changes the updates: convergence can slow, and biased compression can even cause divergence. A known remedy for stochastic gradient descent is to retain compression error and add it back during a later update.

This paper examines that remedy for a class of variance-reduced algorithms that smooth stochastic gradients through a moving average of gradient history. Its analysis shows that correcting with only the previous step's compression error does not fully compensate for the error in this setting. The proposed method instead uses errors from the previous two steps.

The authors show that this two-step correction can recover the same asymptotic convergence rate as training without compression. The result concerns the rate of convergence, giving theoretical support for reducing communication without losing that asymptotic behavior. They also provide a unified analysis framework covering the relevant variance-reduced algorithms both with and without error compensation. This clarifies why the correction must account for how historical gradients enter the update.
summary.tldr: Using compression errors from two previous steps can restore uncompressed asymptotic convergence rates for the analyzed class of variance-reduced algorithms.

title: ErrorCompensatedX: error compensation for variance reduced algorithms

abstract: Structured pruning is a commonly used technique in deploying deep neural networks (DNNs) onto resource-constrained devices. However, the existing pruning methods are usually heuristic, task-specified, and require an extra fine-tuning procedure. To overcome these limitations, we propose a framework that compresses DNNs into slimmer architectures with competitive performances and significant FLOPs reductions by Only-Train-Once (OTO). OTO contains two key steps: (i) we partition the parameters of DNNs into zero-invariant groups, enabling us to prune zero groups without affecting the output; and (ii) to promote zero groups, we then formulate a structured-sparsity optimization problem, and propose a novel optimization algorithm, Half-Space Stochastic Projected Gradient (HSPG), to solve it, which outperforms the standard proximal methods on group sparsity exploration, and maintains comparable convergence. To demonstrate the effectiveness of OTO, we train and compress full models simultaneously from scratch without fine-tuning for inference speedup and parameter reduction, and achieve state-of-the-art results on VGG16 for CIFAR10, ResNet50 for CIFAR10 and Bert for SQuAD and competitive result on ResNet50 for ImageNet. The source code is available at https://github.com/tianyic/only_train_once.

paragraphs: Structured pruning makes neural networks smaller by removing groups of parameters, but it often involves heuristics and a separate fine-tuning stage. Only-Train-Once, or OTO, combines training and compression from scratch. Its aim is to produce slimmer networks with competitive predictive performance and substantially reduced computational requirements.

OTO first divides parameters into zero-invariant groups: when a whole group is zero, removing it leaves the network's output unchanged. It then formulates training as a structured-sparsity optimization problem that encourages such zero groups. The proposed Half-Space Stochastic Projected Gradient algorithm finds group sparsity more effectively than standard proximal methods while maintaining comparable convergence.

The authors demonstrate simultaneous training and compression without subsequent fine-tuning, reporting inference speedups and fewer parameters. Results are state of the art for VGG16 and ResNet50 on CIFAR10 and BERT on SQuAD, with competitive results for ResNet50 on ImageNet. The framework connects safe removal of zero groups to an optimizer designed to create them during the original training process.
summary.tldr: OTO trains and structurally prunes networks in one process by encouraging removable zero-valued parameter groups, avoiding a separate fine-tuning stage.

title: Only Train Once: A One-Shot Neural Network Training And Pruning Framework

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) integrate deep architectures and topological structure modeling in an effective way. However, the performance of existing GNNs would decrease significantly when they stack many layers, because of the over-smoothing issue. Node embeddings tend to converge to similar vectors when GNNs keep recursively aggregating the representations of neighbors. To enable deep GNNs, several methods have been explored recently. But they are developed from either techniques in convolutional neural networks or heuristic strategies. There is no generalizable and theoretical principle to guide the design of deep GNNs. To this end, we analyze the bottleneck of deep GNNs by leveraging the Dirichlet energy of node embeddings, and propose a generalizable principle to guide the training of deep GNNs. Based on it, a novel deep GNN framework -- Energetic Graph Neural Networks (EGNN) is designed. It could provide lower and upper constraints in terms of Dirichlet energy at each layer to avoid over-smoothing. Experimental results demonstrate that EGNN achieves state-of-the-art performance by using deep layers.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks repeatedly combine each node’s representation with information from its neighbors. With many layers, this process can make node embeddings increasingly alike, a problem known as over-smoothing. The paper studies this bottleneck through the Dirichlet energy of node embeddings and uses that analysis to guide the design of deeper networks.

The resulting framework, Energetic Graph Neural Networks, places lower and upper constraints on Dirichlet energy at each layer. Instead of selecting architectural changes solely through heuristics or borrowing techniques from convolutional networks, the approach uses an explicit energy-based principle to regulate the representations as they pass through the network. The intended effect is to avoid the collapse associated with repeated aggregation.

The authors report state-of-the-art experimental performance using deep layers. This supports the usefulness of their proposed training principle in the evaluated setting. The main contribution is both analytical and architectural: a way to describe the depth bottleneck and a corresponding framework that incorporates layer-by-layer constraints aimed at controlling it.
summary.tldr: Energetic Graph Neural Networks constrain layer-wise Dirichlet energy to counter over-smoothing and improve deep GNN performance.

title: Dirichlet Energy Constrained Learning for Deep Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) work well when the graph structure is provided. However, this structure may not always be available in real-world applications. One solution to this problem is to infer a task-specific latent structure and then apply a GNN to the inferred graph. Unfortunately, the space of possible graph structures grows super-exponentially with the number of nodes and so the task-specific supervision may be insufficient for learning both the structure and the GNN parameters. In this work, we propose the Simultaneous Learning of Adjacency and GNN Parameters with Self-supervision, or SLAPS, a method that provides more supervision for inferring a graph structure through self-supervision. A comprehensive experimental study demonstrates that SLAPS scales to large graphs with hundreds of thousands of nodes and outperforms several models that have been proposed to learn a task-specific graph structure on established benchmarks.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks depend on a graph describing relationships between nodes, but that structure is not always available. One response is to learn a task-specific graph alongside the network. This creates a difficult joint learning problem: the task’s labels must help determine both which relationships should exist and how the network should use them.

The paper emphasizes that the space of possible graphs grows super-exponentially with the number of nodes. Task-specific supervision may therefore be insufficient to identify a useful structure while also fitting the network parameters. SLAPS adds self-supervision to provide more learning signal for graph inference, combining adjacency learning and GNN parameter learning within the same method.

A comprehensive experimental study reports that SLAPS scales to graphs containing hundreds of thousands of nodes. It also outperforms several models designed to learn task-specific graph structures on established benchmarks. These findings support additional self-supervision as a practical way to improve joint graph and network learning, particularly when the relationships needed by a GNN must themselves be inferred.
summary.tldr: SLAPS adds self-supervision to jointly learn graph structure and GNN parameters, improving benchmark performance and scaling to large graphs.

title: SLAPS: Self-Supervision Improves Structure Learning for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We propose a multi-agent variant of the classical multi-armed bandit problem, in which there are $N$ agents and $K$ arms, and pulling an arm generates a (possibly different) stochastic reward for each agent. Unlike the classical multi-armed bandit problem, the goal is not to learn the "best arm"; indeed, each agent may perceive a different arm to be the best for her personally. Instead, we seek to learn a fair distribution over the arms. Drawing on a long line of research in economics and computer science, we use the Nash social welfare as our notion of fairness. We design multi-agent variants of three classic multi-armed bandit algorithms and show that they achieve sublinear regret, which is now measured in terms of the lost Nash social welfare. We also extend a classical lower bound, establishing the optimality of one of our algorithms.

paragraphs: In a standard bandit problem, a learner explores uncertain options to discover which produces the best reward. This paper considers multiple agents who receive potentially different rewards from the same chosen option. An arm that is attractive to one agent may therefore be unattractive to another, making a single shared ranking inappropriate.

The goal becomes learning a fair probability distribution over arms. The authors formalize fairness through Nash social welfare and evaluate learning by the welfare lost while rewards are still being discovered. This places the distribution of benefits across agents directly inside the learning objective, rather than treating fairness as a separate assessment after choosing an arm.

The paper adapts three classical bandit algorithms to this multi-agent setting and proves sublinear regret measured in lost Nash social welfare. Consequently, average welfare regret per decision decreases as the interaction grows. An extension of a classical lower bound establishes optimality for one of the algorithms. Together, these results show that uncertainty about rewards can be handled with formal learning guarantees while pursuing the specified collective fairness objective.
summary.tldr: The paper develops bandit algorithms that learn fair distributions over shared options using Nash social welfare, with sublinear regret guarantees.

title: Fair Algorithms for Multi-Agent Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: The prevalence of graph-based data has spurred the rapid development of graph neural networks (GNNs) and related machine learning algorithms. Yet, despite the many datasets naturally modeled as directed graphs, including citation, website, and traffic networks, the vast majority of this research focuses on undirected graphs. In this paper, we propose MagNet, a GNN for directed graphs based on a complex Hermitian matrix known as the magnetic Laplacian. This matrix encodes undirected geometric structure in the magnitude of its entries and directional information in their phase. A charge parameter attunes spectral information to variation among directed cycles. We apply our network to a variety of directed graph node classification and link prediction tasks showing that MagNet performs well on all tasks and that its performance exceeds all other methods on a majority of such tasks. The underlying principles of MagNet are such that it can be adapted to other GNN architectures.

paragraphs: Many networks contain connections with a direction, including citations, website links, and traffic flows. That direction carries information that an undirected graph representation does not explicitly preserve. MagNet is a graph neural network designed to incorporate both connection structure and direction through a mathematical representation called the magnetic Laplacian.

This representation is a complex Hermitian matrix. The magnitudes of its entries encode the underlying undirected geometry, while their phases encode directional information. A charge parameter adjusts how its spectral information responds to differences among directed cycles. This gives the network a structured way to represent direction together with graph geometry within the same underlying matrix.

The authors evaluate MagNet on directed-graph node classification and link prediction. It performs well across the tested tasks and exceeds all compared methods on a majority of them. These results support the usefulness of the magnetic-Laplacian representation for the evaluated directed networks. The authors also state that its underlying principles can be adapted to other graph neural network architectures, extending the design idea beyond this particular network.
summary.tldr: MagNet encodes graph geometry and edge direction in a magnetic Laplacian to support learning on directed networks.

title: MagNet: A Neural Network for Directed Graphs

abstract: We present a new dataset and benchmark with the goal of advancing research in the intersection of brain activities and eye movements. Our dataset, EEGEyeNet, consists of simultaneous Electroencephalography (EEG) and Eye-tracking (ET) recordings from 356 different subjects collected from three different experimental paradigms. Using this dataset, we also propose a benchmark to evaluate gaze prediction from EEG measurements. The benchmark consists of three tasks with an increasing level of difficulty: left-right, angle-amplitude and absolute position. We run extensive experiments on this benchmark in order to provide solid baselines, both based on classical machine learning models and on large neural networks. We release our complete code and data and provide a simple and easy-to-use interface to evaluate new methods.

The dataset records electroencephalography, or EEG, at the same time as eye tracking for 356 participants across three experimental paradigms. Collecting both measurements together supports a concrete prediction problem: estimating gaze from the accompanying EEG measurements.

The benchmark organizes that problem into three tasks of increasing difficulty. The first concerns left-versus-right movement, the second concerns angle and amplitude, and the third concerns absolute position. This progression moves from a coarse directional distinction toward more detailed descriptions of gaze, allowing methods to be assessed at different levels of prediction difficulty.

The authors run extensive experiments with classical machine learning methods and large neural networks to establish reference results. They also release the full dataset, code, and an interface for evaluating new methods. The resulting contribution combines simultaneous recordings with a defined testing procedure, giving researchers a common starting point for comparing approaches to gaze prediction from EEG.
summary.tldr: EEGEyeNet combines simultaneous EEG and eye tracking from 356 participants with three progressively harder gaze prediction tasks.

title: EEGEyeNet: a Simultaneous Electroencephalography and Eye-tracking Dataset and Benchmark for Eye Movement Prediction

abstract: In this work we present a novel approach for computing correspondences between non-rigid objects, by exploiting a reduced representation of deformation fields. Different from existing works that represent deformation fields by training a general-purpose neural network, we advocate for an approximation based on mesh-free methods. By letting the network learn deformation parameters at a sparse set of positions in space (nodes), we reconstruct the continuous deformation field in a closed-form with guaranteed smoothness. With this reduction in degrees of freedom, we show significant improvement in terms of data-efficiency thus enabling limited supervision. Furthermore, our approximation provides direct access to first-order derivatives of deformation fields, which facilitates enforcing desirable regularization effectively. Our resulting model has high expressive power and is able to capture complex deformations. We illustrate its effectiveness through state-of-the-art results across multiple deformable shape matching benchmarks. Our code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/Sentient07/DeformationBasis.

paragraphs: Matching non-rigid objects requires finding corresponding locations despite changes in shape. A deformation field describes how positions move between the objects. This paper proposes learning a reduced representation of that field, with the aim of capturing complex movement while reducing the amount of information that must be learned from supervision.

The network predicts deformation parameters at a sparse set of spatial nodes. A mesh-free approximation then reconstructs the continuous field in closed form with guaranteed smoothness. This reduces the degrees of freedom compared with representing the field through a general-purpose neural network. The representation also provides direct access to first-order derivatives, making it easier to apply regularization to the deformation.

The authors report improved data efficiency that enables learning with limited supervision, while retaining enough expressive power to capture complex deformations. Results across multiple deformable shape-matching benchmarks reach state-of-the-art performance. The approach connects representational structure to learning efficiency: sparse learned parameters and an explicit reconstruction rule jointly determine the full deformation field.
summary.tldr: Learning sparse deformation parameters and reconstructing a smooth continuous field improves data efficiency for non-rigid shape matching.

title: Reduced Representation of Deformation Fields for Effective Non-rigid Shape Matching

abstract: 3D object detection from the LiDAR point cloud is fundamental to autonomous driving. Large-scale outdoor scenes usually feature significant variance in instance scales, thus requiring features rich in long-range and fine-grained information to support accurate detection. Recent detectors leverage the power of window-based transformers to model long-range dependencies but tend to blur out fine-grained details. To mitigate this gap, we present a novel Mixed-scale Sparse Voxel Transformer, named MsSVT, which can well capture both types of information simultaneously by the divide-and-conquer philosophy. Specifically, MsSVT explicitly divides attention heads into multiple groups, each in charge of attending to information within a particular range. All groups' output is merged to obtain the final mixed-scale features. Moreover, we provide a novel chessboard sampling strategy to reduce the computational complexity of applying a window-based transformer in 3D voxel space. To improve efficiency, we also implement the voxel sampling and gathering operations sparsely with a hash map. Endowed by the powerful capability and high efficiency of modeling mixed-scale information, our single-stage detector built on top of MsSVT surprisingly outperforms state-of-the-art two-stage detectors on Waymo. Our project page: https://github.com/dscdyc/MsSVT.

paragraphs: Detecting objects in outdoor LiDAR point clouds requires both broad spatial context and fine detail. Objects vary substantially in size, so a detector needs information at different ranges. Window-based transformers can capture distant relationships, but the paper identifies a tendency to blur the detailed information needed for accurate detection.

MsSVT addresses this by dividing attention heads into groups, with each group attending over a particular range. Their outputs are merged into features that combine multiple scales. This division assigns different spatial responsibilities within the transformer, allowing local detail and longer-range information to contribute to the same final representation.

The authors also introduce chessboard sampling to reduce computation in three-dimensional voxel windows and use hash maps for sparse voxel sampling and gathering. These efficiency measures accompany the mixed-scale attention design. A single-stage detector built with MsSVT outperforms state-of-the-art two-stage detectors on Waymo in the reported evaluation. The result supports the value of combining spatial scales while making the underlying sparse processing efficient.
summary.tldr: MsSVT combines attention at multiple spatial ranges with efficient sparse processing to improve LiDAR-based 3D detection.

title: MsSVT: Mixed-scale Sparse Voxel Transformer for 3D Object Detection on Point Clouds

abstract: The wide adoption of deep neural networks (DNNs) in mission-critical applications has spurred the need for interpretable models that provide explanations of the model's decisions. Unfortunately, previous studies have demonstrated that model explanations facilitate information leakage, rendering DNN models vulnerable to model inversion attacks. These attacks enable the adversary to reconstruct original images based on model explanations, thus leaking privacy-sensitive features. To this end, we present Generative Noise Injector for Model Explanations (GNIME), a novel defense framework that perturbs model explanations to minimize the risk of model inversion attacks while preserving the interpretabilities of the generated explanations. Specifically, we formulate the defense training as a two-player minimax game between the inversion attack network on the one hand, which aims to invert model explanations, and the noise generator network on the other, which aims to inject perturbations to tamper with model inversion attacks. We demonstrate that GNIME significantly decreases the information leakage in model explanations, decreasing transferable classification accuracy in facial recognition models by up to 84.8% while preserving the original functionality of model explanations.

paragraphs: Explanations can reveal more than the reasons behind a neural network's decision. The paper addresses model inversion attacks that reconstruct original images from explanations, potentially exposing sensitive visual information. Its goal is to reduce this leakage while keeping explanations useful for interpreting the model's behavior.

The proposed framework, GNIME, learns to perturb explanations using a noise generator. Training is formulated as a two-player minimax game. An inversion network tries to recover images from explanations, while the generator learns perturbations that interfere with this reconstruction. This makes the defensive changes responsive to the inversion objective, while the framework also seeks to preserve explanation interpretability.

The authors report substantially reduced information leakage while maintaining the original functionality of explanations. In facial recognition models, transferable classification accuracy decreases by up to 84.8%, providing a reported measure of the defense's effect. This is an observed maximum reduction, not a claim of complete privacy. The contribution is a learned approach to balancing explanation usefulness with resistance to reconstruction attacks.
summary.tldr: GNIME learns perturbations that make model explanations harder to invert while preserving their explanatory functionality.

title: Learning to Generate Inversion-Resistant Model Explanations

abstract: The adversarial vulnerability of neural nets, and subsequent techniques to create robust models have attracted significant attention; yet we still lack a full understanding of this phenomenon. Here, we study adversarial examples of trained neural networks through analytical tools afforded by recent theory advances connecting neural networks and kernel methods, namely the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), following a growing body of work that leverages the NTK approximation to successfully analyze important deep learning phenomena and design algorithms for new applications. We show how NTKs allow to generate adversarial examples in a ``training-free'' fashion, and demonstrate that they transfer to fool their finite-width neural net counterparts in the ``lazy'' regime. We leverage this connection to provide an alternative view on robust and non-robust features, which have been suggested to underlie the adversarial brittleness of neural nets. Specifically, we define and study features induced by the eigendecomposition of the kernel to better understand the role of robust and non-robust features, the reliance on both for standard classification and the robustness-accuracy trade-off. We find that such features are surprisingly consistent across architectures, and that robust features tend to correspond to the largest eigenvalues of the model, and thus are learned early during training. Our framework allows us to identify and visualize non-robust yet useful features. Finally, we shed light on the robustness mechanism underlying adversarial training of neural nets used in practice: quantifying the evolution of the associated empirical NTK, we demonstrate that its dynamics falls much earlier into the ``lazy'' regime and manifests a much stronger form of the well known bias to prioritize learning features within the top eigenspaces of the kernel, compared to standard training.

We show how NTKs allow to generate adversarial examples in a ``training-free'' fashion, and demonstrate that they transfer to fool their finite-width neural net counterparts in the ``lazy'' regime. We leverage this connection to provide an alternative view on robust and non-robust features, which have been suggested to underlie the adversarial brittleness of neural nets. Specifically, we define and study features induced by the eigendecomposition of the kernel to better understand the role of robust and non-robust features, the reliance on both for standard classification and the robustness-accuracy trade-off. We find that such features are surprisingly consistent across architectures, and that robust features tend to correspond to the largest eigenvalues of the model, and thus are learned early during training. Our framework allows us to identify and visualize non-robust yet useful features. Finally, we shed light on the robustness mechanism underlying adversarial training of neural nets used in practice: quantifying the evolution of the associated empirical NTK, we demonstrate that its dynamics falls much earlier into the ``lazy'' regime and manifests a much stronger form of the well known bias to prioritize learning features within the top eigenspaces of the kernel, compared to standard training.

It shows that kernel-based tools can generate attacks without training and that these attacks transfer to corresponding finite-width networks in the lazy regime. This ties the attack behavior to a specific connection between networks and kernels.

Robust features tend to correspond to larger eigenvalues and consequently are learned earlier during training. The framework also identifies and visualizes useful but non-robust features, offering a way to examine the accuracy-robustness trade-off.

Compared with standard training, its dynamics enter the lazy regime much earlier and show a stronger preference for learning features in the kernel's top eigenspaces. This supplies a kernel-based account of a mechanism underlying adversarial training, connecting observed robustness behavior with changes in which features training prioritizes.

title: What Can the Neural Tangent Kernel Tell Us About Adversarial Robustness?

abstract: In semi-supervised learning (SSL), a common practice is to learn consistent information from unlabeled data and discriminative information from labeled data to ensure both the immutability and the separability of the classification model. Existing SSL methods suffer from failures in barely-supervised learning (BSL), where only one or two labels per class are available, as the insufficient labels cause the discriminative information being difficult or even infeasible to learn. To bridge this gap, we investigate a simple yet effective way to leverage unlabeled samples for discriminative learning, and propose a novel discriminative information learning module to benefit model training. Specifically, we formulate the learning objective of discriminative information at the super-class level and dynamically assign different classes into different super-classes based on model performance improvement. On top of this on-the-fly process, we further propose a distribution-based loss to learn discriminative information by utilizing the similarity relationship between samples and super-classes. It encourages the unlabeled samples to stay closer to the distribution of their corresponding super-class than those of others. Such a constraint is softer than the direct assignment of pseudo labels, while the latter could be very noisy in BSL. We compare our method with state-of-the-art SSL and BSL methods through extensive experiments on standard SSL benchmarks. Our method can achieve superior results, \eg, an average accuracy of 76.76\% on CIFAR-10 with merely 1 label per class.
