This paper asks how unlabeled data can also supply useful information for separating classes in this barely supervised setting.

The proposed module groups classes into broader super-classes and changes those groupings dynamically according to improvements in model performance. A distribution-based loss uses relationships between samples and super-classes, encouraging each unlabeled sample to be closer to its associated super-class distribution than to others. This provides a softer training constraint than assigning a specific pseudo-label, which can be highly noisy with so few labels.

Experiments compare the method with leading semi-supervised and barely supervised approaches on standard benchmarks. The reported results include average accuracy of 76.76% on CIFAR-10 with one labeled example per class. The findings support using broader, adaptive group distinctions to extract discriminative information from unlabeled samples when fine-grained supervision is extremely scarce.
summary.tldr: Adaptive super-classes help unlabeled examples teach class separation when only one or two labeled examples per class are available.

title: Improving Barely Supervised Learning by Discriminating Unlabeled Samples with Super-Class

abstract: Effective decision making involves flexibly relating past experiences and relevant contextual information to a novel situation. In deep reinforcement learning (RL), the dominant paradigm is for an agent to amortise information that helps decision-making into its network weights via gradient descent on training losses. Here, we pursue an alternative approach in which agents can utilise large-scale context-sensitive database lookups to support their parametric computations. This allows agents to directly learn in an end-to-end manner to utilise relevant information to inform their outputs. In addition, new information can be attended to by the agent, without retraining, by simply augmenting the retrieval dataset. We study this approach for offline RL in 9x9 Go, a challenging game for which the vast combinatorial state space privileges generalisation over direct matching to past experiences. We leverage fast, approximate nearest neighbor techniques in order to retrieve relevant data from a set of tens of millions of expert demonstration states. Attending to this information provides a significant boost to prediction accuracy and game-play performance over simply using these demonstrations as training trajectories, providing a compelling demonstration of the value of large-scale retrieval in offline RL agents.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement-learning agents commonly incorporate useful experience into network weights during training. This paper augments that process with context-sensitive database retrieval, letting an agent consult relevant information while producing its outputs. The retrieval mechanism supports the network's own computations and is learned end to end.

A practical consequence is that the agent can attend to newly added information without retraining, simply by expanding the retrieval dataset. The authors investigate the approach in offline reinforcement learning for 9x9 Go. Fast approximate nearest-neighbor methods retrieve relevant examples from tens of millions of expert demonstration states, making consultation of a very large experience collection feasible.

Go's vast state space makes the task depend on generalization beyond exact matches to previous positions. In the reported study, attending to retrieved information significantly improves prediction accuracy and game-play performance compared with using the demonstrations only as training trajectories. The result demonstrates the value of keeping experience available for direct consultation alongside what the network has already learned in its parameters.
summary.tldr: An offline Go agent improves prediction and play by retrieving relevant expert states from a large database during decision-making.

title: Large-Scale Retrieval for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Video prediction is a challenging task. The quality of video frames from current state-of-the-art (SOTA) generative models tends to be poor and generalization beyond the training data is difficult. Furthermore, existing prediction frameworks are typically not capable of simultaneously handling other video-related tasks such as unconditional generation or interpolation. In this work, we devise a general-purpose framework called Masked Conditional Video Diffusion (MCVD) for all of these video synthesis tasks using a probabilistic conditional score-based denoising diffusion model, conditioned on past and/or future frames. We train the model in a manner where we randomly and independently mask all the past frames or all the future frames. This novel but straightforward setup allows us to train a single model that is capable of executing a broad range of video tasks, specifically: future/past prediction -- when only future/past frames are masked; unconditional generation -- when both past and future frames are masked; and interpolation -- when neither past nor future frames are masked. Our experiments show that this approach can generate high-quality frames for diverse types of videos. Our MCVD models are built from simple non-recurrent 2D-convolutional architectures, conditioning on blocks of frames and generating blocks of frames. We generate videos of arbitrary lengths autoregressively in a block-wise manner. Our approach yields SOTA results across standard video prediction and interpolation benchmarks, with computation times for training models measured in 1-12 days using $\le$ 4 GPUs. paragraphs: MCVD brings several video synthesis tasks into one conditional diffusion framework. Instead of treating future prediction, past prediction, interpolation, and unconditional generation as separate modelling problems, it changes which surrounding frames are available to the same model. The motivation is to improve video synthesis while broadening the tasks a single model can handle.

During training, the method randomly and independently hides the past conditioning frames or the future conditioning frames. With only past frames available, it predicts forward; with only future frames available, it predicts backward. Hiding both gives unconditional generation, while retaining both supports interpolation. The model learns to denoise video content under these different patterns of available context.

The architecture uses non-recurrent two-dimensional convolutions and processes blocks of frames. Generating successive blocks autoregressively allows videos of arbitrary length. The authors report high-quality frames across diverse videos and state-of-the-art results on standard prediction and interpolation benchmarks. Reported training takes one to twelve days using at most four GPUs, providing a concrete computational context for those experimental results.
summary.tldr: MCVD uses random masking of past and future conditioning frames to train one diffusion model for multiple video synthesis tasks.

title: MCVD - Masked Conditional Video Diffusion for Prediction, Generation, and Interpolation

abstract: The choice of activation functions and their motivation is a long-standing issue within the neural network community. Neuronal representations within artificial neural networks are commonly understood as logits, representing the log-odds score of presence of features within the stimulus. We derive logit-space operators equivalent to probabilistic Boolean logic-gates AND, OR, and XNOR for independent probabilities. Such theories are important to formalize more complex dendritic operations in real neurons, and these operations can be used as activation functions within a neural network, introducing probabilistic Boolean-logic as the core operation of the neural network. Since these functions involve taking multiple exponents and logarithms, they are computationally expensive and not well suited to be directly used within neural networks. Consequently, we construct efficient approximations named $\text{AND}_\text{AIL}$ (the AND operator Approximate for Independent Logits), $\text{OR}_\text{AIL}$, and $\text{XNOR}_\text{AIL}$, which utilize only comparison and addition operations, have well-behaved gradients, and can be deployed as activation functions in neural networks. Like MaxOut, $\text{AND}_\text{AIL}$ and $\text{OR}_\text{AIL}$ are generalizations of ReLU to two-dimensions. While our primary aim is to formalize dendritic computations within a logit-space probabilistic-Boolean framework, we deploy these new activation functions, both in isolation and in conjunction to demonstrate their effectiveness on a variety of tasks including tabular classification, image classification, transfer learning, abstract reasoning, and compositional zero-shot learning.

paragraphs: Neural representations are often interpreted as logits: scores expressing the log odds that a feature is present. This paper asks how Boolean operations can be expressed directly in that space. It derives counterparts of probabilistic AND, OR, and XNOR under an independence assumption for the probabilities being combined.

The exact operators require repeated exponentials and logarithms, making them expensive as neural-network activation functions. The authors therefore construct approximate versions that use comparisons and additions and have well-behaved gradients. Their approximate AND and OR functions generalize ReLU to two dimensions, connecting the logical formulation to an established kind of neural activation.

The paper also evaluates the resulting functions, separately and in combinations, on tabular classification, image classification, transfer learning, abstract reasoning, and compositional zero-shot learning. These demonstrations support their practical effectiveness across the tested tasks. The work links an interpretable motivation for combining features with computationally efficient operations usable inside neural networks.
summary.tldr: The paper derives probabilistic Boolean operators in logit space and builds efficient approximations for neural-network activations.

title: Logical Activation Functions: Logit-space equivalents of Probabilistic Boolean Operators

abstract: A central problem in online learning and decision making---from bandits to reinforcement learning---is to understand what modeling assumptions lead to sample-efficient learning guarantees. We consider a general adversarial decision making framework that encompasses (structured) bandit problems with adversarial rewards and reinforcement learning problems with adversarial dynamics. Our main result is to show---via new upper and lower bounds---that the Decision-Estimation Coefficient, a complexity measure introduced by Foster et al. in the stochastic counterpart to our setting, is necessary and sufficient to obtain low regret for adversarial decision making. However, compared to the stochastic setting, one must apply the Decision-Estimation Coefficient to the convex hull of the class of models (or, hypotheses) under consideration. This establishes that the price of accommodating adversarial rewards or dynamics is governed by the behavior of the model class under convexification, and recovers a number of existing results --both positive and negative. En route to obtaining these guarantees, we provide new structural results that connect the Decision-Estimation Coefficient to variants of other well-known complexity measures, including the Information Ratio of Russo and Van Roy and the Exploration-by-Optimization objective of Lattimore and György.

paragraphs: Learning to make good decisions depends on which assumptions are made about the environment. This paper studies a broad adversarial setting covering structured bandits with adversarial rewards and reinforcement learning with adversarial dynamics. Its goal is to characterize when a learner can achieve low regret, rather than providing a guarantee for just one particular problem.

Using upper and lower bounds, the authors show that the Decision-Estimation Coefficient supplies a necessary and sufficient complexity characterization in their framework. The crucial change from the stochastic setting is where this measure must be applied: to the convex hull of the model class, which includes mixtures of the candidate models.

This identifies how accommodating adversarial behavior can make learning harder. The relevant cost depends on what happens to the model class under convexification, and the characterization recovers existing positive and negative results. The paper also establishes structural connections to variants of the Information Ratio and Exploration-by-Optimization objective, linking several ways of describing the difficulty of exploration and decision making.
summary.tldr: Low-regret adversarial decision making is characterized by the Decision-Estimation Coefficient applied to the convex hull of the model class.

title: On the Complexity of Adversarial Decision Making

abstract: Machine learning for point clouds has been attracting much attention, with many applications in various fields, such as shape recognition and material science. For enhancing the accuracy of such machine learning methods, it is often effective to incorporate global topological features, which are typically extracted by persistent homology. In the calculation of persistent homology for a point cloud, we choose a filtration for the point cloud, an increasing sequence of spaces. Since the performance of machine learning methods combined with persistent homology is highly affected by the choice of a filtration, we need to tune it depending on data and tasks. In this paper, we propose a framework that learns a filtration adaptively with the use of neural networks. In order to make the resulting persistent homology isometry-invariant, we develop a neural network architecture with such invariance. Additionally, we show a theoretical result on a finite-dimensional approximation of filtration functions, which justifies the proposed network architecture. Experimental results demonstrated the efficacy of our framework in several classification tasks.

paragraphs: Point clouds describe objects through collections of points, but useful information can also lie in their overall structure. Persistent homology extracts global topological features by examining an increasing sequence of spaces called a filtration. The choice of this sequence strongly affects how useful the resulting features are for a learning task.

The paper proposes learning the filtration with a neural network so that it can adapt to the data and prediction objective. It also develops an architecture designed to make the resulting persistent homology invariant to isometries: transformations that preserve distances. This connects task-specific feature learning with a requirement that equivalent geometric arrangements receive consistent topological descriptions.

A theoretical result concerning finite-dimensional approximations of filtration functions provides justification for the architecture. Experiments on several classification tasks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. The contribution is therefore both a method for adapting topological feature extraction and a principled way to retain geometric invariance while doing so, rather than relying on a fixed filtration choice across tasks.
summary.tldr: The paper learns task-adaptive filtrations for point-cloud topology while preserving invariance to distance-preserving transformations.

title: Adaptive Topological Feature via Persistent Homology: Filtration Learning for Point Clouds

abstract: Capturing semantic information is crucial for accurate long-range time series forecasting, which involves modeling global and local correlations, as well as discovering long- and short-term repetitive patterns. Previous works have partially addressed these issues separately, but have not been able to address all of them simultaneously. Meanwhile, their time and memory complexities are still not sufficiently low for long-range forecasting. To address the challenge of capturing different types of semantic information, we propose a novel Water-wave Information Transmission (WIT) framework. This framework captures both long- and short-term repetitive patterns through bi-granular information transmission. It also models global and local correlations by recursively fusing and selecting information using Horizontal Vertical Gated Selective Unit (HVGSU). In addition, to improve the computing efficiency, we propose a generic Recurrent Acceleration Network (RAN) which reduces the time complexity to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{L})$ while maintaining the memory complexity at $\mathcal{O}(L)$. Our proposed method, called Water-wave Information Transmission and Recurrent Acceleration Network (WITRAN), outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by 5.80% and 14.28% on long-range and ultra-long-range time series forecasting tasks respectively, as demonstrated by experiments on four benchmark datasets. The code is available at: https://github.com/Water2sea/WITRAN.

The contribution connects richer temporal modeling with computational acceleration, addressing the cost of processing long sequences alongside the problem of identifying which recurring and correlated information is useful for prediction.

title: WITRAN: Water-wave Information Transmission and Recurrent Acceleration Network for Long-range Time Series Forecasting

abstract: The storage of continuous variables in working memory is hypothesized to be sustained in the brain by the dynamics of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) whose steady states form continuous manifolds. In some cases, it is thought that the synaptic connectivity supports multiple attractor manifolds, each mapped to a different context or task. For example, in hippocampal area CA3, positions in distinct environments are represented by distinct sets of population activity patterns, each forming a continuum. It has been argued that the embedding of multiple continuous attractors in a single RNN inevitably causes detrimental interference: quenched noise in the synaptic connectivity disrupts the continuity of each attractor, replacing it by a discrete set of steady states that can be conceptualized as lying on local minima of an abstract energy landscape. Consequently, population activity patterns exhibit systematic drifts towards one of these discrete minima, thereby degrading the stored memory over time. Here we show that it is possible to dramatically attenuate these detrimental interference effects by adjusting the synaptic weights. Synaptic weight adjustment are derived from a loss function that quantifies the roughness of the energy landscape along each of the embedded attractor manifolds. By minimizing this loss function, the stability of states can be dramatically improved, without compromising the capacity.

paragraphs: One hypothesis about working memory is that recurrent neural networks preserve continuous quantities through continuous families of stable activity states. A single network may need several such families for different contexts. Interference between them can roughen the network’s energy landscape, causing activity to drift toward isolated stable states and degrading the stored value.

This paper shows that adjusting synaptic weights can substantially reduce that interference. The authors define a loss measuring the roughness of the energy landscape along each embedded attractor manifold. Minimizing this loss directly targets the irregularities associated with drift, rather than treating interference as an unavoidable consequence of storing multiple continuous representations.

The reported result is a dramatic improvement in state stability without sacrificing capacity. This matters for models that need to maintain different continuous memories within the same recurrent network. The contribution demonstrates that suitable weight adjustment can attenuate detrimental interference; it does not require claiming that all interference disappears. The biological framing remains a hypothesis about how continuous working-memory representations may be sustained.
summary.tldr: Optimizing synaptic weights to smooth attractor landscapes can greatly improve continuous-memory stability without reducing network capacity.

title: Simultaneous embedding of multiple attractor manifolds in a recurrent neural network using constrained gradient optimization

abstract: Modern climate projections lack adequate spatial and temporal resolution due to computational constraints. A consequence is inaccurate and imprecise predictions of critical processes such as storms. Hybrid methods that combine physics with machine learning (ML) have introduced a new generation of higher fidelity climate simulators that can sidestep Moore's Law by outsourcing compute-hungry, short, high-resolution simulations to ML emulators. However, this hybrid ML-physics simulation approach requires domain-specific treatment and has been inaccessible to ML experts because of lack of training data and relevant, easy-to-use workflows. We present ClimSim, the largest-ever dataset designed for hybrid ML-physics research. It comprises multi-scale climate simulations, developed by a consortium of climate scientists and ML researchers. It consists of 5.7 billion pairs of multivariate input and output vectors that isolate the influence of locally-nested, high-resolution, high-fidelity physics on a host climate simulator's macro-scale physical state.The dataset is global in coverage, spans multiple years at high sampling frequency, and is designed such that resulting emulators are compatible with downstream coupling into operational climate simulators. We implement a range of deterministic and stochastic regression baselines to highlight the ML challenges and their scoring. The data (https://huggingface.co/datasets/LEAP/ClimSim_high-res) and code (https://leap-stc.github.io/ClimSim) are released openly to support the development of hybrid ML-physics and high-fidelity climate simulations for the benefit of science and society.

We implement a range of deterministic and stochastic regression baselines to highlight the ML challenges and their scoring. The data (https://huggingface.co/datasets/LEAP/ClimSim_high-res) and code (https://leap-stc.github.io/ClimSim) are released openly to support the development of hybrid ML-physics and high-fidelity climate simulations for the benefit of science and society.

paragraphs: Climate simulations face a computational tradeoff: resolving short-lived, local processes in detail is expensive, yet those processes influence larger-scale climate behavior. Hybrid physics and machine-learning systems aim to replace costly high-resolution calculations with learned emulators. ClimSim supplies training data and workflows intended to make this research more accessible to machine-learning researchers.

The dataset contains 5.7 billion pairs of multivariate inputs and outputs from simulations at multiple scales. These pairs isolate how locally embedded, high-resolution physics affects the larger-scale state of a host climate simulator. Coverage is global, extends across multiple years, and uses frequent sampling. The data is designed so that learned emulators can later be coupled to operational climate simulators.

The authors also implement deterministic and stochastic regression baselines to expose the prediction challenges and demonstrate how to score models. The contribution is a shared resource for developing and evaluating emulators, with openly released data and code. Its connection to simulator states makes it especially relevant to research that must eventually integrate learned predictions into a physical simulation.
summary.tldr: ClimSim provides 5.7 billion simulation input-output pairs for learning high-resolution physics emulators compatible with climate simulators.

title: ClimSim: A large multi-scale dataset for hybrid physics-ML climate emulation

abstract: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods are efficient iterative algorithms for solving ill-posed image inverse problems. PnP methods are obtained by using deep Gaussian denoisers instead of the proximal operator or the gradient-descent step within proximal algorithms. Current PnP schemes rely on data-fidelity terms that have either Lipschitz gradients or closed-form proximal operators, which is not applicable to Poisson inverse problems. Based on the observation that the Gaussian noise is not the adequate noise model in this setting, we propose to generalize PnP using the Bregman Proximal Gradient (BPG) method. BPG replaces the Euclidean distance with a Bregman divergence that can better capture the smoothness properties of the problem. We introduce the Bregman Score Denoiser specifically parametrized and trained for the new Bregman geometry and prove that it corresponds to the proximal operator of a nonconvex potential. We propose two PnP algorithms based on the Bregman Score Denoiser for solving Poisson inverse problems. Extending the convergence results of BPG in the nonconvex settings, we show that the proposed methods converge, targeting stationary points of an explicit global functional. Experimental evaluations conducted on various Poisson inverse problems validate the convergence results and showcase effective restoration performance.

title: Convergent Bregman Plug-and-Play Image Restoration for Poisson Inverse Problems

abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets), a class of generative models over discrete and structured sample spaces, have been previously applied to the problem of inferring the marginal posterior distribution over the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of a Bayesian Network, given a dataset of observations. Based on recent advances extending this framework to non-discrete sample spaces, we propose in this paper to approximate the joint posterior over not only the structure of a Bayesian Network, but also the parameters of its conditional probability distributions. We use a single GFlowNet whose sampling policy follows a two-phase process: the DAG is first generated sequentially one edge at a time, and then the corresponding parameters are picked once the full structure is known. Since the parameters are included in the posterior distribution, this leaves more flexibility for the local probability models of the Bayesian Network, making our approach applicable even to non-linear models parametrized by neural networks. We show that our method, called JSP-GFN, offers an accurate approximation of the joint posterior, while comparing favorably against existing methods on both simulated and real data.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network involves uncertainty about both its graph structure and the parameters describing its conditional probabilities. Earlier GFlowNet approaches targeted the posterior over graph structures alone. This paper proposes JSP-GFN, which uses a single generative flow network to approximate the joint posterior over the graph and its associated parameters.

Sampling proceeds in two phases. First, the model constructs a directed acyclic graph sequentially, adding one edge at a time. Once the structure is complete, it selects parameters for that graph’s conditional probability distributions. This arrangement uses extensions of GFlowNets beyond discrete sample spaces to handle structural and parameter uncertainty within one generative model.

Including parameters directly in the posterior allows more flexibility in the network’s local probability models. The approach can therefore accommodate nonlinear models parameterized by neural networks. Experiments on simulated and real data show an accurate approximation to the joint posterior and favorable comparisons with existing methods, supporting the proposed combination of graph generation and parameter sampling.
summary.tldr: JSP-GFN jointly samples Bayesian-network structures and parameters with one GFlowNet, including networks with nonlinear local models.

title: Joint Bayesian Inference of Graphical Structure and Parameters with a Single Generative Flow Network

abstract: In video analysis, an important challenge is insufficient annotated data due to the rare occurrence of the critical patterns, and we need to provide discriminative frame-level representation with limited annotation in some applications. Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is suitable for this scenario. However, many MIL models paid attention to analyzing the relationships between instance representations and aggregating them, but neglecting the critical information from the MIL problem itself, which causes difficultly achieving ideal instance-level performance compared with the supervised model.To address this issue, we propose the $\textbf{\textit{Regressor-Guided MIL network} (RGMIL)}$, which effectively produces discriminative instance-level representations in a general multi-classification scenario. In the proposed method, we make full use of the $\textit{regressor}$ through our newly introduced $\textit{aggregator}$, $\textbf{\textit{Regressor-Guided Pooling} (RGP)}$. RGP focuses on simulating the correct inference process of humans while facing similar problems without introducing new parameters, and the MIL problem can be accurately described through the critical information from the $\textit{regressor}$ in our method. In experiments, RGP shows dominance on more than 20 MIL benchmark datasets, with the average bag-level classification accuracy close to 1. We also perform a series of comprehensive experiments on the MMNIST dataset. Experimental results illustrate that our $\textit{aggregator}$ outperforms existing methods under different challenging circumstances. Instance-level predictions are even possible under the guidance of RGP information table in a long sequence. RGMIL also presents comparable instance-level performance with S-O-T-A supervised models in complicated applications. Statistical results demonstrate the assumption that a MIL model can compete with a supervised model at the instance level, as long as a structure that accurately describes the MIL problem is provided. The codes are available on $\url{https://github.com/LMBDA-design/RGMIL}$.

paragraphs: Multiple-instance learning is useful when labels are available for groups of examples but detailed labels for individual examples are limited. The paper argues that existing methods emphasize relationships and aggregation while overlooking information inherent in the multiple-instance learning problem.

The pooling mechanism adds no new parameters and is designed to reflect how humans reason through similar inference problems. It aims to improve both group-level decisions and the representations needed for individual predictions.

The results support the possibility of competitive instance-level learning when the model structure accurately represents the multiple-instance problem.
summary.tldr: RGMIL uses regressor-guided pooling to improve multiple-instance learning, achieving strong group-level and instance-level results with limited annotation.

title: RGMIL: Guide Your Multiple-Instance Learning Model with Regressor

abstract: Human activities are goal-oriented and hierarchical, comprising primary goals at the top level, sequences of steps and substeps in the middle, and atomic actions at the lowest level. Recognizing human activities thus requires relating atomic actions and steps to their functional objectives (what the actions contribute to) and modeling their sequential and hierarchical dependencies towards achieving the goals. Current activity recognition research has primarily focused on only the lowest levels of this hierarchy, i.e., atomic or low-level actions, often in trimmed videos with annotations spanning only a few seconds. In this work, we introduce Ego4D Goal-Step, a new set of annotations on the recently released Ego4D with a novel hierarchical taxonomy of goal-oriented activity labels. It provides dense annotations for 48K procedural step segments (430 hours) and high-level goal annotations for 2,807 hours of Ego4D videos. Compared to existing procedural video datasets, it is substantially larger in size, contains hierarchical action labels (goals - steps - substeps), and provides goal-oriented auxiliary information including natural language summary description, step completion status, and step-to-goal relevance information. We take a data-driven approach to build our taxonomy, resulting in dense step annotations that do not suffer from poor label-data alignment issues resulting from a taxonomy defined a priori. Through comprehensive evaluations and analyses, we demonstrate how Ego4D Goal-Step supports exploring various questions in procedural activity understanding, including goal inference, step prediction, hierarchical relation learning, and long-term temporal modeling.

The authors construct the taxonomy from the data to avoid poor alignment between observed activities and labels defined in advance. Their evaluations and analyses show how the annotations support goal inference, step prediction, learning hierarchical relationships, and modeling longer time spans. The contribution is a substantial annotation resource for studying purposeful activity beyond recognizing isolated motions or brief action segments.
summary.tldr: Ego4D Goal-Step adds large-scale hierarchical annotations that connect video actions and procedural steps to their broader goals.

title: Ego4D Goal-Step: Toward Hierarchical Understanding of Procedural Activities

abstract: Probabilistic solvers provide a flexible and efficient framework for simulation, uncertainty quantification, and inference in dynamical systems. However, like standard solvers, they suffer performance penalties for certain stiff systems, where small steps are required not for reasons of numerical accuracy but for the sake of stability. This issue is greatly alleviated in semi-linear problems by the probabilistic exponential integrators developed in this paper. By including the fast, linear dynamics in the prior, we arrive at a class of probabilistic integrators with favorable properties. Namely, they are proven to be L-stable, and in a certain case reduce to a classic exponential integrator---with the added benefit of providing a probabilistic account of the numerical error. The method is also generalized to arbitrary non-linear systems by imposing piece-wise semi-linearity on the prior via Jacobians of the vector field at the previous estimates, resulting in probabilistic exponential Rosenbrock methods. We evaluate the proposed methods on multiple stiff differential equations and demonstrate their improved stability and efficiency over established probabilistic solvers. The present contribution thus expands the range of problems that can be effectively tackled within probabilistic numerics.

paragraphs: Probabilistic differential-equation solvers support simulation while representing uncertainty about numerical error. Stiff systems can make them inefficient because stability forces very small steps even when accuracy alone would permit larger ones. This paper develops probabilistic exponential integrators that substantially alleviate that issue for semilinear problems.

The method incorporates fast linear dynamics directly into the solver's prior. The resulting integrators are proved to be L-stable, a stability property relevant to stiff equations. In a particular case, the method reduces to a classical exponential integrator while retaining a probabilistic description of numerical error.

The authors also extend the approach to general nonlinear systems. They use Jacobians evaluated at previous estimates to impose piecewise semilinear structure on the prior, producing probabilistic exponential Rosenbrock methods. Evaluations on multiple stiff differential equations demonstrate improved stability and efficiency compared with established probabilistic solvers. The contribution makes the prior's treatment of dynamics central to handling stiffness while preserving the uncertainty representation that motivates probabilistic numerical methods.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic exponential integrators encode fast linear dynamics in their prior to improve stability and efficiency while quantifying numerical error.

title: Probabilistic Exponential Integrators

abstract: Discovering causal relationship using multivariate functional data has received a significant amount of attention very recently. In this article, we introduce a functional linear structural equation model for causal structure learning when the underlying graph involving the multivariate functions may have cycles. To enhance interpretability, our model involves a low-dimensional causal embedded space such that all the relevant causal information in the multivariate functional data is preserved in this lower-dimensional subspace. We prove that the proposed model is causally identifiable under standard assumptions that are often made in the causal discovery literature. To carry out inference of our model, we develop a fully Bayesian framework with suitable prior specifications and uncertainty quantification through posterior summaries. We illustrate the superior performance of our method over existing methods in terms of causal graph estimation through extensive simulation studies. We also demonstrate the proposed method using a brain EEG dataset.

paragraphs: This paper studies causal relationships among variables that are themselves functions, such as signals varying over time. Its model allows the causal graph to contain directed cycles, so the structure need not follow a one-way ordering. The authors introduce a functional linear structural equation model to learn these relationships from multivariate functional data.

To make the structure easier to interpret, the model uses a lower-dimensional causal representation. Within the proposed formulation, this smaller space preserves the relevant causal information in the original functions. The authors prove causal identifiability under standard assumptions used in causal discovery. That qualification matters: the result establishes when the model's causal structure can be distinguished, rather than promising causal recovery from arbitrary observations.

Inference uses a fully Bayesian framework, with prior specifications and posterior summaries that quantify uncertainty. Simulation studies report better causal graph estimation than existing methods, and an EEG dataset provides an application. Together, the contributions combine cyclic causal modelling, a compact interpretable representation, and uncertainty-aware estimation.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model learns potentially cyclic causal relationships among functional variables, with identifiability under stated assumptions and posterior uncertainty estimates.

title: Directed Cyclic Graph for Causal Discovery from Multivariate Functional Data

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising performance in knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks that require a compound understanding of knowledge. However, deployment of the LLMs in real-world applications can be challenging due to their high computational requirements and concerns on data privacy.Previous studies have focused on building task-specific small Language Models (LMs) by fine-tuning them with labeled data or distilling LLMs. However, these approaches are ill-suited for knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks due to the limited capacity of small LMs in memorizing the knowledge required.Motivated by our theoretical analysis on memorization, we propose Knowledge-Augmented Reasoning Distillation (KARD), a novel method that fine-tunes small LMs to generate rationales obtained from LLMs with augmented knowledge retrieved from an external knowledge base. Moreover, we further propose a neural reranker to obtain documents relevant to rationale generation. We empirically show that KARD significantly improves the performance of small T5 and GPT models on the challenging knowledge-intensive reasoning datasets, namely MedQA-USMLE, StrategyQA, and OpenbookQA.Notably, our method makes the 250M T5 models achieve superior performance against the fine-tuned 3B models, having 12 times larger parameters, on both MedQA-USMLE and StrategyQA benchmarks.

paragraphs: Small language models can be easier to deploy, but knowledge-intensive reasoning places demands on how much information they can memorize. Simply fine-tuning them on answers or distilling a larger model may leave that bottleneck unresolved. This paper uses an analysis of memorization to motivate combining distilled reasoning with retrieved knowledge.

Knowledge-Augmented Reasoning Distillation, or KARD, trains small models to generate rationales obtained from larger language models while supplying information from an external knowledge base. A neural reranker selects documents relevant to generating those rationales. The approach therefore gives the learner both examples of reasoning and access to supporting knowledge.

Experiments show substantial improvements for small T5 and GPT models on MedQA-USMLE, StrategyQA, and OpenbookQA. On the first two benchmarks, a 250-million-parameter T5 model outperforms fine-tuned models with 3 billion parameters. These results support retrieval-augmented reasoning distillation as an effective way to improve smaller models on the studied knowledge-intensive tasks.
summary.tldr: KARD combines retrieved knowledge with distilled reasoning rationales to substantially improve small language models on knowledge-intensive benchmarks.

title: Knowledge-Augmented Reasoning Distillation for Small Language Models in Knowledge-Intensive Tasks

abstract: We consider the problem of traffic accident analysis on a road network based on road network connections and traffic volume. Previous works have designed various deep-learning methods using historical records to predict traffic accident occurrences. However, there is a lack of consensus on how accurate existing methods are, and a fundamental issue is the lack of public accident datasets for comprehensive evaluations. This paper constructs a large-scale, unified dataset of traffic accident records from official reports of various states in the US, totaling 9 million records, accompanied by road networks and traffic volume reports. Using this new dataset, we evaluate existing deep-learning methods for predicting the occurrence of accidents on road networks. Our main finding is that graph neural networks such as GraphSAGE can accurately predict the number of accidents on roads with less than 22% mean absolute error (relative to the actual count) and whether an accident will occur or not with over 87% AUROC, averaged over states. We achieve these results by using multitask learning to account for cross-state variabilities (e.g., availability of accident labels) and transfer learning to combine traffic volume with accident prediction. Ablation studies highlight the importance of road graph-structural features, amongst other features. Lastly, we discuss the implications of the analysis and develop a package for easily using our new dataset.

The paper addresses a shortage of public evaluation data by assembling a unified dataset containing nine million accident records from official reports across US states, accompanied by road networks and traffic-volume reports.

Using this dataset, the authors evaluate deep-learning methods for predicting accident counts and whether accidents occur. Their approach uses multitask learning to handle differences across states, including differences in label availability. Transfer learning connects traffic-volume modeling with accident prediction, allowing those related sources of information to contribute to the task.

These are distinct measures for count prediction and occurrence discrimination. Ablation studies identify road graph structure as an important input alongside other features. The dataset and accompanying package provide a common basis for evaluating how road connectivity and traffic information support accident modeling.
summary.tldr: A unified nine-million-record accident dataset supports evaluations showing strong graph-neural-network results for road accident counts and occurrence.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Road Safety Modeling: Datasets and Evaluations for Accident Analysis

abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved significant success in the last decades, but they are not well-calibrated and often produce unreliable predictions. A large number of literature relies on uncertainty quantification to evaluate the reliability of a learning model, which is particularly important for applications of out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and misclassification detection. We are interested in uncertainty quantification for interdependent node-level classification. We start our analysis based on graph posterior networks (GPNs) that optimize the uncertainty cross-entropy (UCE)-based loss function. We describe the theoretical limitations of the widely-used UCE loss. To alleviate the identified drawbacks, we propose a distance-based regularization that encourages clustered OOD nodes to remain clustered in the latent space. We conduct extensive comparison experiments on eight standard datasets and demonstrate that the proposed regularization outperforms the state-of-the-art in both OOD detection and misclassification detection.

paragraphs: A node classifier must assign labels to interconnected graph nodes, but its predictions also need a useful indication of reliability. This paper focuses on detecting unfamiliar, out-of-distribution nodes and identifying incorrect classifications. These tasks depend on uncertainty estimates that distinguish questionable predictions from trustworthy ones, beyond simply producing a class label.

The authors begin with graph posterior networks trained using uncertainty cross-entropy. They analyze theoretical limitations of this widely used loss and introduce a distance-based regularizer to alleviate the identified problems. The regularizer encourages out-of-distribution nodes that form clusters to remain grouped in the learned latent representation. It therefore constrains the geometry of the representation used for uncertainty estimation.

Experiments on eight standard datasets show that the proposed regularization outperforms state-of-the-art methods for both out-of-distribution detection and misclassification detection. The contribution connects a theoretical critique of the training objective with a targeted change to representation learning. The reported gains indicate that preserving relevant clustering structure can help the studied graph models produce more useful reliability signals.
summary.tldr: Distance-based regularization improves graph-node uncertainty estimates by encouraging clustered out-of-distribution nodes to stay clustered in latent space.

title: Improvements on Uncertainty Quantification for Node Classification via Distance Based Regularization

abstract: Structural causal models (SCMs) are a powerful tool for understanding the complex causal relationships that underlie many real-world systems. As these systems grow in size, the number of variables and complexity of interactions between them does, too. Thus, becoming convoluted and difficult to analyze. This is particularly true in the context of machine learning and artificial intelligence, where an ever increasing amount of data demands for new methods to simplify and compress large scale SCM. While methods for marginalizing and abstracting SCM already exist today, they may destroy the causality of the marginalized model. To alleviate this, we introduce the concept of consolidating causal mechanisms to transform large-scale SCM while preserving consistent interventional behaviour. We show consolidation is a powerful method for simplifying SCM, discuss reduction of computational complexity and give a perspective on generalizing abilities of consolidated SCM.
originalAbstract: Structural causal models (SCMs) are a powerful tool for understanding the complex causal relationships that underlie many real-world systems. As these systems grow in size, the number of variables and complexity of interactions between them does, too. Thus, becoming convoluted and difficult to analyze. This is particularly true in the context of machine learning and artificial intelligence, where an ever increasing amount of data demands for new methods to simplify and compress large scale SCM. While methods for marginalizing and abstracting SCM already exist today, they may destroy the causality of the marginalized model. To alleviate this, we introduce the concept of consolidating causal mechanisms to transform large-scale SCM while preserving consistent interventional behaviour. We show consolidation is a powerful method for simplifying SCM, discuss reduction of computational complexity and give a perspective on generalizing abilities of consolidated SCM.

paragraphs: Structural causal models describe systems through variables and the mechanisms connecting them. As a system grows, those relationships can become difficult to analyze or compute with. This paper addresses how to simplify such models while retaining their causal meaning, especially their behavior when an intervention changes part of the system.

Existing marginalization and abstraction methods can damage the causal behavior of the reduced model. The authors introduce consolidation of causal mechanisms as an alternative transformation. Its defining aim is consistent interventional behavior: simplifying the representation should preserve how the model responds to the interventions covered by the transformation.

The paper shows consolidation to be a useful method for simplifying structural causal models and discusses reductions in computational complexity. It also offers a perspective on how consolidated models might generalize. The central contribution is a way to reason about compression at the level of causal mechanisms, making intervention consistency part of the simplification objective. The discussion of generalization is presented as a perspective, rather than a blanket guarantee for every reduced model.
summary.tldr: Consolidating causal mechanisms simplifies structural causal models while preserving consistent interventional behavior.

title: Do Not Marginalize Mechanisms, Rather Consolidate!

abstract: Recently, open-domain text-to-video (T2V) generation models have made remarkable progress. However, the promising results are mainly shown by the qualitative cases of generated videos, while the quantitative evaluation of T2V models still faces two critical problems. Firstly, existing studies lack fine-grained evaluation of T2V models on different categories of text prompts. Although some benchmarks have categorized the prompts, their categorization either only focuses on a single aspect or fails to consider the temporal information in video generation. Secondly, it is unclear whether the automatic evaluation metrics are consistent with human standards. To address these problems, we propose **FETV**, a benchmark for **F**ine-grained **E**valuation of **T**ext-to-**V**ideo generation. FETV is multi-aspect, categorizing the prompts based on three orthogonal aspects: the major content, the attributes to control and the prompt complexity. FETV is also temporal-aware, which introduces several temporal categories tailored for video generation. Based on FETV, we conduct comprehensive manual evaluations of four representative T2V models, revealing their pros and cons on different categories of prompts from different aspects. We also extend FETV as a testbed to evaluate the reliability of automatic T2V metrics. The multi-aspect categorization of FETV enables fine-grained analysis of the metrics' reliability in different scenarios. We find that existing automatic metrics (e.g., CLIPScore and FVD) correlate poorly with human evaluation. To address this problem, we explore several solutions to improve CLIPScore and FVD, and develop two automatic metrics that exhibit significant higher correlation with humans than existing metrics. Benchmark page: https://github.com/llyx97/FETV.

abstract: Given a graph $G$, a community structure $\mathcal{C}$, and a budget $k$, the fair influence maximization problem aims to select a seed set $S$ ($|S|\leq k$) that maximizes the influence spread while narrowing the influence gap between different communities. While various fairness notions exist, the welfare fairness notion, which balances fairness level and influence spread, has shown promising effectiveness. However, the lack of efficient algorithms for optimizing the welfare fairness objective function restricts its application to small-scale networks with only a few hundred nodes. In this paper, we adopt the objective function of welfare fairness to maximize the exponentially weighted summation over the influenced fraction of all communities. We first introduce an unbiased estimator for the fractional power of the arithmetic mean. Then, by adapting the reverse influence sampling (RIS) approach, we convert the optimization problem to a weighted maximum coverage problem. We also analyze the number of reverse reachable sets needed to approximate the fair influence at a high probability. Further, we present an efficient algorithm that guarantees $1-1/e - \varepsilon$ approximation.

paragraphs: Influence maximization chooses a limited set of starting nodes to spread influence through a network. A fairness-aware version also considers disparities between communities. This paper focuses on welfare fairness, an objective that balances influence spread and fairness, but whose computational cost has previously restricted its use to networks with only a few hundred nodes.

The authors optimize an exponentially weighted sum involving the influenced fraction of each community. Their approach begins with an unbiased estimator for a fractional power of an arithmetic mean. They then adapt reverse influence sampling to transform the original optimization into a weighted maximum coverage problem, creating a route to efficient approximation.

The analysis determines how many reverse reachable sets are needed to approximate fair influence with high probability. The resulting algorithm has a 1 − 1/e − epsilon approximation guarantee. The contribution makes the chosen welfare objective more computationally accessible while providing a formal quality bound; the fairness target remains the specific balance encoded by that objective.
summary.tldr: A sampling-based reduction yields an efficient approximation algorithm for influence maximization under a welfare-fairness objective.

title: Scalable Fair Influence Maximization

abstract: Learning binary classifiers from positive and unlabeled data (PUL) is vital in many real-world applications, especially when verifying negative examples is difficult. Despite the impressive empirical performance of recent PUL methods, challenges like accumulated errors and increased estimation bias persist due to the absence of negative labels. In this paper, we unveil an intriguing yet long-overlooked observation in PUL: \textit{resampling the positive data in each training iteration to ensure a balanced distribution between positive and unlabeled examples results in strong early-stage performance. Furthermore, predictive trends for positive and negative classes display distinctly different patterns.} Specifically, the scores (output probability) of unlabeled negative examples consistently decrease, while those of unlabeled positive examples show largely chaotic trends. Instead of focusing on classification within individual time frames, we innovatively adopt a holistic approach, interpreting the scores of each example as a temporal point process (TPP). This reformulates the core problem of PUL as recognizing trends in these scores. We then propose a novel TPP-inspired measure for trend detection and prove its asymptotic unbiasedness in predicting changes. Notably, our method accomplishes PUL without requiring additional parameter tuning or prior assumptions, offering an alternative perspective for tackling this problem. Extensive experiments verify the superiority of our method, particularly in a highly imbalanced real-world setting, where it achieves improvements of up to $11.3\%$ in key metrics.

paragraphs: Learning from positive and unlabeled data means training a binary classifier without verified negative examples. This can lead to accumulating mistakes and biased estimates. The authors observe that resampling positive examples to balance them with unlabeled examples during each training iteration produces strong performance early in training.

They also find different prediction patterns over time: scores for unlabeled negative examples tend to decrease consistently, whereas scores for unlabeled positive examples fluctuate chaotically. Their method uses this history rather than relying only on an example's prediction at a particular moment. It treats the evolving scores as a temporal point process and introduces a measure for detecting their trends.

The paper proves asymptotic unbiasedness for this measure's prediction of changes and reports that the method requires no additional parameter tuning or prior assumptions. Extensive experiments support its effectiveness, with improvements of up to 11.3% in key metrics in a highly imbalanced real-world setting. The central finding is that training-time prediction trajectories provide useful evidence when negative labels are unavailable.
summary.tldr: Tracking prediction trends across training helps distinguish positive from negative examples when only positive labels are available.

title: Beyond Myopia: Learning from Positive and Unlabeled Data through Holistic Predictive Trends

abstract: A major challenge of reinforcement learning (RL) in real-world applications is the variation between environments, tasks or clients. Meta-RL (MRL) addresses this issue by learning a meta-policy that adapts to new tasks. Standard MRL methods optimize the average return over tasks, but often suffer from poor results in tasks of high risk or difficulty. This limits system reliability since test tasks are not known in advance. In this work, we define a robust MRL objective with a controlled robustness level. Optimization of analogous robust objectives in RL is known to lead to both **biased gradients** and **data inefficiency**. We prove that the gradient bias disappears in our proposed MRL framework. The data inefficiency is addressed via the novel Robust Meta RL algorithm (RoML). RoML is a meta-algorithm that generates a robust version of any given MRL algorithm, by identifying and over-sampling harder tasks throughout training. We demonstrate that RoML achieves robust returns on multiple navigation and continuous control benchmarks.

paragraphs: Meta reinforcement learning trains a policy that can adapt to new tasks, but optimizing average return can leave difficult or high-risk tasks poorly served. Because deployment tasks are not known beforehand, strong average performance may provide an incomplete picture of reliability. This paper introduces a robust meta-learning objective with an adjustable robustness level.

Robust objectives in reinforcement learning can create biased gradient estimates and use training data inefficiently. The authors prove that the gradient bias disappears within their proposed meta reinforcement learning framework. To address data inefficiency, they introduce RoML, a meta-algorithm that identifies harder tasks and samples them more often throughout training.

RoML is designed to produce a robust version of any given meta reinforcement learning algorithm. Experiments on navigation and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate robust returns. The approach connects the training objective with the allocation of experience: prioritizing harder tasks supplies more learning opportunities where an average-focused objective may otherwise leave weaknesses, while the theoretical result addresses the gradient bias associated with analogous robust objectives.
summary.tldr: RoML makes meta reinforcement learning more robust by identifying and oversampling harder tasks during training.

title: Train Hard, Fight Easy: Robust Meta Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper investigates the asymptotic distribution of the maximum-likelihood estimate (MLE) in multinomial logistic models in the high-dimensional regime where dimension and sample size are of the same order. While classical large-sample theory provides asymptotic normality of the MLE under certain conditions, such classical results are expected to fail in high-dimensions as documented for the binary logistic case in the seminal work of Sur and Candès [2019]. We address this issue in classification problems with 3 or more classes, by developing asymptotic normality and asymptotic chi-square results for the multinomial logistic MLE (also known as cross-entropy minimizer) on null covariates. Our theory leads to a new methodology to test the significance of a given feature. Extensive simulation studies on synthetic data corroborate these asymptotic results and confirm the validity of proposed p-values for testing the significance of a given feature.

paragraphs: The paper studies statistical inference for multinomial logistic regression when the number of features and the number of samples are of comparable size. Classical large-sample results are expected to fail in this high-dimensional setting, as previously documented for binary logistic regression. The authors address classification problems with three or more classes.

Their analysis concerns the maximum-likelihood estimator, which also minimizes cross-entropy, on null covariates: features considered under a no-effect hypothesis. They establish asymptotic normality and chi-square results for this setting. These distributions supply a theoretical basis for assessing whether an observed feature estimate provides evidence of significance when dimensionality grows alongside sample size.

The resulting methodology produces feature-significance tests and associated p-values. Extensive experiments on synthetic data corroborate the asymptotic theory and the validity of the proposed p-values. The contribution is specifically about inference on null covariates in high-dimensional multiclass models, extending the statistical analysis beyond the binary case while retaining that stated scope for its guarantees.
summary.tldr: New asymptotic results enable feature-significance testing for null covariates in high-dimensional multinomial logistic regression.

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: Asymptotic Normality on Null Covariates in High-Dimensions

abstract: Preserving training dynamics across batch sizes is an important tool for practical machine learning as it enables the trade-off between batch size and wall-clock time. This trade-off is typically enabled by a scaling rule, for example, in stochastic gradient descent, one should scale the learning rate linearly with the batch size. Another important machine learning tool is the model EMA, a functional copy of a target model, whose parameters move towards those of its target model according to an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) at a rate parameterized by a momentum hyperparameter. This model EMA can improve the robustness and generalization of supervised learning, stabilize pseudo-labeling, and provide a learning signal for Self-Supervised Learning (SSL). Prior works have not considered the optimization of the model EMA when performing scaling, leading to different training dynamics across batch sizes and lower model performance. In this work, we provide a scaling rule for optimization in the presence of a model EMA and demonstrate the rule's validity across a range of architectures, optimizers, and data modalities. We also show the rule's validity where the model EMA contributes to the optimization of the target model, enabling us to train EMA-based pseudo-labeling and SSL methods at small and large batch sizes. For SSL, we enable training of BYOL up to batch size 24,576 without sacrificing performance, a 6$\times$ wall-clock time reduction under idealized hardware settings.

paragraphs: Changing training batch size can reduce elapsed training time, but preserving learning behavior requires adjusting the optimization process. This paper examines a component that earlier scaling approaches overlooked: the exponential moving average of model parameters. This moving-average model follows the target model at a rate controlled by a momentum parameter and can influence both predictions and learning.

The authors provide a scaling rule for optimization involving a model EMA. They validate it across multiple architectures, optimizers, and data modalities. They also examine settings where the moving-average model helps train the target model, including pseudo-labeling and self-supervised learning. They associate this with a sixfold wall-clock reduction under idealized hardware conditions. That qualification matters: the result demonstrates the scaling opportunity without promising the same speedup on every hardware setup.
summary.tldr: An EMA-aware scaling rule preserves training behavior across batch sizes and enables larger-batch self-supervised learning without reported performance loss.

title: How to Scale Your EMA

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) encompasses diverse paradigms, including model-based RL, policy-based RL, and value-based RL, each tailored to approximate the model, optimal policy, and optimal value function, respectively. This work investigates the potential hierarchy of representation complexity among these RL paradigms. By utilizing computational complexity measures, including time complexity and circuit complexity, we theoretically unveil a potential representation complexity hierarchy within RL. We find that representing the model emerges as the easiest task, followed by the optimal policy, while representing the optimal value function presents the most intricate challenge. Additionally, we reaffirm this hierarchy from the perspective of the expressiveness of Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), which align more closely with practical deep RL and contribute to a completely new perspective in theoretical studying representation complexity in RL. Finally, we conduct deep RL experiments to validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning methods can focus on representing the environment, a policy for choosing actions, or a value function describing outcomes. This paper asks whether these targets differ in how difficult they are to represent. That question provides a way to compare major reinforcement learning paradigms through the complexity of what each tries to approximate.

Using time complexity and circuit complexity, the authors identify a potential hierarchy: the environment model is easiest to represent, the optimal policy comes next, and the optimal value function is the most intricate. They also examine the expressive power of multilayer perceptrons and find support for the same ordering, bringing the analysis closer to neural networks used in deep reinforcement learning.

Deep reinforcement learning experiments provide further validation of the theoretical findings. The proposed hierarchy offers a perspective on why different approximation targets can place different demands on a representation. Its scope is representation complexity; the stated findings do not establish that one reinforcement learning paradigm will universally train faster or achieve better decisions in every environment.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies a potential representation-complexity hierarchy from environment models to optimal policies to optimal value functions.

title: Rethinking Model-based, Policy-based, and Value-based Reinforcement Learning via the Lens of Representation Complexity

abstract: We investigate the problem of universal online learning with gradient-variation regret. Universal online learning aims to achieve regret guarantees without prior knowledge of the curvature of the online functions. Moreover, we study the problem-dependent gradient-variation regret as it plays a crucial role in bridging stochastic and adversarial optimization as well as game theory. In this work, we design a universal approach with the *optimal* gradient-variation regret simultaneously for strongly convex, exp-concave, and convex functions, thus addressing an open problem highlighted by [Yan et al. [2023]](https://openreview.net/forum?id=AA1xrgAP5z). Our approach is *simple* since it is algorithmically efficient-to-implement with a two-layer online ensemble structure and only $1$ gradient query per round, and theoretically easy-to-analyze with a novel and alternative analysis to the gradient-variation regret. Concretely, previous works on gradient variations require controlling the algorithmic stability, which is challenging and leads to sub-optimal regret and less efficient algorithm design. Our analysis overcomes this issue by using a Bregman divergence negative term from linearization and a useful smoothness property.

paragraphs: Online learning involves making decisions as functions arrive over time, with regret measuring the accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparison decision. This paper seeks guarantees that adapt to how gradients vary, without requiring advance knowledge of the functions’ curvature. Such guarantees help connect settings ranging from stochastic optimization to adversarial learning and games.

The proposed method uses an ensemble organized into two layers and needs only one gradient query per round. It simultaneously achieves optimal gradient-variation regret for strongly convex, exp-concave, and convex functions. This combination addresses the stated open problem while keeping the algorithm comparatively straightforward to implement.

A central contribution is the proof strategy. Earlier analyses needed to control algorithmic stability, a difficult requirement associated with weaker regret guarantees and less efficient designs. The authors instead exploit a negative Bregman-divergence term arising from linearization, together with a smoothness property. This alternative analysis supports the optimal guarantees and explains how a relatively simple ensemble can adapt across the three curvature classes.
summary.tldr: A two-layer online ensemble achieves optimal gradient-variation regret across three curvature classes using one gradient query per round.

title: A Simple and Optimal Approach for Universal Online Learning with Gradient Variations

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models benefit artists with high-quality image generation. Yet their stochastic nature hinders artists from creating consistent images of the same subject. Existing methods try to tackle this challenge and generate consistent content in various ways. However, they either depend on external restricted data or require expensive tuning of the diffusion model. For this issue, we propose a novel one-shot tuning paradigm, termed OneActor. It efficiently performs consistent subject generation solely driven by prompts via a learned semantic guidance to bypass the laborious backbone tuning. We lead the way to formalize the objective of consistent subject generation from a clustering perspective, and thus design a cluster-conditioned model. To mitigate the overfitting challenge shared by one-shot tuning pipelines, we augment the tuning with auxiliary samples and devise two inference strategies: semantic interpolation and cluster guidance. These techniques are later verified to significantly improve the generation quality. Comprehensive experiments show that our method outperforms a variety of baselines with satisfactory subject consistency, superior prompt conformity as well as high image quality. Our method is capable of multi-subject generation and compatible with popular diffusion extensions. Besides, we achieve a $4\times$ faster tuning speed than tuning-based baselines and, if desired, avoid increasing the inference time. Furthermore, our method can be naturally utilized to pre-train a consistent subject generation network from scratch, which will implement this research task into more practical applications. (Project page: https://johnneywang.github.io/OneActor-webpage/)

OneActor addresses this with a prompt-driven, one-shot tuning approach. It learns semantic guidance for consistent subject generation while avoiding expensive tuning of the diffusion backbone.

summary.tldr: OneActor learns cluster-conditioned semantic guidance for consistent subject generation, reporting strong image quality and fourfold faster tuning than tuning-based baselines.

abstract: We present Preference Flow Matching (PFM), a new framework for preference alignment that streamlines the integration of preferences into an arbitrary class of pre-trained models. Existing alignment methods require fine-tuning pre-trained models, which presents challenges such as scalability, inefficiency, and the need for model modifications, especially with black-box APIs like GPT-4. In contrast, PFM utilizes flow matching techniques to directly learn from preference data, thereby reducing the dependency on extensive fine-tuning of pre-trained models. By leveraging flow-based models, PFM transforms less preferred data into preferred outcomes, and effectively aligns model outputs with human preferences without relying on explicit or implicit reward function estimation, thus avoiding common issues like overfitting in reward models. We provide theoretical insights that support our method’s alignment with standard preference alignment objectives. Experimental results indicate the practical effectiveness of our method, offering a new direction in aligning a pre-trained model to preference. Our code is available at https://github.com/jadehaus/preference-flow-matching.

Existing alignment methods require fine-tuning pre-trained models, which presents challenges such as scalability, inefficiency, and the need for model modifications, especially with black-box APIs like GPT-4. In contrast, PFM utilizes flow matching techniques to directly learn from preference data, thereby reducing the dependency on extensive fine-tuning of pre-trained models. By leveraging flow-based models, PFM transforms less preferred data into preferred outcomes, and effectively aligns model outputs with human preferences without relying on explicit or implicit reward function estimation, thus avoiding common issues like overfitting in reward models. We provide theoretical insights that support our method’s alignment with standard preference alignment objectives. Experimental results indicate the practical effectiveness of our method, offering a new direction in aligning a pre-trained model to preference. Our code is available at https://github.com/jadehaus/preference-flow-matching.

paragraphs: Aligning a pretrained model with human preferences commonly involves fine-tuning that model. This can be cumbersome when modifying the model is expensive or access is limited to a black-box API. Preference Flow Matching proposes learning directly from preference data through a flow-based transformation, reducing reliance on extensive fine-tuning of the underlying model.

The framework learns to transform less preferred data into preferred outcomes. It does so without estimating an explicit or implicit reward function. This removes the need for a reward model whose fitting could introduce problems such as reward-model overfitting. The alignment mechanism is therefore organized around learning a transformation between preference levels rather than learning a reward estimate to optimize.

The authors provide theoretical insights connecting the method with standard preference-alignment objectives, alongside experiments indicating practical effectiveness. The framework is presented as applicable to an arbitrary class of pretrained models. Its central significance is an alternative interface for alignment: preferences guide a learned flow that changes outcomes, making direct modification of the original model less central to the process.
summary.tldr: Preference Flow Matching learns transformations from less preferred to preferred outcomes without estimating reward functions or relying on extensive base-model fine-tuning.

title: Preference Alignment with Flow Matching

abstract: We introduce a novel implicit field representation tailored for multi-person interaction geometry in 3D spaces, capable of simultaneously reconstructing occupancy, instance identification (ID) tags, and contact fields. Volumetric representation of interacting human bodies presents significant challenges, including inaccurately captured geometries, varying degrees of occlusion, and data scarcity. Existing multi-view methods, which either reconstruct each subject in isolation or merge nearby 3D surfaces into a single unified mesh, often fail to capture the intricate geometry between interacting bodies and exploit on datasets with many views and a small group of people for training. Our approach utilizes an implicit representation for interaction geometry contextualized by a multi-view local-global feature module. This module adeptly aggregates both local and global information from individual views and interacting groups, enabling precise modeling of close physical interactions through dense point retrieval in small areas, supported by the implicit fields. Furthermore, we develop a synthetic dataset encompassing diverse multi-person interaction scenarios to enhance the robustness of our geometry estimation. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method to accurately reconstruct human geometries and ID tags within three-dimensional spaces, outperforming conventional multi-view techniques. Notably, our method facilitates unsupervised estimation of contact points without the need for specific training data on contact supervision.
