paragraphs: Pseudo-labels provide supervision when segmentation annotations are scarce, but incorrect one-hot labels can be reinforced during training. ECOCSeg replaces that all-or-nothing class representation with error-correcting output codes, allowing each class to be expressed through multiple attributes or bits.

The classifier can tolerate some incorrect bits rather than treating any error as a completely wrong class signal. A bit-level denoising mechanism improves the pseudo-labels used for unlabeled images, providing more stable training targets.

The method integrates with existing architectures and improves multiple unsupervised-domain-adaptation and semisupervised benchmarks. Its contribution is to modify how uncertainty and error enter the supervision itself. A partially inaccurate code can still retain useful class information, giving the learning process a way to recover from imperfect predictions instead of repeatedly amplifying one mistaken categorical assignment.
summary.tldr: ECOCSeg uses error-correcting class codes and bit-level denoising to stabilize segmentation pseudo-labels.

title: Towards Robust Pseudo-Label Learning in Semantic Segmentation: An Encoding Perspective

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has proven to be an effective post-training strategy for enhancing reasoning in vision–language models (VLMs). Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a recent prominent method that encourages models to generate complete reasoning traces before answering, leading to increased token usage and computational cost. Inspired by the human-like thinking process—where people skip reasoning for easy questions but think carefully when needed—we explore how to enable VLMs to first decide *when reasoning is necessary*. To realize this, we propose \ours, a two-stage training strategy: **(i)** a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage with a simple yet effective “**thought dropout**” operation, where reasoning traces are randomly replaced with empty thoughts. This introduces a think-or-not format that serves as a cold start for selective reasoning; **(ii)** a GRPO stage that enables the model to freely explore when to think or not, while maximizing task-aware outcome rewards. Experimental results show that \ours can *reduce the completion length by up to **90%** compared to vanilla GRPO, without sacrificing performance or even improving it*. Further evaluations across LLM (GSM8K), VLM (CLEVR, Super-CLEVR, GeoQA), and Agentic (AITZ) tasks—covering a range of reasoning difficulties under both 3B and 7B models—consistently reveal that the \textit{model progressively learns to bypass unnecessary reasoning steps as training advances}. These findings shed light on the path toward human-like reasoning patterns in RL approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/kokolerk/TON.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can improve vision-language reasoning while encouraging models to produce lengthy reasoning traces for every answer. This paper studies whether a model can learn when such a trace is useful. The aim is selective reasoning: spending output tokens on thought when needed and bypassing unnecessary reasoning on easier questions.

The training strategy has two stages. During supervised fine-tuning, thought dropout randomly replaces reasoning traces with empty thoughts, introducing a format that permits either reasoning or a direct answer. Group Relative Policy Optimization then allows the model to explore both choices while optimizing task-aware outcome rewards. The first stage provides a starting behavior; the second learns how to use it.

Experiments report completion-length reductions of up to 90% relative to vanilla GRPO, with performance maintained or sometimes improved. Evaluations span language, vision-language, and agentic tasks using models with three billion and seven billion parameters. Across these settings, the models increasingly bypass unnecessary reasoning as training progresses, supporting learned control over when to generate explicit thought.
summary.tldr: Thought dropout followed by reinforcement learning teaches selective reasoning, reducing completion length by up to 90% without sacrificing reported task performance.

title: Think or Not? Selective Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Language Models

abstract: Understanding and explaining the behavior of machine learning models is essential for building transparent and trustworthy AI systems. We introduce DEXTER, a data-free framework that employs diffusion models and large language models to generate global, textual explanations of visual classifiers. DEXTER operates by optimizing text prompts to synthesize class-conditional images that strongly activate a target classifier. These synthetic samples are then used to elicit detailed natural language reports that describe class-specific decision patterns and biases. Unlike prior work, DEXTER enables natural language explanation about a classifier's decision process without access to training data or ground-truth labels. We demonstrate DEXTER's flexibility across three tasks—activation maximization, slice discovery and debiasing, and bias explanation—each illustrating its ability to uncover the internal mechanisms of visual classifiers. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations, including a user study, show that DEXTER produces accurate, interpretable outputs. Experiments on ImageNet, Waterbirds, CelebA, and FairFaces confirm that DEXTER outperforms existing approaches in global model explanation and class-level bias reporting. Code is available at https://github.com/perceivelab/dexter.

paragraphs: DEXTER aims to explain the broader behavior of visual classifiers in natural language. Its explanations describe class-specific decision patterns and biases rather than focusing only on an individual prediction. The framework operates without access to the classifier’s training data or ground-truth labels, making that access requirement central to its contribution.

The method optimizes text prompts so that a diffusion model generates images that strongly activate a target classifier for particular classes. Those synthetic images provide material for a large language model to produce detailed reports. This connects what the classifier responds to with descriptions that people can inspect and interpret.

The authors demonstrate the framework through activation maximization, slice discovery and debiasing, and bias explanation. Quantitative evaluations, qualitative assessments, and a user study support the accuracy and interpretability of its outputs. Experiments involving ImageNet, Waterbirds, CelebA, and FairFaces report improvements over existing approaches in global explanations and class-level bias reporting, supporting the usefulness of synthetic probing for these explanation tasks.
summary.tldr: DEXTER uses generated images and language models to explain visual classifiers’ class-level behavior without training data or ground-truth labels.

title: DEXTER: Diffusion-Guided EXplanations with TExtual Reasoning for Vision Models

abstract: We address the challenge of Small Object Image Retrieval (SoIR), where the goal is to retrieve images containing a specific small object, in a cluttered scene. The key challenge in this setting is constructing a single image descriptor, for scalable and efficient search, that effectively represents all objects in the image. In this paper, we first analyze the limitations of existing methods on this challenging task and then introduce new benchmarks to support SoIR evaluation. Next, we introduce \ours (\oursMI), a novel retrieval framework which incorporates a dedicated multi-object pre-training phase. This is followed by a refinement process that leverages attention-based feature extraction with object masks, integrating them into a single unified image descriptor. Our \oursMI approach significantly outperforms existing retrieval methods and strong baselines, achieving notable improvements in both zero-shot and lightweight multi-object fine-tuning. We hope this work will pave the way and inspire further research to enhance retrieval performance for this highly practical task.

paragraphs: Small Object Image Retrieval asks a search system to find images containing a particular small object within a cluttered scene. The difficulty is representing all relevant objects using a single descriptor for each image. That compact representation supports efficient search, but it must still preserve information about objects occupying only a small part of the scene.

The paper first examines weaknesses in existing retrieval methods and introduces benchmarks for this task. Its proposed framework uses a dedicated multi-object pretraining stage, followed by refinement with attention-based feature extraction and object masks. Information from multiple objects is integrated into one unified descriptor, keeping the representation suited to scalable image retrieval.

The authors report substantial improvements over existing retrieval methods and strong baselines in both zero-shot evaluation and lightweight multi-object fine-tuning. These results suggest that explicitly preparing a representation to capture multiple objects helps small objects remain useful for retrieval. The work contributes both an evaluation setting for this search problem and a training-and-refinement approach designed around its central representation challenge.
summary.tldr: Multi-object pretraining and mask-guided attention improve retrieval of images containing small objects while retaining one descriptor per image.

title: Find your Needle: Small Object Image Retrieval via Multi-Object Attention Optimization

abstract: The ability of robots to interpret human instructions and execute manipulation tasks necessitates the availability of task-relevant tabletop scenes for training. However, traditional methods for creating these scenes rely on time-consuming manual layout design or purely randomized layouts, which are limited in terms of plausibility or alignment with the tasks. In this paper, we formulate a novel task, namely task-oriented tabletop scene generation, which poses significant challenges due to the substantial gap between high-level task instructions and the tabletop scenes. To support research on such a challenging task, we introduce \textbf{MesaTask-10K}, a large-scale dataset comprising approximately 10,700 synthetic tabletop scenes with \emph{manually crafted layouts} that ensure realistic layouts and intricate inter-object relations. To bridge the gap between tasks and scenes, we propose a \textbf{Spatial Reasoning Chain} that decomposes the generation process into object inference, spatial interrelation reasoning, and scene graph construction for the final 3D layout. We present \textbf{MesaTask}, an LLM-based framework that utilizes this reasoning chain and is further enhanced with DPO algorithms to generate physically plausible tabletop scenes that align well with given task descriptions. Exhaustive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of MesaTask compared to baselines in generating task-conforming tabletop scenes with realistic layouts.

paragraphs: MesaTask addresses the creation of tabletop scenes suited to particular robot manipulation instructions. A useful training scene must contain appropriate objects and arrange them in ways that fit the task. Manual layout construction is slow, while purely random placement can produce scenes that are implausible or poorly connected to the requested activity.

The paper introduces MesaTask-10K, a dataset of approximately 10,700 synthetic scenes with manually crafted layouts and detailed relations among objects. It also proposes a Spatial Reasoning Chain that breaks scene generation into three stages: inferring the required objects, reasoning about their spatial relationships, and constructing a scene graph for the final three-dimensional layout.

MesaTask uses a language model to follow this chain and incorporates direct preference optimization to improve generation. Experiments report better task conformity and layout realism than the evaluated baselines. The contribution connects high-level instructions to explicit spatial structure, making object relationships part of the generation process. The dataset supplies examples of those relationships, while the framework uses structured reasoning to produce task-relevant scenes.
summary.tldr: MesaTask combines a curated tabletop dataset with staged spatial reasoning to generate realistic scenes aligned with robot-task descriptions.

title: MesaTask: Towards Task-Driven Tabletop Scene Generation via 3D Spatial Reasoning

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become popular in machine learning, boosting performance by partitioning tasks across multiple experts. However, the need for several experts often results in high computational costs, limiting their application on resource-constrained devices with stringent real-time requirements, such as cochlear implants (CIs). We introduce the Omni-Expert (OE) – a simple and efficient solution that leverages feature transformations to achieve the 'divide-and-conquer' functionality of a full MoE ensemble in a single expert model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the OE using phoneme-specific time-frequency masking for speech dereverberation in a CI. Empirical results show that the OE delivers statistically significant improvements in objective intelligibility measures of CI vocoded speech at different levels of reverberation across various speech datasets at a much reduced computational cost relative to a counterpart MoE.

paragraphs: The Omni-Expert aims to obtain the task-specialization benefits of a mixture of experts using a single expert model. Multiple experts can improve performance by dividing work among specialized components, but their computational demands can be difficult to accommodate in devices with strict resource and timing requirements. Cochlear implants provide the paper's motivating application.

The proposed method uses feature transformations to provide a divide-and-conquer capability within one model. The authors demonstrate it through phoneme-specific time-frequency masking for speech dereverberation in a cochlear implant setting. This task connects the approach to speech processing where reducing reverberation and keeping computation manageable are both relevant goals.

Across multiple speech datasets and reverberation levels, the Omni-Expert yields statistically significant improvements in objective intelligibility measures for cochlear-implant-vocoded speech. It also has substantially lower computational cost than a corresponding mixture-of-experts model. The evidence supports feature transformation as an efficient route to specialization in this application. The reported intelligibility findings concern objective measures of the processed speech.
summary.tldr: The Omni-Expert uses feature transformations to deliver efficient specialization in a single model for cochlear-implant speech dereverberation.

title: The Omni-Expert: A Computationally Efficient Approach to Achieve a Mixture of Experts in a Single Expert Model

abstract: Robust verbal confidence generated by large language models (LLMs) is crucial for the deployment of LLMs to help ensure transparency, trust, and safety in many applications, including those involving human-AI interactions. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive study on the robustness of verbal confidence under adversarial attacks. We introduce attack frameworks targeting verbal confidence scores through both perturbation and jailbreak-based methods, and demonstrate that these attacks can significantly impair verbal confidence estimates and lead to frequent answer changes. We examine a variety of prompting strategies, model sizes, and application domains, revealing that current verbal confidence is vulnerable and that commonly used defence techniques are largely ineffective or counterproductive. Our findings underscore the need to design robust mechanisms for confidence expression in LLMs, as even subtle semantic-preserving modifications can lead to misleading confidence in responses.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether a language model's stated confidence remains dependable when its input is adversarially modified. Confidence expressions can influence how users interpret and trust an answer, so their robustness matters alongside answer quality. The study focuses specifically on attacks against verbal confidence scores and how those attacks affect the accompanying responses.

The authors introduce two kinds of attack framework: perturbation-based methods and jailbreak-based methods. They investigate their effects across different prompting strategies, model sizes, and application domains. The attacks can substantially distort confidence estimates and frequently change answers. Even subtle changes that preserve the input's meaning can produce misleading confidence, showing that meaningful stability cannot be assumed from semantic similarity alone.

The evaluation also finds that commonly used defenses are largely ineffective or can make the problem worse. The findings therefore concern both the vulnerability of confidence expression and the shortcomings of existing mitigation strategies. They motivate mechanisms specifically designed to make expressed confidence robust, especially when users rely on those expressions to judge whether an answer deserves trust.
summary.tldr: Adversarial input changes can distort LLMs' stated confidence and alter answers, while common defenses often fail or backfire.

title: On the Robustness of Verbal Confidence of LLMs in Adversarial Attacks

abstract: We introduce a new graph diffusion model for small drug molecule generation which simultaneously offers a 10-fold reduction in the number of diffusion steps when compared to existing methods, preservation of small molecule graph motifs via motif compression, and an average 3\% improvement in SMILES validity over the DiGress model across all real-world molecule benchmarking datasets. Furthermore, our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art DeFoG method with respect to motif-conservation by roughly 4\%, as evidenced by high ChEMBL-likeness, QED and newly introduced shingles distance scores. The key ideas behind the approach are to use a combination of deterministic and random subgraph perturbations, so that the node and edge noise schedules are codependent; to modify the loss function of the training process in order to exploit the deterministic component of the schedule; and, to ''compress'' a collection of highly relevant carbon ring and other motif structures into supernodes in a way that allows for simple subsequent integration into the molecular scaffold.

Furthermore, our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art DeFoG method with respect to motif-conservation by roughly 4\%, as evidenced by high ChEMBL-likeness, QED and newly introduced shingles distance scores. The key ideas behind the approach are to use a combination of deterministic and random subgraph perturbations, so that the node and edge noise schedules are codependent; to modify the loss function of the training process in order to exploit the deterministic component of the schedule; and, to ''compress'' a collection of highly relevant carbon ring and other motif structures into supernodes in a way that allows for simple subsequent integration into the molecular scaffold.

paragraphs: DMol generates small drug molecules using diffusion over molecular graphs. The approach addresses both the number of generation steps and the preservation of important chemical patterns. Its central design choice is to represent selected carbon rings and other relevant motifs as supernodes, keeping these structures together during generation and allowing their subsequent integration into a molecular scaffold.

The model also combines deterministic and random perturbations of subgraphs, coupling the noise schedules for nodes and edges. Its training loss is modified to exploit the deterministic part of that process. These choices make motif handling and the diffusion procedure work together, rather than treating chemical structure preservation as an unrelated final check.

The authors report tenfold fewer diffusion steps than existing methods and an average three percent improvement in SMILES validity over DiGress across the real-world benchmarks studied. They also report roughly four percent better motif conservation than DeFoG, supported by ChEMBL-likeness, QED, and a newly introduced shingles-distance measure. The findings concern generation efficiency, structural validity, and conservation of molecular motifs.
summary.tldr: DMol combines motif compression with coordinated graph diffusion to reduce generation steps and improve reported molecular validity and motif conservation.

title: DMol: A Highly Efficient and Chemical Motif-Preserving Molecule Generation Platform

abstract: Transformers have been widely regarded as a promising direction for breaking through the performance bottlenecks of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), primarily due to their global receptive fields. However, a recent empirical study suggests that tuned classical GNNs can match or even outperform state-of-the-art Graph Transformers (GTs) on standard node classification benchmarks. Motivated by this fact, we deconstruct several representative GTs to examine how global attention components influence node representations. We find that the global attention module does not provide significant performance gains and may even exacerbate test error oscillations. Consequently, we consider that the Transformer is barely able to learn connectivity patterns that meaningfully complement the original graph topology. Interestingly, we further observe that mitigating such oscillations enables the Transformer to improve generalization in GNNs. In a nutshell, we reinterpret the Transformer through the lens of graph spectrum and reformulate it as a global-aware graph filter with band-pass characteristics and linear complexity. This unique perspective introduces multi-channel filtering constraints that effectively suppress test error oscillations. Extensive experiments (17 homophilous, heterophilous graphs) provide comprehensive empirical evidence for our perspective. This work clarifies the role of Transformers in GNNs and suggests that advancing modern GNN research may still require a return to the graph itself.

paragraphs: Graph transformers offer global access to nodes, which might help overcome the local reach of conventional graph neural networks. Yet well-tuned classical models can match or exceed them on standard node classification benchmarks. This paper investigates that discrepancy by examining how global attention affects node representations in several representative graph transformers.

The authors find that global attention offers little performance improvement in their analysis and can worsen oscillations in test error. They interpret this as difficulty learning connectivity that usefully complements the given graph. However, reducing those oscillations allows transformer components to improve generalization. This motivates reinterpreting the component through the graph spectrum as a global-aware filter with band-pass behavior.

The resulting formulation has linear complexity and uses multi-channel filtering constraints to suppress test-error oscillations. Experiments on seventeen graphs, including settings with similar and dissimilar connected nodes, support the perspective. The contribution is a more constrained way to incorporate global information, grounded in the graph's structure and spectral behavior rather than assuming that unrestricted global attention will improve classification.
summary.tldr: Recasting graph-transformer components as constrained spectral filters improves generalization by controlling test-error oscillations.

title: Restricted Global-Aware Graph Filters Bridging GNNs and Transformer for Node Classification

abstract: Medical time-series data play a vital role in disease diagnosis but suffer from limited labeled samples and single-center bias, which hinder model generalization and lead to overfitting. To address these challenges, we propose DAAC (Discrepancy-Aware Adaptive Contrastive learning), a learnable multi-view contrastive framework that integrates external normal samples and enhances feature learning through adaptive contrastive strategies. DAAC consists of two key modules: (1) a Discrepancy Estimator, built upon a GAN-enhanced encoder-decoder architecture, captures the distribution of normal data and computes reconstruction errors as indicators of abnormality. These discrepancy features augment the target dataset to mitigate overfitting. (2) an Adaptive Contrastive Learner uses multi-head attention to extract discriminative representations by contrasting embeddings across multiple views and data granularities (subject, trial, epoch, and temporal levels), eliminating the need for handcrafted positive-negative sample pairs. Extensive experiments on three clinical datasets—covering Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and myocardial infarction—demonstrate that DAAC significantly outperforms existing methods, even when only 10\% of labeled data is available, showing strong generalization and diagnostic performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/CUHKSZ-MED-BioE/DAAC.

paragraphs: Medical time-series models can overfit when labeled examples are scarce and data come from a single center. DAAC addresses these problems by incorporating external normal samples and learning representations through an adaptive contrastive framework. Its design connects a model of normal patterns with comparisons across several views of the target data.

Reconstruction errors serve as indicators of abnormality, and the resulting discrepancy features augment the target dataset. They report significant improvements over existing methods, including when only 10% of labeled data is available. These findings support the proposed combination of external normal-data information and adaptive representation learning for the evaluated diagnostic tasks, particularly under limited supervision.
summary.tldr: DAAC combines external normal signals with adaptive contrastive learning to improve medical time-series classification under limited labeled data.

title: DAAC: Discrepancy-Aware Adaptive Contrastive Learning for Medical Time series

abstract: Multi-task model merging aims to consolidate knowledge from multiple fine-tuned task-specific experts into a unified model while minimizing performance degradation. Existing methods primarily approach this by minimizing differences between task-specific experts and the unified model, either from a parameter-level or a task-loss perspective. However, parameter-level methods exhibit a significant performance gap compared to the upper bound, while task-loss approaches entail costly secondary training procedures. In contrast, we observe that performance degradation closely correlates with feature drift, i.e., differences in feature representations of the same sample caused by model merging. Motivated by this observation, we propose Layer-wise Optimal Task Vector Merging (LOT Merging), a technique that explicitly minimizes feature drift between task-specific experts and the unified model in a layer-by-layer manner. LOT Merging can be formulated as a convex quadratic optimization problem, enabling us to analytically derive closed-form solutions for the parameters of linear and normalization layers. Consequently, LOT Merging achieves efficient model consolidation through basic matrix operations. Extensive experiments across vision and vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that LOT Merging significantly outperforms baseline methods, achieving improvements of up to 4.4% (ViT-B/32) over state-of-the-art approaches. The source code is available at https://github.com/SunWenJu123/model-merging.

paragraphs: Model merging combines several task-specific experts into one model, but the combined model can lose performance. This paper observes a close correlation between that loss and feature drift: changes in the internal representations produced for the same input after merging. That observation motivates preserving representations more directly during consolidation.

Layer-wise Optimal Task Vector Merging minimizes feature drift between the experts and the merged model one layer at a time. The authors formulate this as a convex quadratic optimization problem and derive closed-form parameter solutions for linear and normalization layers. This allows merging through basic matrix operations, addressing the cost associated with approaches that require secondary training.

Experiments on vision and vision-language benchmarks show substantial improvements over baseline merging methods, including gains of up to 4.4% for ViT-B/32 over state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is an efficient optimization target tied to the model’s internal behavior. The observed correlation motivates the design, while the experiments provide evidence that reducing drift improves merging in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: LOT Merging combines task experts by analytically minimizing layer-wise feature drift, improving benchmark performance with basic matrix operations.

title: Towards Minimizing Feature Drift in Model Merging: Layer-wise Task Vector Fusion for Adaptive Knowledge Integration

abstract: Training Deep Neural Networks is complicated by the fact that the distribution of each layer’s inputs changes during training, as the parameters of the previous layers change. This slows down the training by requiring lower learning rates and careful parameter initialization, and makes it notoriously hard to train models with saturating nonlinearities. We refer to this phenomenon as internal covariate shift, and address the problem by normalizing layer inputs. Our method draws its strength from making normalization a part of the model architecture and performing the normalization for each training mini-batch. Batch Normalization allows us to use much higher learning rates and be less careful about initialization, and in some cases eliminates the need for Dropout. Applied to a stateof-the-art image classification model, Batch Normalization achieves the same accuracy with 14 times fewer training steps, and beats the original model by a significant margin. Using an ensemble of batch-normalized networks, we improve upon the best published result on ImageNet classification: reaching 4.82% top-5 test error, exceeding the accuracy of human raters.

paragraphs: The paper starts from a training difficulty: as earlier network layers change, the inputs received by later layers change too. The authors call this internal covariate shift and connect it to slow training, sensitivity to initialization, and difficulties with saturating nonlinearities. Their proposed response is to normalize inputs within the network.

Batch Normalization makes normalization part of the model architecture and performs it separately for each training mini-batch. The authors report that this permits much larger learning rates and reduces the care needed in initialization. They also find that it can remove the need for Dropout in some cases, making that benefit explicitly dependent on the setting.

On an image classification model, the method reaches the original accuracy with fourteen times fewer training steps and also improves final accuracy. An ensemble achieves 4.82% top-5 test error on ImageNet, exceeding the reported human-rater accuracy on that benchmark. These results demonstrate training and classification benefits in the evaluated systems, while the paper’s explanation centers on changing internal input distributions.
summary.tldr: Batch Normalization normalizes layer inputs within mini-batches and substantially accelerates training in the reported image-classification experiments.

title: Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift

abstract: In this paper we consider the collaborative ranking setting: a pool of users each provides a set of pairwise preferences over a small subset of the set of d possible items; from these we need to predict each user’s preferences for items s/he has not yet seen. We do so via fitting a rank r score matrix to the pairwise data, and provide two main contributions: (a) We show that an algorithm based on convex optimization provides good generalization guarantees once each user provides as few as O(r \log^2 d) pairwise comparisons — essentially matching the sample complexity required in the related matrix completion setting (which uses actual numerical as opposed to pairwise information), and also matching a lower bound we establish here. (b) We develop a large-scale non-convex implementation, which we call AltSVM, which trains a factored form of the matrix via alternating minimization (which we show reduces to alternating SVM problems), and scales and parallelizes very well to large problem settings. It also outperforms common baselines on many moderately large popular collaborative filtering datasets in both NDCG and other measures of ranking performance.

We do so via fitting a rank r score matrix to the pairwise data, and provide two main contributions: (a) We show that an algorithm based on convex optimization provides good generalization guarantees once each user provides as few as O(r \log^2 d) pairwise comparisons — essentially matching the sample complexity required in the related matrix completion setting (which uses actual numerical as opposed to pairwise information), and also matching a lower bound we establish here. (b) We develop a large-scale non-convex implementation, which we call AltSVM, which trains a factored form of the matrix via alternating minimization (which we show reduces to alternating SVM problems), and scales and parallelizes very well to large problem settings. It also outperforms common baselines on many moderately large popular collaborative filtering datasets in both NDCG and other measures of ranking performance.

paragraphs: Collaborative ranking predicts a user's preferences for unseen items from comparisons involving a small subset of available items. The paper fits a rank-r score matrix to these pairwise choices. This provides a shared representation of users' scores while working with relative preferences rather than requiring numerical ratings.

For a convex optimization algorithm, the authors give generalization guarantees with as few as O(r log² d) comparisons per user, where d is the number of items. This essentially matches the sample complexity of related matrix completion methods using numerical observations, as well as a lower bound established in the paper. The result quantifies how informative pairwise feedback can be.

For larger problems, the authors develop a separate nonconvex implementation called AltSVM. It learns a factored matrix through alternating minimization, with each stage reducing to an SVM problem. AltSVM scales and parallelizes well, and outperforms common baselines on many evaluated collaborative filtering datasets in NDCG and other ranking measures.
summary.tldr: Low-rank preference completion provides sample-efficiency guarantees for pairwise feedback and a scalable alternating-SVM implementation.

title: Preference Completion: Large-scale Collaborative Ranking from Pairwise Comparisons

abstract: Inspired by recent work in machine translation and object detection, we introduce an attention based model that automatically learns to describe the content of images. We describe how we can train this model in a deterministic manner using standard backpropagation techniques and stochastically by maximizing a variational lower bound. We also show through visualization how the model is able to automatically learn to fix its gaze on salient objects while generating the corresponding words in the output sequence. We validate the use of attention with state-of-the-art performance on three benchmark datasets: Flickr8k, Flickr30k and MS COCO.
originalAbstract: Inspired by recent work in machine translation and object detection, we introduce an attention based model that automatically learns to describe the content of images. We describe how we can train this model in a deterministic manner using standard backpropagation techniques and stochastically by maximizing a variational lower bound. We also show through visualization how the model is able to automatically learn to fix its gaze on salient objects while generating the corresponding words in the output sequence. We validate the use of attention with state-of-the-art performance on three benchmark datasets: Flickr8k, Flickr30k and MS COCO.

paragraphs: Generating an image caption requires connecting visual content to a sequence of words. This paper introduces a model that learns to describe images using attention. Attention gives the caption-generation process a way to focus on salient image content as it produces the corresponding parts of a description.

The authors present two training approaches. A deterministic approach uses standard backpropagation, while a stochastic approach maximizes a variational lower bound. These offer different ways to train the attention-based model within the same overall image-description task. The contribution includes both the visual-attention model and methods for learning its behavior.

Visualizations show that the model can learn to direct its gaze toward salient objects while generating words associated with them. This connects the learned attention behavior to the content of its captions. Evaluation on Flickr8k, Flickr30k, and MS COCO achieves state-of-the-art performance, supporting the use of attention across the three tested image-captioning benchmarks.
summary.tldr: An attention-based captioning model learns to focus on salient image objects while generating words and achieves strong benchmark results.

title: Show, Attend and Tell: Neural Image Caption Generation with Visual Attention

abstract: Many high dimensional sparse learning problems are formulated as nonconvex optimization. A popular approach to solve these nonconvex optimization problems is through convex relaxations such as linear and semidefinite programming. In this paper, we study the statistical limits of convex relaxations. Particularly, we consider two problems: Mean estimation for sparse principal submatrix and edge probability estimation for stochastic block model. We exploit the sum-of-squares relaxation hierarchy to sharply characterize the limits of a broad class of convex relaxations. Our result shows statistical optimality needs to be compromised for achieving computational tractability using convex relaxations. Compared with existing results on computational lower bounds for statistical problems, which consider general polynomial-time algorithms and rely on computational hardness hypotheses on problems like planted clique detection, our theory focuses on a broad class of convex relaxations and does not rely on unproven hypotheses.

paragraphs: Many sparse learning problems are naturally expressed as nonconvex optimization, motivating the use of more tractable convex relaxations. This paper asks what statistical accuracy can be lost through that choice. It studies mean estimation for a sparse principal submatrix and edge-probability estimation for a stochastic block model.

The analysis uses the sum-of-squares hierarchy to characterize the limits of a broad class of convex relaxations. In the problems examined, achieving computational tractability through these relaxations requires compromising statistical optimality. The result therefore concerns the relationship between an optimization approach and the accuracy it can attain, rather than only the time needed to solve its optimization problem.

A distinguishing feature is that the theory does not depend on unproven computational-hardness assumptions. Other lower-bound approaches discussed in the abstract address general polynomial-time algorithms using hypotheses about problems such as planted clique detection. Here, the scope is narrower—a broad class of convex relaxations—but the conclusions within that scope avoid those hypotheses. This provides a different form of evidence for a computation–accuracy tradeoff.
summary.tldr: The paper proves statistical limits for a broad class of tractable convex relaxations without relying on unproven hardness assumptions.

title: On the Statistical Limits of Convex Relaxations

abstract: Critically ill patients in regular wards are vulnerable to unanticipated adverse events which require prompt transfer to the intensive care unit (ICU). To allow for accurate prognosis of deteriorating patients, we develop a novel continuous-time probabilistic model for a monitored patient’s temporal sequence of physiological data. Our model captures “informatively sampled” patient episodes: the clinicians’ decisions on when to observe a hospitalized patient’s vital signs and lab tests over time are represented by a marked Hawkes process, with intensity parameters that are modulated by the patient’s latent clinical states, and with observable physiological data (mark process) modeled as a switching multi-task Gaussian process. In addition, our model captures “informatively censored” patient episodes by representing the patient’s latent clinical states as an absorbing semi-Markov jump process. The model parameters are learned from offline patient episodes in the electronic health records via an EM-based algorithm. Experiments conducted on a cohort of patients admitted to a major medical center over a 3-year period show that risk prognosis based on our model significantly outperforms the currently deployed medical risk scores and other baseline machine learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Predicting deterioration in hospitalized patients requires interpreting both physiological measurements and the circumstances in which they were collected. This paper models clinicians' decisions about when to take vital signs or order laboratory tests as informative. The timing of observations becomes part of a continuous-time model for prognosis, alongside the measured values themselves.

A marked Hawkes process represents observation timing, with its intensity controlled by unobserved clinical states. A switching multitask Gaussian process models the physiological observations. An absorbing semi-Markov process represents the hidden clinical states and captures informative censoring, so the way a patient episode ends is also included in the model.

The parameters are learned from previously recorded electronic health record episodes using an EM-based algorithm. Evaluation uses a cohort admitted to a major medical center over three years. The authors report significantly better risk prognosis than deployed medical risk scores and other baseline machine-learning algorithms. The findings support jointly modeling patient physiology, observation timing, and episode termination in that evaluated cohort.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time patient model uses physiology, clinicians' observation timing, and informative episode endings to improve risk prognosis in a hospital cohort.

title: Learning from Clinical Judgments: Semi-Markov-Modulated Marked Hawkes Processes for Risk Prognosis

abstract: Sophisticated gated recurrent neural network architectures like LSTMs and GRUs have been shown to be highly effective in a myriad of applications. We develop an un-gated unit, the statistical recurrent unit (SRU), that is able to learn long term dependencies in data by only keeping moving averages of statistics. The SRU’s architecture is simple, un-gated, and contains a comparable number of parameters to LSTMs; yet, SRUs perform favorably to more sophisticated LSTM and GRU alternatives, often outperforming one or both in various tasks. We show the efficacy of SRUs as compared to LSTMs and GRUs in an unbiased manner by optimizing respective architectures’ hyperparameters for both synthetic and real-world tasks.

We develop an un-gated unit, the statistical recurrent unit (SRU), that is able to learn long term dependencies in data by only keeping moving averages of statistics. The SRU’s architecture is simple, un-gated, and contains a comparable number of parameters to LSTMs; yet, SRUs perform favorably to more sophisticated LSTM and GRU alternatives, often outperforming one or both in various tasks. We show the efficacy of SRUs as compared to LSTMs and GRUs in an unbiased manner by optimizing respective architectures’ hyperparameters for both synthetic and real-world tasks.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks must retain information from earlier inputs to learn dependencies over time. LSTMs and GRUs address this with sophisticated gated architectures. This paper introduces the statistical recurrent unit, or SRU, which learns long-term dependencies using moving averages of statistics without a gating mechanism.

The design makes running statistical summaries the basis of its memory. Although the architecture is simpler and ungated, its parameter count is comparable to that of LSTMs. The comparison therefore explores whether a different way of maintaining information can be competitive with more elaborate recurrent units, without claiming that simplicity necessarily means fewer parameters.

The authors evaluate synthetic and real-world tasks, optimizing the hyperparameters of each architecture to make the comparison fair. SRUs perform favorably against LSTMs and GRUs and often outperform one or both. These findings show that moving statistical summaries can support effective recurrent learning across the tested tasks. They provide empirical support for the architecture without asserting that it wins every comparison.
summary.tldr: The ungated statistical recurrent unit learns long-term dependencies through moving averages and performs competitively with LSTMs and GRUs.

title: The Statistical Recurrent Unit

abstract: We introduce a stochastic version of the non-reversible, rejection-free Bouncy Particle Sampler (BPS), a Markov process whose sample trajectories are piecewise linear, to efficiently sample Bayesian posteriors in big datasets. We prove that in the BPS no bias is introduced by noisy evaluations of the log-likelihood gradient. On the other hand, we argue that efficiency considerations favor a small, controllable bias, in exchange for faster mixing. We introduce a simple method that controls this trade-off. We illustrate these ideas in several examples which outperform previous approaches.
originalAbstract: We introduce a stochastic version of the non-reversible, rejection-free Bouncy Particle Sampler (BPS), a Markov process whose sample trajectories are piecewise linear, to efficiently sample Bayesian posteriors in big datasets. We prove that in the BPS no bias is introduced by noisy evaluations of the log-likelihood gradient. On the other hand, we argue that efficiency considerations favor a small, controllable bias, in exchange for faster mixing. We introduce a simple method that controls this trade-off. We illustrate these ideas in several examples which outperform previous approaches.

paragraphs: The paper develops a stochastic version of the Bouncy Particle Sampler for Bayesian posterior sampling on large datasets. The underlying sampler is a non-reversible, rejection-free Markov process whose trajectories consist of straight segments joined by changes in direction. The proposed extension focuses on making this sampling approach computationally efficient at large scale.

A central theoretical result is that noisy evaluations of the log-likelihood gradient do not introduce bias in the Bouncy Particle Sampler. This matters because it separates gradient noise from unavoidable sampling bias within the analyzed process. The authors then argue that insisting on no bias is not always the most efficient operating choice.

They propose allowing a small, controllable amount of bias in exchange for faster mixing, meaning faster movement through the target distribution. A simple method controls this trade-off. Several examples outperform previous approaches, illustrating the practical value of the idea. The paper thus distinguishes its no-bias result for noisy gradients from its deliberate use of controlled bias to improve efficiency.
summary.tldr: A stochastic Bouncy Particle Sampler tolerates noisy gradients without bias and offers a controlled bias–mixing trade-off for greater efficiency.

title: Stochastic Bouncy Particle Sampler

abstract: Learning under a Wasserstein loss, a.k.a. Wasserstein loss minimization (WLM), is an emerging research topic for gaining insights from a large set of structured objects. Despite being conceptually simple, WLM problems are computationally challenging because they involve minimizing over functions of quantities (i.e. Wasserstein distances) that themselves require numerical algorithms to compute. In this paper, we introduce a stochastic approach based on simulated annealing for solving WLMs. Particularly, we have developed a Gibbs sampler to approximate effectively and efficiently the partial gradients of a sequence of Wasserstein losses. Our new approach has the advantages of numerical stability and readiness for warm starts. These characteristics are valuable for WLM problems that often require multiple levels of iterations in which the oracle for computing the value and gradient of a loss function is embedded. We applied the method to optimal transport with Coulomb cost and the Wasserstein non-negative matrix factorization problem, and made comparisons with the existing method of entropy regularization.

In this paper, we introduce a stochastic approach based on simulated annealing for solving WLMs. Particularly, we have developed a Gibbs sampler to approximate effectively and efficiently the partial gradients of a sequence of Wasserstein losses. Our new approach has the advantages of numerical stability and readiness for warm starts. These characteristics are valuable for WLM problems that often require multiple levels of iterations in which the oracle for computing the value and gradient of a loss function is embedded. We applied the method to optimal transport with Coulomb cost and the Wasserstein non-negative matrix factorization problem, and made comparisons with the existing method of entropy regularization.

paragraphs: Wasserstein loss minimization involves an optimization problem inside another optimization problem. The outer learning procedure depends on Wasserstein distances, but computing those distances already requires numerical work. Repeatedly obtaining the loss information needed for learning can therefore become a computational bottleneck, particularly when several levels of iteration are involved.

The paper proposes a stochastic approach based on simulated annealing. Its central computational component is a Gibbs sampler that approximates partial gradients for a sequence of Wasserstein losses. This supplies an inexact oracle: a procedure that provides approximate information needed by the surrounding optimization process, rather than requiring exact calculations at every call.

The authors emphasize numerical stability and the ability to warm-start the computation using earlier work. These properties matter when related calculations recur throughout training. They apply the method to optimal transport with Coulomb cost and Wasserstein non-negative matrix factorization, comparing it with entropy regularization. The abstract describes these comparisons without asserting a universal performance advantage.
summary.tldr: A simulated annealing approach uses Gibbs sampling to approximate Wasserstein-loss gradients with numerical stability and warm-start support.

title: A Simulated Annealing Based Inexact Oracle for Wasserstein Loss Minimization

abstract: We study streaming algorithms for principal component analysis (PCA) in noisy settings. We present computationally efficient algorithms with sub-linear regret bounds for PCA in the presence of noise, missing data, and gross outliers.
originalAbstract: We study streaming algorithms for principal component analysis (PCA) in noisy settings. We present computationally efficient algorithms with sub-linear regret bounds for PCA in the presence of noise, missing data, and gross outliers.
title: Streaming Principal Component Analysis in Noisy Setting

abstract: We study the problem of generalization guarantees for dropout training. A general framework is first proposed for learning procedures with random perturbation on model parameters. The generalization error is bounded by sum of two offset Rademacher complexities: the main term is Rademacher complexity of the hypothesis class with minus offset induced by the perturbation variance, which characterizes data-dependent regularization by the random perturbation; the auxiliary term is offset Rademacher complexity for the variance class, controlling the degree to which this regularization effect can be weakened. For neural networks, we estimate upper and lower bounds for the variance induced by truthful dropout, a variant of dropout that we propose to ensure unbiased output and fit into our framework, and the variance bounds exhibits connection to adaptive regularization methods. By applying our framework to ReLU networks with one hidden layer, a generalization upper bound is derived with no assumptions on the parameter norms or data distribution, with $O(1/n)$ fast rate and adaptivity to geometry of data points being achieved at the same time.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of generalization guarantees for dropout training. A general framework is first proposed for learning procedures with random perturbation on model parameters. The generalization error is bounded by sum of two offset Rademacher complexities: the main term is Rademacher complexity of the hypothesis class with minus offset induced by the perturbation variance, which characterizes data-dependent regularization by the random perturbation; the auxiliary term is offset Rademacher complexity for the variance class, controlling the degree to which this regularization effect can be weakened. For neural networks, we estimate upper and lower bounds for the variance induced by truthful dropout, a variant of dropout that we propose to ensure unbiased output and fit into our framework, and the variance bounds exhibits connection to adaptive regularization methods. By applying our framework to ReLU networks with one hidden layer, a generalization upper bound is derived with no assumptions on the parameter norms or data distribution, with $O(1/n)$ fast rate and adaptivity to geometry of data points being achieved at the same time.

paragraphs: This paper develops generalization guarantees for training procedures that randomly perturb model parameters, with dropout as its main application. The central question is how randomness during training acts as regularization and how that effect depends on the data. The analysis expresses generalization error through two offset Rademacher complexity terms.

The main term incorporates a subtractive contribution from perturbation variance, capturing the regularizing effect. An auxiliary term controls how much that benefit can weaken. For neural networks, the authors introduce truthful dropout, a variant designed to preserve an unbiased output and fit the framework. They bound the variance it induces and connect those bounds with adaptive regularization.

For ReLU networks with one hidden layer, the framework yields a generalization upper bound without assumptions on parameter norms or the data distribution. The stated result combines a fast O(1/n) rate with adaptation to the geometry of the data points. Its significance is a mathematical account of how appropriately structured training randomness can produce data-sensitive generalization control.
summary.tldr: A perturbation-based framework explains dropout’s data-dependent regularization and yields a fast generalization bound for one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.

title: Dropout Training, Data-dependent Regularization, and Generalization Bounds

abstract: In many real-world settings, a team of agents must coordinate their behaviour while acting in a decentralised way. At the same time, it is often possible to train the agents in a centralised fashion in a simulated or laboratory setting, where global state information is available and communication constraints are lifted. Learning joint action-values conditioned on extra state information is an attractive way to exploit centralised learning, but the best strategy for then extracting decentralised policies is unclear. Our solution is QMIX, a novel value-based method that can train decentralised policies in a centralised end-to-end fashion. QMIX employs a network that estimates joint action-values as a complex non-linear combination of per-agent values that condition only on local observations. We structurally enforce that the joint-action value is monotonic in the per-agent values, which allows tractable maximisation of the joint action-value in off-policy learning, and guarantees consistency between the centralised and decentralised policies. We evaluate QMIX on a challenging set of StarCraft II micromanagement tasks, and show that QMIX significantly outperforms existing value-based multi-agent reinforcement learning methods.

paragraphs: A team of agents may have access to global information during training while each agent must act using only local observations after training. QMIX addresses how to exploit that richer training information while obtaining coordinated policies that can run in a decentralized way.

The method estimates a joint action-value by combining individual agents' values through a nonlinear network. Each individual value depends only on local observations. QMIX constrains the combination to be monotonic in those values. This structure makes joint-value maximization tractable during off-policy learning and guarantees consistency between the centralized and decentralized policies.

The authors evaluate QMIX on challenging StarCraft II micromanagement tasks and report significant improvements over existing value-based multiagent methods. The findings support the combination of expressive nonlinear mixing with a structural constraint that keeps decentralized choices consistent with the central value estimate. The guarantee concerns that consistency; the reported performance advantage comes from the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: QMIX mixes local agent values monotonically to support centralized training and consistent decentralized decisions, improving reported StarCraft II performance.

title: QMIX: Monotonic Value Function Factorisation for Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Over the last few years, the phenomenon of adversarial examples — maliciously constructed inputs that fool trained machine learning models — has captured the attention of the research community, especially when restricted to small modifications of a correctly handled input. Less surprisingly, image classifiers also lack human-level performance on randomly corrupted images, such as images with additive Gaussian noise. In this paper we provide both empirical and theoretical evidence that these are two manifestations of the same underlying phenomenon, and therefore the adversarial robustness and corruption robustness research programs are closely related. This suggests that improving adversarial robustness should go hand in hand with improving performance in the presence of more general and realistic image corruptions. This yields a computationally tractable evaluation metric for defenses to consider: test error in noisy image distributions.

paragraphs: A classifier can fail when an input is deliberately modified to fool it, even if the original input was classified correctly. It can also fail when an image receives random corruption, such as additive Gaussian noise. This paper investigates whether these apparently different weaknesses reflect a shared underlying phenomenon.

The authors provide both theoretical and empirical evidence connecting adversarial examples with errors on noisy inputs. Their analysis brings adversarial robustness and corruption robustness into a common discussion: the model's behavior under random disturbance is relevant to understanding its vulnerability to deliberately chosen disturbance. The claimed connection concerns these forms of failure, rather than merely their similar appearance.

This perspective suggests that progress against adversarial examples should accompany better performance under broader, realistic image corruptions. It also motivates test error on noisy image distributions as a computationally manageable metric for evaluating defenses. The proposed metric gives researchers another way to examine robustness, while the evidence supports a relationship between the two research directions rather than an unconditional promise about every defense.
summary.tldr: Theoretical and empirical evidence links adversarial vulnerability to errors under random noise, motivating noisy test error as a defense evaluation metric.

title: Adversarial Examples Are a Natural Consequence of Test Error in Noise

abstract: While policy-based reinforcement learning (RL) achieves tremendous successes in practice, it is significantly less understood in theory, especially compared with value-based RL. In particular, it remains elusive how to design a provably efficient policy optimization algorithm that incorporates exploration. To bridge such a gap, this paper proposes an Optimistic variant of the Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm (OPPO), which follows an “optimistic version” of the policy gradient direction. This paper proves that, in the problem of episodic Markov decision process with linear function approximation, unknown transition, and adversarial reward with full-information feedback, OPPO achieves $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d^2 H^3 T})$ regret. Here $d$ is the feature dimension, $H$ is the episode horizon, and $T$ is the total number of steps. To the best of our knowledge, OPPO is the first provably efficient policy optimization algorithm that explores.

paragraphs: Policy-based reinforcement learning has achieved substantial practical success, but its theoretical treatment of exploration is less developed than that of value-based methods. This paper asks how policy optimization can incorporate exploration while retaining an efficiency guarantee. It proposes OPPO, an optimistic variant of Proximal Policy Optimization, to connect policy improvement with a principled exploration mechanism.

OPPO follows an optimistic version of the policy-gradient direction. The authors analyze episodic Markov decision processes with linear function approximation, unknown transitions, and adversarial rewards under full-information feedback. These conditions define the setting of the result; in particular, the reward-feedback assumption is part of the guarantee rather than an incidental implementation detail.

The regret bound is Õ(√(d²H³T)), where d is feature dimension, H is episode length, and T is the total number of interaction steps. For fixed dimension and horizon, this bound grows sublinearly in interaction time. The authors identify OPPO, to their knowledge, as the first provably efficient policy-optimization algorithm that explores. The contribution is a theoretical exploration guarantee for policy optimization in the specified setting.
summary.tldr: OPPO adds optimism to policy optimization and proves a sublinear regret bound for exploration in a specified linear episodic reinforcement-learning setting.

title: Provably Efficient Exploration in Policy Optimization

abstract: Parameter estimation, statistical tests and conﬁdence sets are the cornerstones of classical statistics that allow scientists to make inferences about the underlying process that generated the observed data. A key question is whether one can still construct hypothesis tests and conﬁdence sets with proper coverage and high power in a so-called likelihood-free inference (LFI) setting; that is, a setting where the likelihood is not explicitly known but one can forward-simulate observable data according to a stochastic model. In this paper, we present ACORE (Approximate Computation via Odds Ratio Estimation), a frequentist approach to LFI that ﬁrst formulates the classical likelihood ratio test (LRT) as a parametrized classiﬁcation problem, and then uses the equivalence of tests and conﬁdence sets to build conﬁdence regions for parameters of interest. We also present a goodness-of-ﬁt procedure for checking whether the constructed tests and conﬁdence regions are valid. ACORE is based on the key observation that the LRT statistic, the rejection probability of the test, and the coverage of the conﬁdence set are conditional distribution functions which often vary smoothly as a function of the parameters of interest. Hence, instead of relying solely on samples simulated at ﬁxed parameter settings (as is the convention in standard Monte Carlo solutions), one can leverage machine learning tools and data simulated in the neighborhood of a parameter to improve estimates of quantities of interest. We demonstrate the efﬁcacy of ACORE with both theoretical and empirical results. Our implementation is available on Github.

paragraphs: Some scientific models can simulate observations even when their likelihood cannot be evaluated explicitly. This paper asks how to construct useful hypothesis tests and confidence regions in that setting. The challenge is to retain statistical validity and the ability to detect alternatives while relying on simulated data.

The proposed method, ACORE, recasts the likelihood-ratio test as a classification problem parameterized by the quantities being inferred. It then uses the relationship between tests and confidence sets to construct parameter regions. A separate goodness-of-fit procedure checks whether the resulting tests and confidence regions are valid, making validation an explicit part of the approach.

The method exploits the observation that relevant statistical quantities often vary smoothly with model parameters. Machine learning can therefore use simulations from nearby parameter settings to improve estimates, instead of relying only on simulations at one fixed setting. The authors provide theoretical and empirical support for this strategy. The claimed opportunity comes from sharing information across parameter values where that smoothness is available.
summary.tldr: ACORE uses classification and shared information across simulated parameter settings to build and check likelihood-free tests and confidence regions.

title: Confidence Sets and Hypothesis Testing in a Likelihood-Free Inference Setting

abstract: We study whether a neural network optimizes to the same, linearly connected minimum under different samples of SGD noise (e.g., random data order and augmentation). We find that standard vision models become stable to SGD noise in this way early in training. From then on, the outcome of optimization is determined to a linearly connected region. We use this technique to study iterative magnitude pruning (IMP), the procedure used by work on the lottery ticket hypothesis to identify subnetworks that could have trained in isolation to full accuracy. We find that these subnetworks only reach full accuracy when they are stable to SGD noise, which either occurs at initialization for small-scale settings (MNIST) or early in training for large-scale settings (ResNet-50 and Inception-v3 on ImageNet).

paragraphs: Training a neural network involves randomness from sources such as data ordering and augmentation. This paper asks whether different realizations of that SGD noise lead to solutions in the same linearly connected region. Linear connectivity provides a way to assess whether training outcomes remain closely related even when the random choices differ.

The authors find that standard vision models become stable to SGD noise early in training. After this point, optimization outcomes are confined to a linearly connected region in the sense studied. They apply the same test to iterative magnitude pruning, the procedure used to identify sparse subnetworks associated with the lottery ticket hypothesis.

In their findings, these subnetworks reach full accuracy only when they are stable to SGD noise. That stability is present at initialization in the small-scale MNIST setting, but emerges early in training for ResNet-50 and Inception-v3 on ImageNet. The results connect the success of the studied sparse subnetworks to training stability and show that the timing of this stability differs across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Pruned subnetworks empirically reach full accuracy only once their training outcomes become stable to SGD noise through linear connectivity.

title: Linear Mode Connectivity and the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis

abstract: We present a description of the function space and the smoothness class associated with a convolutional network using the machinery of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. We show that the mapping associated with a convolutional network expands into a sum involving elementary functions akin to spherical harmonics. This functional decomposition can be related to the functional ANOVA decomposition in nonparametric statistics. Building off our functional characterization of convolutional networks, we obtain statistical bounds highlighting an interesting trade-off between the approximation error and the estimation error.

paragraphs: This paper studies convolutional networks through the functions they represent and the smoothness of those functions. It uses reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces as the mathematical framework for that description. The goal is to characterize the resulting function space, providing a way to reason about the network’s representational properties through a functional analysis.

The authors show that the mapping associated with a convolutional network can be expanded as a sum of elementary functions resembling spherical harmonics. This decomposition provides components with which to describe the network’s overall function. They also relate it to functional ANOVA decomposition from nonparametric statistics, connecting the network characterization to another established approach for breaking functions into constituent parts.

From this characterization, the paper derives statistical bounds exposing a trade-off between approximation error and estimation error. These concern how well the function space can represent a target and how accurately it can be learned from data. The contribution links the structure of convolutional representations to that statistical balance, rather than stopping at an algebraic decomposition.
summary.tldr: A harmonic-style decomposition characterizes convolutional-network function spaces and yields bounds linking approximation and estimation error.

title: Harmonic Decompositions of Convolutional Networks

abstract: Many automated machine learning methods, such as those for hyperparameter and neural architecture optimization, are computationally expensive because they involve training many different model configurations. In this work, we present a new method that saves computational budget by terminating poor configurations early on in the training. In contrast to existing methods, we consider this task as a ranking and transfer learning problem. We qualitatively show that by optimizing a pairwise ranking loss and leveraging learning curves from other data sets, our model is able to effectively rank learning curves without having to observe many or very long learning curves. We further demonstrate that our method can be used to accelerate a neural architecture search by a factor of up to 100 without a significant performance degradation of the discovered architecture. In further experiments we analyze the quality of ranking, the influence of different model components as well as the predictive behavior of the model.

paragraphs: Automated searches over hyperparameters and neural architectures can be expensive because they train many candidate models. This paper aims to save computation by stopping poor candidates early. The challenge is deciding which training runs are unpromising when only limited information about their learning progress has been observed.

The authors frame this decision as a ranking and transfer learning problem. Their model optimizes a pairwise ranking loss and uses learning curves from other datasets. The desired output is a useful ordering of candidate curves. Qualitative results show that the model can rank effectively without requiring many observed curves or long training histories.

In a neural architecture search experiment, the method achieves acceleration of up to a factor of 100 without significant degradation in the discovered architecture's performance. Further experiments examine ranking quality, individual model components, and predictive behavior. The reported speedup is an experimental result rather than a guarantee for every search. The contribution is a way to reuse prior training experience to make earlier computational allocation decisions.
summary.tldr: Learning to rank partial training curves across datasets enables early stopping and speeds up the reported architecture search by up to 100 times.

title: Learning to Rank Learning Curves

abstract: Centralized training with decentralized execution has become an important paradigm in multi-agent learning. Though practical, current methods rely on restrictive assumptions to decompose the centralized value function across agents for execution. In this paper, we eliminate this restriction by proposing multi-agent determinantal Q-learning. Our method is established on Q-DPP, a novel extension of determinantal point process (DPP) to multi-agent setting. Q-DPP promotes agents to acquire diverse behavioral models; this allows a natural factorization of the joint Q-functions with no need for \emph{a priori} structural constraints on the value function or special network architectures. We demonstrate that Q-DPP generalizes major solutions including VDN, QMIX, and QTRAN on decentralizable cooperative tasks. To efficiently draw samples from Q-DPP, we develop a linear-time sampler with theoretical approximation guarantee. Our sampler also benefits exploration by coordinating agents to cover orthogonal directions in the state space during training. We evaluate our algorithm on multiple cooperative benchmarks; its effectiveness has been demonstrated when compared with the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Multi-agent learning often trains agents together but requires them to act separately afterward. Decomposing a centralized value function for that purpose can impose restrictive structural assumptions. This paper proposes multi-agent determinantal Q-learning, built around Q-DPP, an extension of determinantal point processes to the multi-agent setting.

Q-DPP encourages agents to learn diverse behavioral models. According to the paper, this supports a natural factorization of joint Q-functions without prescribing structural constraints on the value function or requiring special network architectures. The framework also generalizes VDN, QMIX, and QTRAN on decentralizable cooperative tasks, connecting the proposed formulation to several established ways of coordinating agents.

The sampling procedure also supports exploration by coordinating agents toward orthogonal directions in the state space during training. Evaluations on multiple cooperative benchmarks demonstrate effectiveness against state-of-the-art comparisons. The method therefore connects behavioral diversity to both value decomposition and coordinated exploration within centralized training.
summary.tldr: Q-DPP uses diverse agent behaviors to support joint-value factorization and coordinated exploration without prescribed value-function structure.

title: Multi-Agent Determinantal Q-Learning

abstract: Current deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are still highly task-specific and lack the ability to generalize to new environments. Lifelong learning (LLL), however, aims at solving multiple tasks sequentially by efficiently transferring and using knowledge between tasks. Despite a surge of interest in lifelong RL in recent years, the lack of a realistic testbed makes robust evaluation of LLL algorithms difficult. Multi-agent RL (MARL), on the other hand, can be seen as a natural scenario for lifelong RL due to its inherent non-stationarity, since the agents’ policies change over time. In this work, we introduce a multi-agent lifelong learning testbed that supports both zero-shot and few-shot settings. Our setup is based on Hanabi {—} a partially-observable, fully cooperative multi-agent game that has been shown to be challenging for zero-shot coordination. Its large strategy space makes it a desirable environment for lifelong RL tasks. We evaluate several recent MARL methods, and benchmark state-of-the-art LLL algorithms in limited memory and computation regimes to shed light on their strengths and weaknesses. This continual learning paradigm also provides us with a pragmatic way of going beyond centralized training which is the most commonly used training protocol in MARL. We empirically show that the agents trained in our setup are able to coordinate well with unseen agents, without any additional assumptions made by previous works. The code and all pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/chandar-lab/Lifelong-Hanabi.
