paragraphs: Lifelong reinforcement learning asks an agent to carry useful knowledge across a sequence of tasks. Evaluating that ability requires settings where change is meaningful and ongoing. This paper proposes coordination with other learning agents as such a setting: because their policies evolve, the behavior an agent must coordinate with changes over time.

The authors build a testbed around Hanabi, a cooperative game in which players have incomplete information. Its large range of possible strategies provides varied coordination challenges. The testbed supports both zero-shot coordination and few-shot adaptation, allowing evaluation of agents facing new partners with either no additional learning or limited opportunities to adapt.

The study benchmarks multi-agent and lifelong learning methods under restricted memory and computation. Empirically, agents trained in this setup coordinate well with previously unseen agents without additional assumptions used in earlier work. The contribution is both an evaluation environment and a practical route beyond centralized training, grounded in the continuing need to adapt to other agents.
summary.tldr: A lifelong-learning testbed based on Hanabi evaluates continual coordination and produces agents that coordinate well with unseen partners.

title: Continuous Coordination As a Realistic Scenario for Lifelong Learning

abstract: Generative probabilistic modeling of biological sequences has widespread existing and potential application across biology and biomedicine, from evolutionary biology to epidemiology to protein design. Many standard sequence analysis methods preprocess data using a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) algorithm, one of the most widely used computational methods in all of science. However, as we show in this article, training generative probabilistic models with MSA preprocessing leads to statistical pathologies in the context of sequence prediction and forecasting. To address these problems, we propose a principled drop-in alternative to MSA preprocessing in the form of a structured observation distribution (the "MuE" distribution). We prove theoretically that the MuE distribution comprehensively generalizes popular methods for inferring biological sequence alignments, and provide a precise characterization of how such biological models have differed from natural language latent alignment models. We show empirically that models that use the MuE as an observation distribution outperform comparable methods across a variety of datasets, and apply MuE models to a novel problem for generative probabilistic sequence models: forecasting pathogen evolution.

paragraphs: Biological sequence models often begin with multiple sequence alignment, a preprocessing step that arranges sequences for comparison. The paper shows that this familiar workflow can create statistical problems when training generative probabilistic models for sequence prediction and forecasting. Its focus is therefore on how observed sequences enter the model, rather than only on the model's predictive machinery.

The proposed MuE distribution replaces alignment preprocessing with a structured observation distribution. This gives generative models a principled alternative for handling sequence structure. The authors prove that MuE generalizes popular biological alignment methods and precisely characterize how those methods differ from latent alignment models used in natural language.

Across several datasets, models using MuE outperform comparable methods in the reported experiments. The paper also applies them to forecasting pathogen evolution, presented as a new application for generative probabilistic sequence models. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support integrating alignment-related structure into probabilistic modeling when the goal is to predict future or unseen sequences.
summary.tldr: MuE replaces biological sequence alignment preprocessing with a structured probabilistic observation model that improves prediction and supports pathogen-evolution forecasting.

title: A Structured Observation Distribution for Generative Biological Sequence Prediction and Forecasting

abstract: The estimation of time-varying quantities is a fundamental component of decision making in fields such as healthcare and finance. However, the practical utility of such estimates is limited by how accurately they quantify predictive uncertainty. In this work, we address the problem of estimating the joint predictive distribution of high-dimensional multivariate time series. We propose a versatile method, based on the transformer architecture, that estimates joint distributions using an attention-based decoder that provably learns to mimic the properties of non-parametric copulas. The resulting model has several desirable properties: it can scale to hundreds of time series, supports both forecasting and interpolation, can handle unaligned and non-uniformly sampled data, and can seamlessly adapt to missing data during training. We demonstrate these properties empirically and show that our model produces state-of-the-art predictions on multiple real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Forecasting many related time series requires more than predicting a separate value for each one. Decision-making also needs uncertainty about how their values may vary together. TACTiS targets this joint predictive distribution, aiming to represent dependencies across a high-dimensional collection of time-varying quantities.

The model uses a transformer with an attention-based decoder. The authors prove that the decoder learns to mimic properties of non-parametric copulas, which describe dependence within a joint distribution. This provides a foundation for modeling relationships among predicted quantities. The architecture supports hundreds of time series and accommodates data whose observations are neither aligned across series nor sampled at uniform intervals.

TACTiS handles both forecasting future values and interpolating values within observed time spans, and it adapts to missing data during training. Experiments demonstrate these capabilities and report state-of-the-art predictions on multiple real-world datasets. The contribution combines joint uncertainty modeling with flexibility for irregular observations, allowing a single approach to address several common time-series estimation settings.
summary.tldr: TACTiS models joint uncertainty across many time series while supporting forecasting, interpolation, irregular sampling, and missing data.

title: TACTiS: Transformer-Attentional Copulas for Time Series

abstract: Multi-layer perceptrons (MLP) have proven to be effective scene encoders when combined with higher-dimensional projections of the input, commonly referred to as positional encoding. However, scenes with a wide frequency spectrum remain a challenge: choosing high frequencies for positional encoding introduces noise in low structure areas, while low frequencies results in poor fitting of detailed regions. To address this, we propose a progressive positional encoding, exposing a hierarchical MLP structure to incremental sets of frequency encodings. Our model accurately reconstructs scenes with wide frequency bands and learns a scene representation at progressive level of detail without explicit per-level supervision. The architecture is modular: each level encodes a continuous implicit representation that can be leveraged separately for its respective resolution, meaning a smaller network for coarser reconstructions. Experiments on several 2D and 3D datasets shows improvements in reconstruction accuracy, representational capacity and training speed compared to baselines.

Our model accurately reconstructs scenes with wide frequency bands and learns a scene representation at progressive level of detail without explicit per-level supervision. Experiments on several 2D and 3D datasets shows improvements in reconstruction accuracy, representational capacity and training speed compared to baselines.

paragraphs: Neural scene representations often use positional encoding to help a multilayer perceptron capture spatial detail. Choosing the encoding’s frequencies creates a trade-off: high frequencies can introduce noise in simple regions, while low frequencies can miss fine detail. This paper addresses scenes that contain both kinds of structure across a wide frequency range.

Progressive Implicit Networks expose a hierarchical network to progressively expanded sets of frequency encodings. The model learns multiple levels of scene detail without requiring explicit supervision for each level. Each level also defines its own continuous implicit representation, so a representation can be used separately at the resolution it supports.

This modularity means that a coarser reconstruction can use a smaller network. Experiments on several two-dimensional and three-dimensional datasets report improvements in reconstruction accuracy, representational capacity, and training speed relative to the baselines. The approach connects frequency selection with network hierarchy, allowing one learned model to represent scenes progressively while making its individual levels useful for different reconstruction resolutions.
summary.tldr: PINs progressively introduce frequency encodings into a hierarchical network to learn modular scene representations at multiple levels of detail.

title: PINs: Progressive Implicit Networks for Multi-Scale Neural Representations

abstract: Optimal transport is a framework for comparing measures whereby a cost is incurred for transporting one measure to another. Recent works have aimed to improve optimal transport plans through the introduction of various forms of structure. We introduce novel order constraints into the optimal transport formulation to allow for the incorporation of structure. We define an efficient method for obtaining explainable solutions to the new formulation that scales far better than standard approaches. The theoretical properties of the method are provided. We demonstrate experimentally that order constraints improve explainability using the e-SNLI (Stanford Natural Language Inference) dataset that includes human-annotated rationales as well as on several image color transfer examples.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares measures by finding how to move one into another while accounting for transportation cost. This paper adds order constraints to that formulation so a transport plan can reflect additional structure. The objective is to make the resulting solutions more explainable by incorporating structure directly into the optimization problem.

Introducing constraints also creates a computational problem: the structured formulation needs a practical solution method. The authors develop an efficient procedure for obtaining explainable solutions and report that it scales substantially better than standard approaches. They also provide theoretical properties of the method, pairing the new formulation with analysis of how it can be solved.

The experiments examine explainability on e-SNLI, a natural-language inference dataset with human-annotated rationales, and on several image color-transfer examples. In these settings, the authors find that order constraints improve explainability. The contribution thus joins a way to express structure in transport plans with a scalable method and empirical evidence from both language and image applications.
summary.tldr: Order constraints incorporate structure into optimal transport, with an efficient solver and demonstrated explainability gains in language and image examples.

title: Order Constraints in Optimal Transport

abstract: Certifying the robustness of model performance under bounded data distribution drifts has recently attracted intensive interest under the umbrella of distributional robustness. However, existing techniques either make strong assumptions on the model class and loss functions that can be certified, such as smoothness expressed via Lipschitz continuity of gradients, or require to solve complex optimization problems. As a result, the wider application of these techniques is currently limited by its scalability and flexibility — these techniques often do not scale to large-scale datasets with modern deep neural networks or cannot handle loss functions which may be non-smooth such as the 0-1 loss. In this paper, we focus on the problem of certifying distributional robustness for blackbox models and bounded loss functions, and propose a novel certification framework based on the Hellinger distance. Our certification technique scales to ImageNet-scale datasets, complex models, and a diverse set of loss functions. We then focus on one specific application enabled by such scalability and flexibility, i.e., certifying out-of-domain generalization for large neural networks and loss functions such as accuracy and AUC. We experimentally validate our certification method on a number of datasets, ranging from ImageNet, where we provide the first non-vacuous certified out-of-domain generalization, to smaller classification tasks where we are able to compare with the state-of-the-art and show that our method performs considerably better.

paragraphs: A distributional robustness certificate bounds how model performance can change when the data distribution shifts within a specified range. Existing certification approaches can require restrictive smoothness assumptions or difficult optimization. These requirements make it hard to handle large neural networks and performance measures that change abruptly, including the loss associated with an incorrect classification.

This paper proposes a certification framework based on Hellinger distance, which measures differences between probability distributions. It targets blackbox models and bounded loss functions, broadening the models and evaluation criteria that can be handled. The resulting guarantees concern bounded distribution shifts; they do not establish performance under every possible change in the deployment environment.

The method scales to ImageNet-sized data and supports out-of-domain certification for measures including accuracy and AUC. Experiments report a non-vacuous certificate on ImageNet, meaning the bound supplies meaningful information rather than an uninformative guarantee. On smaller classification tasks, where comparisons are possible, the method performs considerably better than the competing approaches evaluated. Its central contribution is making certification useful across a broader practical setting.
summary.tldr: A Hellinger-distance framework certifies performance under bounded distribution shifts for blackbox models and bounded losses at large scale.

title: Certifying Out-of-Domain Generalization for Blackbox Functions

abstract: In federated learning (FL), multiple clients collaborate to train machine learning models together while keeping their data decentralized. Through utilizing more training data, FL suffers from the potential negative transfer problem: the global FL model may even perform worse than the models trained with local data only. In this paper, we propose FedCollab, a novel FL framework that alleviates negative transfer by clustering clients into non-overlapping coalitions based on their distribution distances and data quantities. As a result, each client only collaborates with the clients having similar data distributions, and tends to collaborate with more clients when it has less data. We evaluate our framework with a variety of datasets, models, and types of non-IIDness. Our results demonstrate that FedCollab effectively mitigates negative transfer across a wide range of FL algorithms and consistently outperforms other clustered FL algorithms.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train collaboratively while keeping their data decentralized. More participating data does not always help every client: a shared model can perform worse than one trained only on local data. This negative transfer problem motivates FedCollab, which changes the collaboration structure instead of assuming that all clients should train together.

FedCollab groups clients into non-overlapping coalitions using both distances between their data distributions and the quantities of data they hold. Clients consequently collaborate with others whose distributions are similar. Those with less data tend to collaborate more broadly. The grouping therefore considers both compatibility between collaborators and the amount of additional data a client may benefit from.

The framework is evaluated across different datasets, models, and forms of non-identically distributed client data. Reported results show reduced negative transfer across a wide range of federated learning algorithms and consistent improvements over other clustered federated methods. These findings support treating the choice of collaborators as part of the learning problem, with distribution similarity and local data quantity jointly informing that choice.
summary.tldr: FedCollab reduces negative transfer by grouping federated clients according to both data-distribution similarity and local data quantity.

title: Optimizing the Collaboration Structure in Cross-Silo Federated Learning

abstract: Characterizing neural networks in terms of better-understood formal systems has the potential to yield new insights into the power and limitations of these networks. Doing so for transformers remains an active area of research. Bhattamishra and others have shown that transformer encoders are at least as expressive as a certain kind of counter machine, while Merrill and Sabharwal have shown that fixed-precision transformer encoders recognize only languages in uniform $TC^0$. We connect and strengthen these results by identifying a variant of first-order logic with counting quantifiers that is simultaneously an upper bound for fixed-precision transformer encoders and a lower bound for transformer encoders. This brings us much closer than before to an exact characterization of the languages that transformer encoders recognize.

paragraphs: Understanding transformer expressivity means identifying which formal languages a transformer encoder can recognize. Connecting neural networks to formal computational systems gives a more precise way to discuss their capabilities. This paper narrows the gap between established lower and upper bounds on that recognition power.

Previous results connected transformer encoders to a type of counter machine and placed fixed-precision encoders within the complexity class uniform TC⁰. The authors link and strengthen these findings using a variant of first-order logic with counting quantifiers. This logical system becomes a common reference point for expressing what encoders can and cannot recognize.

Specifically, the logic provides an upper bound for fixed-precision transformer encoders and a lower bound for transformer encoders. The precision qualification matters because the two bounds are stated for differently qualified encoder settings. The result brings the field closer to an exact characterization without claiming that the remaining distinction has disappeared. Its contribution is a tighter formal description of recognition ability, rather than an empirical comparison of trained models.
summary.tldr: A counting-based logical system tightens upper and lower bounds on the formal-language recognition power of transformer encoders.

title: Tighter Bounds on the Expressivity of Transformer Encoders

abstract: Minimizing the difference of two submodular (DS) functions is a problem that naturally occurs in various machine learning problems. Although it is well known that a DS problem can be equivalently formulated as the minimization of the difference of two convex (DC) functions, existing algorithms do not fully exploit this connection. A classical algorithm for DC problems is called the DC algorithm (DCA). We introduce variants of DCA and its complete form (CDCA) that we apply to the DC program corresponding to DS minimization. We extend existing convergence properties of DCA, and connect them to convergence properties on the DS problem. Our results on DCA match the theoretical guarantees satisfied by existing DS algorithms, while providing a more complete characterization of convergence properties. In the case of CDCA, we obtain a stronger local minimality guarantee. Our numerical results show that our proposed algorithms outperform existing baselines on two applications: speech corpus selection and feature selection.

paragraphs: Some machine learning selection problems require minimizing the difference between two submodular functions. A known mathematical connection rewrites this as minimizing the difference between two convex functions. The paper argues that existing algorithms have not fully used this connection and develops methods that make it central to optimization.

The authors adapt the classical difference-of-convex algorithm, DCA, and its complete form, CDCA, to the corresponding continuous formulation. They extend convergence results for DCA and connect those results back to the original submodular problem. This step matters because guarantees about the reformulated problem need to explain what happens in the selection problem itself.

For DCA, the resulting guarantees match those of existing submodular-difference algorithms while describing convergence more fully. CDCA provides a stronger guarantee of local minimality, which concerns the quality of a solution relative to nearby alternatives. Numerical experiments on speech corpus selection and feature selection show the proposed algorithms outperforming existing baselines. Together, the theory and experiments support exploiting the convex connection more directly.
summary.tldr: Adapting difference-of-convex optimization improves convergence understanding and yields stronger local guarantees for minimizing differences of submodular functions.

title: Difference of submodular minimization via DC programming

abstract: We propose global context vision transformer (GC ViT), a novel architecture that enhances parameter and compute utilization for computer vision. Our method leverages global context self-attention modules, joint with standard local self-attention, to effectively and efficiently model both long and short-range spatial interactions, without the need for expensive operations such as computing attention masks or shifting local windows. In addition, we address the lack of the inductive bias in ViTs, and propose to leverage a modified fused inverted residual blocks in our architecture. Our proposed GC ViT achieves state-of-the-art results across image classification, object detection and semantic segmentation tasks. On ImageNet-1K dataset for classification, the variants of GC ViT with 51M, 90M and 201M parameters achieve 84.3%, 85.0% and 85.7% Top-1 accuracy, respectively, at 224 image resolution and without any pre-training, hence surpassing comparably-sized prior art such as CNN-based ConvNeXt and ViT-based MaxViT and Swin Transformer by a large margin. Pre-trained GC ViT backbones in downstream tasks of object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation using MS COCO and ADE20K datasets outperform prior work consistently. Specifically, GC ViT with a 4-scale DINO detection head achieves a box AP of 58.3 on MS COCO dataset.

paragraphs: Visual recognition requires both nearby details and relationships across an image. Global Context Vision Transformer, or GC ViT, combines local self-attention with global-context attention to model these two scales efficiently. The architecture avoids expensive operations such as attention-mask computation and shifted local windows, aiming to make better use of parameters and computation.

The model also incorporates modified fused inverted residual blocks to introduce useful structural biases into the vision transformer. Its design therefore addresses both information exchange across spatial distances and the architectural assumptions that guide visual learning. The authors evaluate the resulting architecture on classification and use pretrained backbones for detection and segmentation tasks.

On ImageNet-1K at 224 resolution without pretraining, variants with 51 million, 90 million, and 201 million parameters achieve 84.3%, 85.0%, and 85.7% top-1 accuracy, respectively. The paper reports state-of-the-art results across the evaluated task families and consistent downstream improvements on MS COCO and ADE20K. These findings support the proposed combination of local interactions, global context, and architectural bias as an effective visual backbone.
summary.tldr: GC ViT combines local and global-context attention with structural visual biases, reporting strong efficiency and state-of-the-art vision results.

title: Global Context Vision Transformers

abstract: User embeddings (vectorized representations of a user) are essential in recommendation systems. Numerous approaches have been proposed to construct a representation for the user in order to find similar items for retrieval tasks, and they have been proven effective in industrial recommendation systems. Recently people have discovered the power of using multiple embeddings to represent a user, with the hope that each embedding represents the user’s interest in a certain topic. With multi-interest representation, it’s important to model the user’s preference over the different topics and how the preference changes with time. However, existing approaches either fail to estimate the user’s affinity to each interest or unreasonably assume every interest of every user fades at an equal rate with time, thus hurting the performance of candidate retrieval. In this paper, we propose the Multi-Interest Preference (MIP) model, an approach that not only produces multi-interest for users by using the user’s sequential engagement more effectively but also automatically learns a set of weights to represent the preference over each embedding so that the candidates can be retrieved from each interest proportionally. Extensive experiments have been done on various industrial-scale datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

Recently people have discovered the power of using multiple embeddings to represent a user, with the hope that each embedding represents the user’s interest in a certain topic. Extensive experiments have been done on various industrial-scale datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems use user vectors to retrieve relevant items, and multiple vectors can represent a person’s different interests. Having several interests represented, however, leaves another question: how much should each interest influence the recommendations now? The paper argues that existing approaches can miss these preferences or assume that every interest fades at the same rate.

The Multi-Interest Preference model uses a user’s sequence of engagement to construct multiple interest representations and learn a weight for each one. Those weights express the user’s relative preference across the representations. Retrieval then draws candidates from the different interests proportionally, connecting the learned preferences directly to which items enter the candidate set.

This approach matters because identifying a topic of interest and deciding how strongly to prioritize it are separate parts of recommendation. MIP models both within its retrieval approach, using sequential behavior more effectively. Experiments on several industrial-scale datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The reported evidence supports weighted multi-interest retrieval without establishing that all users’ interests follow a single shared pattern of change.
summary.tldr: MIP learns multiple user interests and their relative weights so recommendation candidates can be retrieved in proportion to user preferences.

title: Everyone’s Preference Changes Differently: A Weighted Multi-Interest Model For Retrieval

abstract: We uncover how SGD interacts with batch normalization and can exhibit undesirable training dynamics such as divergence. More precisely, we study how Single Shuffle (SS) and Random Reshuffle (RR)—two widely used variants of SGD—interact surprisingly differently in the presence of batch normalization: RR leads to much more stable evolution of training loss than SS. As a concrete example, for regression using a linear network with batch normalized inputs, we prove that SS and RR converge to distinct global optima that are “distorted” away from gradient descent. Thereafter, for classification we characterize conditions under which training divergence for SS and RR can, and cannot occur. We present explicit constructions to show how SS leads to distorted optima in regression and divergence for classification, whereas RR avoids both distortion and divergence. We validate our results empirically in realistic settings, and conclude that the separation between SS and RR used with batch normalization is relevant in practice.

paragraphs: The order in which SGD encounters examples can interact strongly with batch normalization. This paper compares Single Shuffle, which uses a single shuffled ordering, with Random Reshuffle, which refreshes the ordering. It finds that Random Reshuffle produces substantially more stable training-loss evolution, showing that these two common variants can behave quite differently.

For regression with a linear network and batch-normalized inputs, the authors prove that the two methods converge to distinct global optima displaced from the gradient-descent solution. For classification, they characterize conditions under which either method can or cannot diverge. These analyses distinguish changes in the solution reached from failures of training to remain stable.

The paper also gives explicit constructions in which Single Shuffle produces distorted regression optima or classification divergence while Random Reshuffle avoids those problems. This does not turn the broader analysis into an unconditional guarantee for reshuffling. Empirical tests in realistic settings support the practical relevance of the separation. The findings make the shuffling procedure part of understanding optimization behavior when batch normalization is present.
summary.tldr: Batch normalization can make Single Shuffle and Random Reshuffle behave differently, with reshuffling showing greater stability in the studied settings.

title: On the Training Instability of Shuffling SGD with Batch Normalization

abstract: We study semiparametrically efficient estimation in off-policy evaluation (OPE) where the underlying Markov decision process (MDP) is linear with a known feature map. We characterize the variance lower bound for regular estimators in the linear MDP setting and propose an efficient estimator whose variance achieves that lower bound. Consistency and asymptotic normality of our estimator are established under mild conditions, which merely requires the only infinite-dimensional nuisance parameter to be estimated at a $n^{-1/4}$ convergence rate. We also construct an asymptotically valid confidence interval for statistical inference and conduct simulation studies to validate our results. To our knowledge, this is the first work that concerns efficient estimation in the presence of a known structure of MDPs in the OPE literature.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates a policy’s performance using data collected under a different policy. This paper studies how precisely that evaluation can be done when the environment is a linear Markov decision process with a known feature map. The known structure is central because it informs both the achievable precision and the estimator’s construction.

The authors characterize a variance lower bound for regular estimators in this setting and propose an estimator that attains it. This is the sense in which the method is semiparametrically efficient: it reaches the stated statistical precision limit. They also establish consistency and asymptotic normality under mild conditions, requiring the sole infinite-dimensional nuisance parameter to be estimated at a convergence rate of n to the power of minus one quarter.

The analysis leads to an asymptotically valid confidence interval, allowing uncertainty to accompany the policy-value estimate. Simulation studies validate the results. The contribution combines an efficiency benchmark, an estimator that reaches it, and an inference procedure, showing how known MDP structure can inform statistically precise policy evaluation.
summary.tldr: For linear MDPs with known features, the paper derives a variance limit and an efficient policy-value estimator with asymptotically valid confidence intervals.

title: Semiparametrically Efficient Off-Policy Evaluation in Linear Markov Decision Processes

abstract: In recent years, multiple notions of algorithmic fairness have arisen. One such notion is individual fairness (IF), which requires that individuals who are similar receive similar treatment. In parallel, matrix estimation (ME) has emerged as a natural paradigm for handling noisy data with missing values. In this work, we connect the two concepts. We show that pre-processing data using ME can improve an algorithm’s IF without sacrificing performance. Specifically, we show that using a popular ME method known as singular value thresholding (SVT) to pre-process the data provides a strong IF guarantee under appropriate conditions. We then show that, under analogous conditions, SVT pre-processing also yields estimates that are consistent and approximately minimax optimal. As such, the ME pre-processing step does not, under the stated conditions, increase the prediction error of the base algorithm, i.e., does not impose a fairness-performance trade-off. We verify these results on synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: Individual fairness asks an algorithm to treat similar individuals similarly. Matrix estimation addresses another problem: recovering useful information from data containing noise and missing values. This paper connects the two by asking whether improving the data before prediction can also improve an algorithm's individual fairness.

The proposed preprocessing step uses singular value thresholding, a matrix estimation method. Under appropriate conditions, the authors prove that this step provides a strong individual-fairness guarantee. Fairness is therefore addressed through the data supplied to a base algorithm, with the theoretical result explaining when that intervention can improve the similarity of treatment.

Under analogous conditions, the estimates are also consistent and approximately minimax optimal, meaning they have strong statistical accuracy properties. The paper concludes that, under its stated conditions, preprocessing does not increase the base algorithm's prediction error and therefore does not impose a fairness-performance trade-off. Experiments on synthetic and real data support these results. The conditional guarantees are central: they establish circumstances in which fairness and predictive performance can improve together.
summary.tldr: Under suitable conditions, singular value thresholding improves individual fairness without increasing prediction error.

title: Matrix Estimation for Individual Fairness

abstract: Reasoning from sequences of raw sensory data is a ubiquitous problem across fields ranging from medical devices to robotics. These problems often involve using long sequences of raw sensor data (e.g. magnetometers, piezoresistors) to predict sequences of desirable physical quantities (e.g. force, inertial measurements). While classical approaches are powerful for locally-linear prediction problems, they often fall short when using real-world sensors. These sensors are typically non-linear, are affected by extraneous variables (e.g. vibration), and exhibit data-dependent drift. For many problems, the prediction task is exacerbated by small labeled datasets since obtaining ground-truth labels requires expensive equipment. In this work, we present Hierarchical State-Space models (HiSS), a conceptually simple, new technique for continuous sequential prediction. HiSS stacks structured state-space models on top of each other to create a temporal hierarchy. Across six real-world sensor datasets, from tactile-based state prediction to accelerometer-based inertial measurement, HiSS outperforms state-of-the-art sequence models such as causal Transformers, LSTMs, S4, and Mamba by at least 23% on MSE. Our experiments further indicate that HiSS demonstrates efficient scaling to smaller datasets and is compatible with existing data-filtering techniques. Code, datasets and videos can be found on https://hiss-csp.github.io.

The paper introduces Hierarchical State-Space models, or HiSS. The method stacks structured state-space models to build a hierarchy over time for continuous sequence prediction. This architecture is intended for tasks that transform sensor readings into sequences of physical estimates, such as tactile state prediction or inertial measurement from accelerometers.

Across six real-world sensor datasets, HiSS improves mean squared error by at least 23% over the compared sequence models, including causal Transformers, LSTMs, S4, and Mamba. Further experiments indicate effective scaling to smaller datasets and compatibility with existing filtering techniques. These findings support temporal hierarchy as a useful architectural choice for the evaluated sensing problems, including settings where labeled measurements are scarce.
summary.tldr: HiSS stacks state-space models into a temporal hierarchy, improving sensor-sequence prediction error by at least 23% across six evaluated datasets.

title: Hierarchical State Space Models for Continuous Sequence-to-Sequence Modeling

abstract: We study the problem of unsupervised representation learning in slightly misspecified settings, and thus formalize the study of robustness of nonlinear representation learning. We focus on the case where the mixing is close to a local isometry in a suitable distance and show based on existing rigidity results that the mixing can be identified up to linear transformations and small errors. In a second step, we investigate Independent Component Analysis (ICA) with observations generated according to $x=f(s)=As+h(s)$ where $A$ is an invertible mixing matrix and $h$ a small perturbation. We show that we can approximately recover the matrix $A$ and the independent components. Together, these two results show approximate identifiability of nonlinear ICA with almost isometric mixing functions. Those results are a step towards identifiability results for unsupervised representation learning for real-world data that do not follow restrictive model classes.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether unsupervised representation learning remains identifiable when the data only approximately satisfy a model’s assumptions. The authors formalize robustness to slight misspecification through two related analyses of nonlinear mixing functions.

First, they consider mixing that is close, in a suitable distance, to a local isometry. Using existing rigidity results, they show that this mixing can be identified up to linear transformations and small errors. Second, they analyze independent component analysis when observations are an invertible linear mixture plus a small nonlinear perturbation, showing approximate recovery of both the mixing matrix and independent components.

The significance is that exact membership in a restrictive model class can be relaxed in the studied settings. The guarantees retain specific closeness and perturbation assumptions, providing a step toward understanding real-world misspecification rather than unrestricted nonlinear recovery.
summary.tldr: The paper proves approximate identifiability for nonlinear ICA under almost-isometric mixing and analyzes recovery under small nonlinear perturbations.

title: Robustness of Nonlinear Representation Learning

abstract: Designing deep neural network classifiers that perform robustly on distributions differing from the available training data is an active area of machine learning research. However, out-of-distribution generalization for regression—the analogous problem for modeling continuous targets—remains relatively unexplored. To tackle this problem, we return to first principles and analyze how the closed-form solution for Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression is sensitive to covariate shift. We characterize the out-of-distribution risk of the OLS model in terms of the eigenspectrum decomposition of the source and target data. We then use this insight to propose a method called Spectral Adapted Regressor (SpAR) for adapting the weights of the last layer of a pre-trained neural regression model to perform better on input data originating from a different distribution. We demonstrate how this lightweight spectral adaptation procedure can improve out-of-distribution performance for synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Regression models predict continuous quantities, and their performance can deteriorate when inputs come from a different distribution than the training data. This paper studies that problem by returning to ordinary least squares, whose explicit solution makes it possible to analyze sensitivity to covariate shift.

This spectral perspective describes how the geometry of the two distributions relates to the behavior of the fitted regression model. It provides the analytical basis for deciding how a model’s regression weights should adapt.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the procedure can improve performance on shifted inputs. The contribution links an interpretable analysis of linear regression with a practical adjustment for neural models facing a different input distribution.
summary.tldr: SpAR uses a spectral analysis of distribution shift to adapt a neural regressor’s final layer and improve tested out-of-distribution performance.

title: Out of the Ordinary: Spectrally Adapting Regression for Covariate Shift

abstract: Studying the complex interactions between different brain regions is crucial in neuroscience. Various statistical methods have explored the latent communication across multiple brain regions. Two main categories are the Gaussian Process (GP) and Linear Dynamical System (LDS), each with unique strengths. The GP-based approach effectively discovers latent variables with frequency bands and communication directions. Conversely, the LDS-based approach is computationally efficient but lacks powerful expressiveness in latent representation. In this study, we merge both methodologies by creating an LDS mirroring a multi-output GP, termed Multi-Region Markovian Gaussian Process (MRM-GP). Our work establishes a connection between an LDS and a multi-output GP that explicitly models frequencies and phase delays within the latent space of neural recordings. Consequently, the model achieves a linear inference cost over time points and provides an interpretable low-dimensional representation, revealing communication directions across brain regions and separating oscillatory communications into different frequency bands.

summary.tldr: MRM-GP connects Gaussian processes with linear dynamical systems to infer frequency-specific directional brain communication at linear cost in recording length.

title: Multi-Region Markovian Gaussian Process: An Efficient Method to Discover Directional Communications Across Multiple Brain Regions

abstract: Solving large-scale linear programming (LP) problems is an important task in various areas such as communication networks, power systems, finance and logistics. Recently, two distinct approaches have emerged to expedite LP solving: (i) First-order methods (FOMs); (ii) Learning to optimize (L2O). In this work, we propose an FOM-unrolled neural network (NN) called PDHG-Net, and propose a two-stage L2O method to solve large-scale LP problems. The new architecture PDHG-Net is designed by unrolling the recently emerged PDHG method into a neural network, combined with channel-expansion techniques borrowed from graph neural networks. We prove that the proposed PDHG-Net can recover PDHG algorithm, thus can approximate optimal solutions of LP instances with a polynomial number of neurons. We propose a two-stage inference approach: first use PDHG-Net to generate an approximate solution, and then apply PDHG algorithm to further improve the solution. Experiments show that our approach can significantly accelerate LP solving, achieving up to a 3$\times$ speedup compared to FOMs for large-scale LP problems.

title: PDHG-Unrolled Learning-to-Optimize Method for Large-Scale Linear Programming

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have attracted great attention for their energy-efficient operations and biologically inspired structures, offering potential advantages over Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) in terms of energy efficiency and interpretability. Nonetheless, similar to ANNs, the robustness of SNNs remains a challenge, especially when facing adversarial attacks. Existing techniques, whether adapted from ANNs or specifically designed for SNNs, exhibit limitations in training SNNs or defending against strong attacks. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to enhance the robustness of SNNs through gradient sparsity regularization. We observe that SNNs exhibit greater resilience to random perturbations compared to adversarial perturbations, even at larger scales. Motivated by this, we aim to narrow the gap between SNNs under adversarial and random perturbations, thereby improving their overall robustness. To achieve this, we theoretically prove that this performance gap is upper bounded by the gradient sparsity of the probability associated with the true label concerning the input image, laying the groundwork for a practical strategy to train robust SNNs by regularizing the gradient sparsity. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on both image-based and event-based datasets. The results demonstrate notable improvements in the robustness of SNNs. Our work highlights the importance of gradient sparsity in SNNs and its role in enhancing robustness.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer potential energy-efficiency and interpretability advantages, but they remain vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. This paper starts from an observation about that vulnerability: the networks tolerate random perturbations better than deliberately adversarial ones, even when the random changes are larger. The authors aim to narrow this performance gap.

Their analysis connects the gap to the input gradient of the probability assigned to the true label. This gradient describes how that probability responds to changes in the input image. They prove an upper bound on the gap involving gradient sparsity, providing a theoretical basis for a training strategy that regularizes this property.

The resulting method adds gradient sparsity regularization to improve robustness. Experiments on both image-based and event-based datasets report notable improvements, supporting the usefulness of the theoretical connection in practical training. The contribution links a measurable aspect of input sensitivity to the difference between random and adversarial disturbances, then uses that link to shape how spiking networks learn.
summary.tldr: Gradient sparsity regularization improves spiking-network robustness, motivated by a bound connecting gradient sparsity to the random-versus-adversarial performance gap.

title: Enhancing Adversarial Robustness in SNNs with Sparse Gradients

abstract: Recently, Cutkosky et al. introduce the online-to-non-convex framework, which utilizes online learning methods to solve non-smooth non-convex optimization problems, and achieves an $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}\delta^{-1})$ gradient complexity for finding $(\delta,\epsilon)$-stationary points. However, their results rely on the bounded variance assumption of stochastic gradients and only hold in expectation. To address these limitations, we investigate the case that stochastic gradients obey heavy-tailed distributions with finite $\mathfrak{p}$-th moments for some $\mathfrak{p}\in(1,2]$, and propose a novel algorithm which is able to identify a $(\delta,\epsilon)$-stationary point with high probability, after consuming $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-\frac{2\mathfrak{p}-1}{\mathfrak{p}-1}}\delta^{-1})$ stochastic gradients. The key idea is first incorporating the gradient clipping technique into the online-to-non-convex framework to produce a sequence of points, the averaged gradient norms of which is no greater than $\epsilon$. Then, we propose a validation method to select one $(\delta,\epsilon)$-stationary point among the candidates. When gradient distributions have bounded variance, i.e., $\mathfrak{p}=2$, our result turns into $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3}\delta^{-1})$, which improves the existing $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-4}\delta^{-1})$ high-probability bound. When the objective is smooth, our algorithm can also find an $\epsilon$-stationary point with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-\frac{3\mathfrak{p}-2}{\mathfrak{p}-1}})$ gradient queries.

paragraphs: Optimizing a non-smooth, non-convex objective is difficult when stochastic gradients can have large, heavy-tailed fluctuations. Earlier online-to-non-convex results assumed bounded gradient variance and provided guarantees in expectation. This paper seeks a stationary point with high probability under the weaker requirement of a finite p-th gradient moment, for p between one and two.

The algorithm first adds gradient clipping to the online-to-non-convex framework, limiting extreme gradient contributions while generating candidate points. It then uses a validation procedure to select a candidate meeting the required stationarity criterion. This second step turns a guarantee about the generated sequence into a high-probability statement about a selected output.

The resulting gradient complexity is approximately epsilon raised to minus (2p−1)/(p−1), multiplied by delta inverse, with logarithmic factors suppressed. When p equals two, the bound becomes approximately epsilon to minus three times delta inverse, improving the prior high-probability epsilon-to-minus-four dependence. The authors also establish a separate bound for smooth objectives. These guarantees concern approximate stationarity under the stated moment conditions.
summary.tldr: Gradient clipping and candidate validation yield improved high-probability stationarity guarantees for stochastic optimization with heavy-tailed gradients.

title: High-Probability Bound for Non-Smooth Non-Convex Stochastic Optimization with Heavy Tails

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) holds the promise of sample-efficient learning by utilizing a world model, which models how the environment works and typically encompasses components for two tasks: observation modeling and reward modeling. In this paper, through a dedicated empirical investigation, we gain a deeper understanding of the role each task plays in world models and uncover the overlooked potential of sample-efficient MBRL by mitigating the domination of either observation or reward modeling. Our key insight is that while prevalent approaches of explicit MBRL attempt to restore abundant details of the environment via observation models, it is difficult due to the environment’s complexity and limited model capacity. On the other hand, reward models, while dominating implicit MBRL and adept at learning compact task-centric dynamics, are inadequate for sample-efficient learning without richer learning signals. Motivated by these insights and discoveries, we propose a simple yet effective approach, HarmonyDream, which automatically adjusts loss coefficients to maintain task harmonization, i.e. a dynamic equilibrium between the two tasks in world model learning. Our experiments show that the base MBRL method equipped with HarmonyDream gains 10%-69% absolute performance boosts on visual robotic tasks and sets a new state-of-the-art result on the Atari 100K benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/thuml/HarmonyDream.

paragraphs: A world model helps a reinforcement-learning agent learn how its environment behaves. Training it typically involves modeling observations and rewards. This paper investigates what happens when either objective dominates, finding that the balance between them can substantially affect how efficiently the agent learns from experience.

Observation modeling supplies rich information but can demand more environmental detail than a limited-capacity model can capture. Reward modeling focuses on task-relevant dynamics, yet the authors find that it lacks sufficiently rich learning signals on its own for sample-efficient learning. HarmonyDream responds by automatically adjusting the coefficients of these two training losses, maintaining a changing balance as learning proceeds.

Experiments report absolute performance gains of 10%–69% when HarmonyDream is added to the base method on visual robotic tasks, alongside a new state-of-the-art result on Atari 100K. The findings suggest that better use of existing world-model objectives can unlock substantial performance improvements. The mechanism matters because it addresses how competing learning signals share model capacity, rather than simply asking the model to reconstruct more detail.
summary.tldr: HarmonyDream automatically balances observation and reward learning inside world models, improving sample-efficient reinforcement learning in the reported benchmarks.

title: HarmonyDream: Task Harmonization Inside World Models

abstract: An effective approach for learning both safety constraints and control policies is Inverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning (ICRL). Previous ICRL algorithms commonly employ an online learning framework that permits unlimited sampling from an interactive environment. This setting, however, is infeasible in many realistic applications where data collection is dangerous and expensive. To address this challenge, we propose Inverse Constrained Superior Distribution Correction Estimation (ICSDICE) as an offline ICRL solver. ICSDICE extracts feasible constraints from superior distributions, thereby highlighting policies with expert-exceeding rewards maximization ability. To estimate these distributions, ICSDICE solves a regularized dual optimization problem for safe control by exploiting the observed reward signals and expert preferences. Striving for transferable constraints and unbiased estimations, ICSDICE actively encourages sparsity and incorporates a discounting effect within the learned and observed distributions. Empirical studies show that ICSDICE outperforms other baselines by accurately recovering the constraints and adapting to high-dimensional environments. The code is available at https://github.com/quangr/ICSDICE.

paragraphs: Inverse constrained reinforcement learning aims to infer safety constraints as well as control policies. Many existing methods assume ongoing access to an interactive environment for extensive data collection. That assumption is difficult to satisfy when collecting more experience is dangerous or costly, motivating a method that learns from offline demonstrations.

ICSDICE estimates superior distributions and extracts feasible constraints from them. These distributions emphasize policies with the capacity to achieve rewards beyond those of the expert. The method estimates them through a regularized dual optimization problem, drawing on both observed reward signals and expert preferences to guide safe control.

The approach encourages sparsity and accounts for discounting within its learned and observed distributions, with the goals of obtaining transferable constraints and unbiased estimates. Empirical studies report better constraint recovery than the compared baselines and successful adaptation to high-dimensional environments. The contribution is an offline route to learning constraints while seeking reward-improving policies, reducing reliance on the interactive sampling assumed by earlier approaches.
summary.tldr: ICSDICE learns safety constraints from offline demonstrations using reward signals and expert preferences to identify promising feasible policies.

title: Learning Constraints from Offline Demonstrations via Superior Distribution Correction Estimation

abstract: The computational difficulties of large language model (LLM) inference remain a significant obstacle to their widespread deployment. The need for many applications to support long input sequences and process them in large batches typically causes token-generation to be bottlenecked by data transfer. For this reason, we introduce SparQ Attention, a technique for increasing the inference throughput of LLMs by utilising memory bandwidth more efficiently within the attention layers, through selective fetching of the cached history. Our proposed technique can be applied directly to off-the-shelf LLMs during inference, without requiring any modification to the pre-training setup or additional fine-tuning. We show that SparQ Attention brings up to 8x savings in attention data transfers without substantial drops in accuracy, by evaluating Llama 2 and 3, Mistral, Gemma and Pythia models on a wide range of downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Generating tokens with large language models can be limited by moving data rather than by computation alone. The paper highlights this bottleneck for applications that combine long input sequences with large batches. Attention must access cached history during generation, making the amount of transferred data an important target for improving inference throughput.

SparQ Attention addresses that target by selectively fetching cached history inside attention layers. The technique uses memory bandwidth more efficiently and can be applied directly to existing language models during inference. It requires neither changes to their pre-training setup nor additional fine-tuning, so its use does not depend on retraining a model specifically for the method.

Evaluations cover Llama 2 and 3, Mistral, Gemma, and Pythia across a range of downstream tasks. The reported savings reach up to eightfold in attention data transfers without substantial accuracy drops. That result concerns attention's transfer requirements, demonstrating that selective access can reduce a key inference bottleneck while retaining accuracy in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SparQ Attention selectively fetches cached history, reducing attention data transfers by up to eightfold without substantial accuracy drops in evaluated models.

title: SparQ Attention: Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference

abstract: Machine learning models fail catastrophically under distribution shift, but a surprisingly effective way to empirically improve robustness to some types of shift (e.g., Imagenet-A/C) is to use stronger open-vocabulary classifiers derived from foundation models. In this work, we first note that for shifts governed by spurious correlations (features spuriously correlated with the label on the training data, but not on test), the zero-shot and few-shot performance of foundation models is no better than ERM models, and remains unchanged when pretrained data/model size is scaled. Secondly, even in these situations, foundation models are quite accurate at predicting the value of the spurious feature. In a simplified setup, we theoretically analyze both these findings. Specifically, we show that during contrastive pretraining, the simplicity bias of foundation models tends to result in the learning of features that mostly rely on the spurious attribute, compared to more robust features. We leverage these observations to propose Prompting for Robustness (PfR) which first uses foundation models to zero-shot predict the spurious attribute on labeled examples, and then learns a classifier with balanced performance across different groups of labels and spurious attribute. Across 5 vision and language tasks, we show that PfR’s performance nearly equals that of an oracle algorithm (group DRO) that leverages human labeled spurious attributes.

paragraphs: Foundation models can handle some distribution shifts well, but this paper finds that spurious correlations remain a problem. When training-time associations between labels and irrelevant features break at test time, zero-shot and few-shot performance is no better than empirical-risk-minimization models in the studied settings. Increasing pretraining data or model size leaves this performance unchanged.

The authors also observe that foundation models can accurately predict the spurious feature itself. summary.tldr: Prompting for Robustness uses foundation-model predictions of spurious attributes to train classifiers with more balanced group performance.

title: Prompting is a Double-Edged Sword: Improving Worst-Group Robustness of Foundation Models

abstract: Equivariant neural networks require explicit knowledge of the symmetry group. Automatic symmetry discovery methods aim to relax this constraint and learn invariance and equivariance from data. However, existing symmetry discovery methods are limited to simple linear symmetries and cannot handle the complexity of real-world data. We propose a novel generative model, Latent LieGAN (LaLiGAN), which can discover symmetries of nonlinear group actions. It learns a mapping from the data space to a latent space where the symmetries become linear and simultaneously discovers symmetries in the latent space. Theoretically, we show that our model can express nonlinear symmetries under some conditions about the group action. Experimentally, we demonstrate that our method can accurately discover the intrinsic symmetry in high-dimensional dynamical systems. LaLiGAN also results in a well-structured latent space that is useful for downstream tasks including equation discovery and long-term forecasting.

title: Latent Space Symmetry Discovery

abstract: We present DriveGPT, a scalable behavior model for autonomous driving. We model driving as a sequential decision-making task, and learn a transformer model to predict future agent states as tokens in an autoregressive fashion. We scale up our model parameters and training data by multiple orders of magnitude, enabling us to explore the scaling properties in terms of dataset size, model parameters, and compute. We evaluate DriveGPT across different scales in a planning task, through both quantitative metrics and qualitative examples, including closed-loop driving in complex real-world scenarios. In a separate prediction task, DriveGPT outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and exhibits improved performance by pretraining on a large-scale dataset, further validating the benefits of data scaling.

This formulation creates a behavior model whose capacity and training data can be expanded systematically.

The authors increase both model parameters and dataset size by multiple orders of magnitude. This lets them study how performance relates to model size, data volume, and computation. They evaluate models at different scales on a planning task using quantitative measures and qualitative examples, including closed-loop driving in complex real-world scenarios.

DriveGPT outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines used in that task, and pretraining on a large dataset further improves performance. summary.tldr: DriveGPT models driving through autoregressive state prediction and finds benefits from scaling training data, including stronger results on a separate prediction task.

title: DriveGPT: Scaling Autoregressive Behavior Models for Driving

abstract: The subset selection problem with a monotone and submodular objective function under a linear cost constraint has wide applications, such as maximum coverage, influence maximization, and feature selection, just to name a few. Various greedy algorithms have been proposed with good performance both theoretically and empirically. Recently, evolutionary algorithms (EAs), inspired by Darwin’s evolution theory, have emerged as a prominent methodology, offering both empirical advantages and theoretical guarantees. Among these, the multi-objective EA, POMC, has demonstrated the best empirical performance to date, achieving an approximation guarantee of $(1/2)(1-1/e)$. However, there remains a gap in the approximation bounds of EAs compared to greedy algorithms, and their full theoretical potential is yet to be realized. In this paper, we re-analyze the approximation performance of POMC theoretically, and derive an improved guarantee of $1/2$, which thus provides theoretical justification for its encouraging empirical performance. Furthermore, we propose a novel multi-objective EA, EPOL, which not only achieves the best-known practical approximation guarantee of $0.6174$, but also delivers superior empirical performance in applications of maximum coverage and influence maximization. We hope this work can help better solving the subset selection problem, but also enhance our theoretical understanding of EAs.

paragraphs: The paper studies selecting a useful subset while keeping its total cost within a budget. Its objective is monotone and submodular: adding items does not reduce value, and additional items have diminishing returns. This setting includes maximum coverage, influence maximization, and feature selection, where evolutionary methods already offer promising practical performance.

The authors first revisit POMC, an existing multi-objective evolutionary algorithm. A new analysis raises its approximation guarantee from one-half times one minus one over e to one-half. This is a stronger theoretical guarantee for the existing algorithm, helping explain its encouraging empirical performance without requiring a change to the method itself.

It also reports superior empirical performance on maximum coverage and influence maximization. Together, the results strengthen both the theoretical case for evolutionary subset selection and its demonstrated effectiveness, narrowing the gap between favorable practical behavior and what analysis can guarantee under the stated objective and cost constraints.
summary.tldr: A stronger analysis of POMC and the new EPOL algorithm improve guarantees for budget-constrained submodular subset selection.

title: Improved Theoretically-Grounded Evolutionary Algorithms for Subset Selection with a Linear Cost Constraint

abstract: Scientific equation discovery is a fundamental task in the history of scientific progress, enabling the derivation of laws governing natural phenomena. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained interest for this task due to their potential to leverage embedded scientific knowledge for hypothesis generation. However, evaluating the true discovery capabilities of these methods remains challenging, as existing benchmarks often rely on common equations that are susceptible to memorization by LLMs, leading to inflated performance metrics that do not reflect actual discovery. In this paper, we introduce LLM-SRBench, a comprehensive benchmark with 239 challenging problems across four scientific domains specifically designed to evaluate LLM-based scientific equation discovery methods while preventing trivial memorization. Our benchmark comprises two main categories: LSR-Transform, which transforms common physical models into less common mathematical representations to test reasoning beyond memorization, and LSR-Synth, which introduces synthetic, discovery-driven problems requiring data-driven reasoning. Through extensive evaluation of several state-of-the-art methods on LLM-SRBench, using both open and closed LLMs, we find that the best-performing system so far achieves only 31.5% symbolic accuracy. These findings highlight the challenges of scientific equation discovery, positioning LLM-SRBench as a valuable resource for future research.

title: LLM-SRBench: A New Benchmark for Scientific Equation Discovery with Large Language Models

abstract: Developing generative models to create or conditionally create symbolic music presents unique challenges due to the combination of limited data availability and the need for high precision in note pitch. To address these challenges, we introduce an efficient Fine-Grained Guidance (FGG) approach within diffusion models. FGG guides the diffusion models to generate music that aligns more closely with the control and intent of expert composers, which is critical to improve the accuracy, listenability, and quality of generated music. This approach empowers diffusion models to excel in advanced applications such as improvisation, and interactive music creation. We derive theoretical characterizations for both the challenges in symbolic music generation and the effects of the FGG approach. We provide numerical experiments and subjective evaluation to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. We have published a demo page to showcase performances, which enables real-time interactive generation.

A generated piece also needs to reflect the composer’s intentions to be useful in controlled creation. This paper introduces Fine-Grained Guidance, or FGG, as an efficient way to steer diffusion models toward those musical requirements.

FGG guides generation to align more closely with expert composers’ control and intent. The authors connect this guidance to accuracy, listenability, and overall musical quality. The intended applications include improvisation and interactive creation, where a system must support active musical direction rather than merely produce an unconstrained sequence.

The paper provides theoretical characterizations of both the difficulties of symbolic music generation and the effects of its guidance method. Numerical experiments and subjective evaluation support the approach’s effectiveness. A demonstration also supports real-time interactive generation. Together, these contributions connect an analysis of the generation problem with a control mechanism and evaluations that address both technical behavior and perceived musical results.
summary.tldr: Fine-Grained Guidance steers diffusion-based symbolic music generation toward composers’ intentions, with theoretical and experimental support.

title: Efficient Fine-Grained Guidance for Diffusion Model Based Symbolic Music Generation

abstract: Convergence in high-probability (HP) has attracted increasing interest, due to implying exponentially decaying tail bounds and strong guarantees for individual runs of an algorithm. While many works study HP guarantees in centralized settings, much less is understood in the decentralized setup, where existing works require strong assumptions, like uniformly bounded gradients, or asymptotically vanishing noise. This results in a significant gap between the assumptions used to establish convergence in the HP and the mean-squared error (MSE) sense, and is also contrary to centralized settings, where it is known that $\mathtt{SGD}$ converges in HP under the same conditions on the cost function as needed for MSE convergence. Motivated by these observations, we study the HP convergence of Decentralized $\mathtt{SGD}$ ($\mathtt{DSGD}$) in the presence of light-tailed noise, providing several strong results. First, we show that $\mathtt{DSGD}$ converges in HP under the same conditions on the cost as in the MSE sense, removing the restrictive assumptions used in prior works. Second, our sharp analysis yields order-optimal rates for both non-convex and strongly convex costs. Third, we establish a linear speed-up in the number of users, leading to matching or strictly better transient times than those obtained from MSE results, further underlining the tightness of our analysis. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that shows $\mathtt{DSGD}$ achieves a linear speed-up in the HP sense. Our relaxed assumptions and sharp rates stem from several technical results of independent interest, including a result on the variance-reduction effect of decentralized methods in the HP sense, as well as a novel bound on the moment-generating function of strongly convex costs, of interest even in centralized settings. Numerical experiments validate our theory.

summary.tldr: Under light-tailed noise, decentralized SGD achieves sharp high-probability convergence and linear user-count speed-up with relaxed cost-function assumptions.

title: High-Probability Convergence Guarantees of Decentralized SGD

abstract: As context windows in large language models continue to expand, it is essential to characterize how attention behaves at extreme sequence lengths. We introduce token sample complexity: the rate at which attention computed on $n$ tokens converges to its infinite-token limit. We estimate finite-$n$ convergence bounds at two levels: pointwise uniform convergence of the attention map, and convergence of moments for the transformed token distribution. For compactly supported (and more generally sub-Gaussian) distributions, our first result shows that the attention map converges uniformly on a ball of radius $R$ at rate $C(R)/\sqrt{n}$, where $C(R)$ grows exponentially with $R$. For large $R$, this estimate loses practical value, and our second result addresses this issue by establishing convergence rates for the moments of the transformed distribution (the token output of the attention layer). In this case, the rate is $C’(R)/n^{\beta}$ with $\beta<\tfrac{1}{2}$, and $C’(R)$ depends polynomially on the size of the support of the distribution. The exponent $\beta$ depends on the attention geometry and the spectral properties of the token distribution. We also examine the regime in which the attention parameter tends to infinity and the softmax approaches a hardmax, and in this setting, we establish a logarithmic rate of convergence. Experiments on synthetic and real data support our predictions and show that the predicted slowdown is reflected in downstream accuracy.

These results show that increasing token count can yield convergence whose pace depends strongly on the attention regime and token distribution.
summary.tldr: Token sample complexity quantifies how attention approaches its infinite-context limit and reveals geometry-dependent slowdowns, especially near hardmax.

title: Token Sample Complexity of Attention

abstract: Amodal instance segmentation is hindered by the scarcity of scalable and transferable annotations. We introduce MaviGen, an automated 3D retail scene modeling and rendering framework that generates photorealistic multi-view images with complete amodal masks. Building on MaviGen, we present the IRAIS dataset, a sim-to-real benchmark comprising a large-scale synthetic multi-view set (3D-IRAIS) and a human-annotated real image set (Real-IRAIS), both sharing unified label definitions and evaluation protocols to facilitate rigorous transfer studies. We propose EUREKA, an encoder-only, query-efficient network for amodal instance segmentation that performs full-image multi-task inference via unified amodal/visible queries and dual mask heads. The dual heads enable mutual supervision between complete and visible masks, while the conditional masked self-attention mechanism further strengthens occlusion reasoning. Experiments establish strong baselines on IRAIS and achieve state-of-the-art performance on D2SA and COCOA-cls, demonstrating substantial improvements in sim-to-real transfer.

paragraphs: Amodal instance segmentation aims to identify an object’s complete extent, including portions hidden behind other objects. Training this capability is difficult because complete object annotations are scarce and may transfer poorly between synthetic and real images. This paper addresses the data and modeling sides of that problem together.

MaviGen automatically builds and renders three-dimensional retail scenes, producing realistic images from multiple viewpoints with complete object masks. The resulting IRAIS benchmark pairs a large synthetic collection with human-annotated real images. Shared label definitions and evaluation procedures make it possible to study transfer between the two collections using a consistent setup.

The proposed EUREKA network predicts visible and complete masks through linked queries and separate mask heads that supervise each other. Conditional masked self-attention further supports reasoning about occlusion. Experiments establish baselines on IRAIS, report state-of-the-art performance on D2SA and COCOA-cls, and show substantial transfer improvements. The contribution combines scalable annotation generation, a transfer benchmark, and an architecture designed around hidden object regions.
summary.tldr: A synthetic-to-real benchmark and a network that jointly predicts visible and complete masks improve segmentation of partially hidden objects.

title: Amodal Instance Segmentation with IRAIS Dataset for Sim-to-Real Transfer

abstract: The remarkable success of the Adam in training neural networks has naturally led to the widespread use of its descent-ascent counterpart, Adam-DA, for solving zero-sum games. Despite its popularity in practice, a rigorous theoretical understanding of Adam-DA still lags behind. In this paper, we derive ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that serve as continuous-time limits of the Adam-DA. These ODEs closely approximate the discrete-time dynamics of Adam-DA, providing a tractable analytical framework for understanding its behavior in zero-sum games. Using this ODE approach, we investigate two fundamental aspects of Adam-DA: local convergence and implicit gradient regularization. Our analysis reveals that the roles of the first- and second-order momentum parameters in zero-sum games are exactly the opposite of their well-documented effects in minimization problems. We validate these predictions through GAN experiments across multiple architectures and datasets, demonstrating the practical implications of this reversed momentum effect.

The paper investigates this Adam-DA optimizer theoretically. Its motivation is that practical popularity has outpaced a rigorous understanding of how the optimizer behaves in competitive learning.
