The paper’s evidence links its local dynamical analysis to practical adversarial training, while keeping the continuous-time equations as approximations of the discrete optimizer.
summary.tldr: An ODE analysis of Adam-DA finds momentum effects opposite to those in minimization, with supporting experiments in adversarial network training.

title: Understanding Dynamics of Adam in Zero-Sum Games: An ODE Approach

abstract: We introduce a multi-scale Image Super Resolution (ISR) method building on recent advances in Visual Auto-Regressive (VAR) modeling. VAR models break image tokenization into additive, gradually increasing scales, using Residual Quantization (RQ), an approach that aligns perfectly with our target ISR task. Previous works taking advantage of this synergy suffer from two main shortcomings. First, due to the limitations in RQ, they only generate images at a predefined fixed scale, failing to map intermediate outputs to the corresponding image scales. They also rely on large backbones or a large corpus of annotated data to achieve better performance. To address both shortcomings, we introduce two novel components to the VAR training for ISR, aiming at increasing its flexibility and reducing its complexity. In particular, we introduce a) a Hierarchical Image Tokenization (HIT) approach that progressively represents images at different scales while enforcing token overlap across scales, and b) a Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) regularization term that, relying solely on the (LR,HR) pair, encourages the transformer to produce the latter over the former. Our proposed HIT acts as a strong inductive bias for the VAR training, resulting in a small model (300M params vs 1B params of VARSR), that achieves state-of-the-art results without external training data, and that delivers multi-scale outputs with a single forward pass.

paragraphs: Visual autoregressive models build image representations through progressively finer scales, making them a natural fit for increasing image resolution. However, earlier approaches using residual quantization produce images at a predefined scale, with intermediate representations not necessarily corresponding to images at intermediate resolutions. They also depend on large models or substantial annotated training data.

This paper introduces Hierarchical Image Tokenization, which represents images progressively while enforcing overlap between tokens across scales. That structure encourages the model to learn representations useful for multiple output resolutions. A second component adds a direct preference optimization regularizer that uses only the low-resolution and high-resolution image pair, encouraging generation of the high-resolution version.

Together, these components let the method produce several image scales in a single forward pass. The authors report state-of-the-art results without external training data using a 300-million-parameter model, compared with the one-billion-parameter VARSR model. The results connect a more suitable token representation to both flexible output resolution and reduced model size, rather than treating these as separate design goals.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical tokenization and preference regularization enable a smaller super-resolution model to generate multiple image scales in one pass.

title: Hierarchical Image Tokenization for Multi-Scale Image Super Resolution

abstract: The dynamics of gradient-based training in neural networks often exhibit nontrivial structures; hence, understanding them remains a central challenge in theoretical machine learning. In particular, the concept of feature unlearning, in which a neural network progressively loses previously learned features over long training, has gained attention. In this study, we consider the infinite-width limit of a two-layer neural network trained with a large-batch stochastic gradient, then derive differential equations with different time scales, revealing the mechanism and conditions for feature unlearning to occur. Specifically, we utilize the fast-slow dynamics: while an alignment of first-layer weights develops rapidly, the second-layer weights develop slowly. The direction of the flow on a critical manifold, determined by the slow dynamics, decides whether feature unlearning occurs. We give numerical validation of the result and derive theoretical grounding and scaling laws for the feature unlearning. Our results yield the following insights: (i) the strength of the primary nonlinear term in the data induces the feature unlearning, and (ii) an initial scale of the second-layer weights mitigates the feature unlearning. Our result should be understood as a population loss of alignment rather than finite-sample overfitting. Technically, our analysis utilizes Tensor Programs and singular perturbation theory.
originalAbstract: The dynamics of gradient-based training in neural networks often exhibit nontrivial structures; hence, understanding them remains a central challenge in theoretical machine learning. In particular, the concept of feature unlearning, in which a neural network progressively loses previously learned features over long training, has gained attention. In this study, we consider the infinite-width limit of a two-layer neural network trained with a large-batch stochastic gradient, then derive differential equations with different time scales, revealing the mechanism and conditions for feature unlearning to occur. Specifically, we utilize the fast-slow dynamics: while an alignment of first-layer weights develops rapidly, the second-layer weights develop slowly. The direction of the flow on a critical manifold, determined by the slow dynamics, decides whether feature unlearning occurs. We give numerical validation of the result and derive theoretical grounding and scaling laws for the feature unlearning. Our results yield the following insights: (i) the strength of the primary nonlinear term in the data induces the feature unlearning, and (ii) an initial scale of the second-layer weights mitigates the feature unlearning. Our result should be understood as a population loss of alignment rather than finite-sample overfitting. Technically, our analysis utilizes Tensor Programs and singular perturbation theory.

paragraphs: A network can acquire useful feature alignment early in training and then lose it as training continues. This paper analyzes that phenomenon in the infinite-width limit of a two-layer network trained with large-batch stochastic gradients. Its focus is a loss of alignment at the population level, rather than overfitting a finite training sample.

The analysis separates training into fast and slow processes. First-layer weights develop alignment quickly, while second-layer weights evolve more slowly. The slow process determines the direction of movement along a critical manifold, a structure governing the coupled dynamics, and thereby determines whether previously acquired alignment is lost.

Using Tensor Programs and singular perturbation theory, the authors derive equations, conditions, and scaling laws for this behavior, with numerical validation. They find that the strength of the leading nonlinear term in the data can induce feature unlearning, while the initial scale of second-layer weights can mitigate it. These results explain how continued optimization can undo earlier feature learning within the analyzed regime, and identify properties of both the data and initialization that influence the outcome.
summary.tldr: A fast–slow analysis explains when infinite-width two-layer networks lose learned feature alignment and how initialization can mitigate that loss.

title: Dichotomy of Feature Learning and Unlearning: Fast-Slow Analysis on Neural Networks with Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Sparse tangent portfolio optimization aims to learn an interpretable, low-cardinality portfolio in the tangency direction of the mean-variance frontier. However, the associated cardinality-constrained formulation is NP-hard, and standard predict-then-optimize pipelines often misalign forecasting accuracy with downstream portfolio quality. We propose an end-to-end decision-focused learning framework that reformulates Sharpe ratio maximization as a Disciplined Parametrized Programming (DPP)-compliant convex programming layer and replaces discrete selection with a smooth top-$k$ operator enforcing an exact cardinality $k$. This enables gradient flow through prediction, asset selection, and re-optimization, allowing the predictive model to directly optimize portfolio performance. Across four major equity markets, our method achieves competitive and often superior out-of-sample Sharpe ratios compared with historical and prediction-focused baselines, with particularly strong gains in larger asset universes. Our code is publicly available.

The limited asset count supports interpretability, but the corresponding discrete optimization is NP-hard. A separate difficulty arises when predictions are trained for forecast accuracy: better forecasts need not translate into better portfolio decisions.

The paper connects prediction, asset selection, and portfolio re-optimization in one trainable system. It reformulates Sharpe ratio maximization as a convex programming layer compatible with Disciplined Parametrized Programming. A smooth top-k operator replaces discrete selection while enforcing exactly k selected assets. These components let gradients pass through the decision process so the predictive model can learn directly from portfolio performance.

Across four major equity markets, the approach obtains competitive and often better out-of-sample Sharpe ratios than historical and prediction-focused baselines. Gains are particularly strong when choosing among larger asset universes. The stated findings support aligning the training objective with the eventual portfolio decision, while retaining explicit control over how many assets the portfolio contains.
summary.tldr: An end-to-end portfolio model learns predictions and exact-size asset selections directly for downstream Sharpe ratio performance.

title: Decision-focused Sparse Tangent Portfolio Optimization

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback is the leading approach to aligning powerful AI systems so that they can be safe and helpful for humanity. While RLHF is typically modelled as a problem of learning a single preference ranking from noisy feedback, true human preferences are complex and often conflicting, representing substantive disagreements stemming from the diversity of individual human values. With this motivation, a recent line of research has studied RLHF from the perspective of social choice theory, which provides a set of well-established desirable properties for aggregating diverse preferences. Seen through this lens, the standard learning objective in RLHF is equivalent to aggregating diverse human preferences via the Borda count rule. At the same time, several new RLHF algorithms have been proposed, which turn out to be equivalent to the von Neumann winner social choice rule. However, the connection between social choice theory and RLHF has thus far ignored the critical role of regularization to prevent divergence from a reference policy, which is utilized in essentially all practical RLHF algorithms. In this paper, we study how regularization affects the social choice axioms satisfied by different RLHF algorithms, and prove that regularization improves the axiomatic properties of the von Neumann winner rule. In contrast, the Borda count rule still fails to satisfy key social choice axioms even when regularized. These results provide a principled argument grounded in social choice theory for utilizing practical RLHF algorithms that correspond to the von Neumann winner, rather than the standard RLHF objective.

The contribution concerns the formal properties of aggregating conflicting preferences, showing that regularization affects more than the policy’s distance from its reference.
summary.tldr: Regularization improves the social choice properties of von Neumann winner RLHF methods, while regularized Borda-based objectives still fail key axioms.

title: The Axiomatic Value of Regularization in AI Alignment from Human Preferences

abstract: While plan-and-infill decoding in Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) shows promise for mathematical and code reasoning, performance remains highly sensitive to slot infilling order, often yielding substantial output variance. We introduce DiffuSearch, a framework that formulates slot selection as decision making and optimises infilling orders through Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). DiffuSearch uses look-ahead simulations to evaluate partial completions before commitment, systematically exploring the combinatorial space of generation orders. Experiments show an average improvement of 3.2% over autoregressive baselines and 8.0% over baseline plan-and-infill, with notable gains of 19.5% on MBPP and 4.9% on MATH500. Our analysis reveals that while DiffuSearch predominantly follows sequential ordering, incorporating non-sequential generation is essential for maximising performance. We observe that larger exploration constants, rather than increased simulations, are necessary to overcome model confidence biases and discover effective orderings. These findings establish MCTS-based planning as an effective approach for enhancing generation quality in MDMs.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion language models can generate a response by filling open positions in a planned sequence. For mathematical and coding tasks, the order of those choices can substantially affect the final answer. DiffuSearch treats choosing the next position as a planning problem, making generation order an explicit part of the decoding method.

The framework uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to explore possible filling orders. Look-ahead simulations evaluate partial completions before the system commits to a choice. This lets the search consider consequences beyond the model’s immediate preference, while exploring the many possible ways to complete a sequence.

Experiments report average improvements of 3.2% over autoregressive baselines and 8.0% over baseline plan-and-infill, with gains of 19.5% on MBPP and 4.9% on MATH500. The observed orders remain mostly sequential, but non-sequential choices matter for maximum performance. The analysis also finds that stronger exploration, rather than simply more simulations, is necessary to overcome model confidence biases in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: DiffuSearch uses tree search to choose filling orders that improve masked diffusion models’ mathematical and coding outputs.

title: Can I Have Your Order? Monte-Carlo Tree Search for Slot Filling Ordering in Diffusion Language Models

abstract: In this paper, we study a structured class of nonconvex constrained stochastic problems with difference-of-convex (DC) regularization, where the feasible set is possibly nonconvex and the concave part of the DC regularizer is allowed to be nonsmooth. The fundamental challenge lies in maintaining feasibility for nonconvex constraints while achieving favorable oracle complexity. Although single-loop algorithms efficiently solve unconstrained DC optimization problems, their potential for constrained optimization with DC structure remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we develop MoSSP, a Momentum-based Single-loop Stochastic Penalty method for such problems with provable complexity guarantees. The key idea is to apply a single stochastic proximal-gradient step to the Moreau envelope of the penalty plus the convex DC part, with the concave part’s proximal mapping computed in parallel. We derive two algorithm variants: a Polyak-momentum version with $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ oracle complexity for finding stochastic $\varepsilon$-KKT points, and an improved $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ version incorporating recursive momentum. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: MoSSP studies stochastic optimization problems with constraints and difference-of-convex regularization. Such a regularizer combines a convex component with a subtracted convex component. The setting permits a nonconvex feasible region and a nonsmooth concave contribution, making it difficult to respect constraints while keeping the number of required optimization queries manageable.

The proposed method uses a single-loop stochastic penalty approach with momentum. Each iteration takes one stochastic proximal-gradient step on a Moreau-envelope representation of the penalty and the convex regularizer component. It computes the proximal mapping associated with the concave component in parallel. This organizes the constrained problem into updates that retain the efficiency motivation of single-loop methods.

The paper establishes two complexity guarantees for reaching stochastic ε-KKT points, which express approximate constrained optimality conditions. A Polyak-momentum variant requires O(ε^-4) oracle calls, while recursive momentum improves this to O(ε^-3). Experiments demonstrate the algorithms’ effectiveness. The theoretical improvement concerns the query cost of attaining these approximate conditions within the structured problem class, rather than a guarantee of finding a global optimum.
summary.tldr: MoSSP offers single-loop momentum methods with provable oracle complexity for constrained stochastic optimization with difference-of-convex regularization.

title: MoSSP: A Momentum-Based Single-Loop Stochastic Penalty Method for Nonconvex Constrained DC-regularized Optimization

abstract: This paper presents a theoretical investigation into the generalization capabilities of cross-domain knowledge distillation. Utilizing a high-dimensional asymptotic analysis of a linear teacher–student model, we characterize the excess risk while accounting for both model and covariate shifts. Our results provide a formal guarantee for the efficacy of distillation: even when the source and target domains differ substantially, there still may exist a regime where the student model achieves superior generalization ability over the student-only baseline. Moreover, we identify a crossed double descent phenomenon: the excess risk can vary non-monotonically with the teacher’s and student’s dimension-to-sample-size ratios. These results provide rigorous insight into when and why distillation helps across domains.

Our results provide a formal guarantee for the efficacy of distillation: even when the source and target domains differ substantially, there still may exist a regime where the student model achieves superior generalization ability over the student-only baseline. Moreover, we identify a crossed double descent phenomenon: the excess risk can vary non-monotonically with the teacher’s and student’s dimension-to-sample-size ratios. paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers information from a teacher model to a student, but the teacher and student may operate in different domains. This paper studies when that transfer can still improve generalization. It analyzes a linear teacher–student model in a high-dimensional asymptotic setting, explicitly accounting for both model shift and changes in input distributions.

The analysis characterizes excess risk and establishes that useful distillation regimes may exist even when the source and target domains differ substantially. In those regimes, the student can generalize better than a baseline trained without the teacher. The qualification matters: the result identifies circumstances where cross-domain transfer helps, rather than claiming that any teacher remains beneficial under any domain mismatch.

The authors also identify crossed double descent. Excess risk can change non-monotonically as either the teacher’s or the student’s ratio of model dimension to sample size varies. Consequently, the theoretical picture depends on both sides of the transfer. Together, the results explain how domain shifts and the relative scale of the two learning problems influence whether distillation is useful.
summary.tldr: A high-dimensional linear analysis identifies regimes where distillation helps despite domain shift and reveals non-monotonic risk across teacher and student scales.

title: Quantifying Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation in the Presence of Domain Shift

abstract: This paper considers the problem of converting a given dense linear layer to low precision. The tradeoff between compressed length and output discrepancy is analyzed information theoretically (IT). It is shown that a popular GPTQ algorithm may have an arbitrarily large gap to the IT limit. To alleviate this problem, a novel algorithm, termed "WaterSIC", is proposed and is shown to be within a rate gap of 0.255 bits to the IT limit, uniformly over all possible covariance matrices of input activations. The key innovation of WaterSIC’s is to allocate different quantization rates to different columns (in-features) of the weight matrix, mimicking the classical IT solution known as “waterfilling”. Applying WaterSIC to the Llama and Qwen family of LLMs establishes new state-of-the-art performance for all quantization rates from 1 to 4 bits. Our code is available at https://github.com/egorlifar/watersic.

paragraphs: WaterSIC examines how much a dense linear layer can be compressed while controlling changes to its outputs. The paper analyzes this trade-off using information theory, giving a reference limit for the compressed length needed at a given output discrepancy. It shows that GPTQ can have an arbitrarily large gap to that limit.

The proposed algorithm assigns different quantization rates to different columns of the weight matrix, corresponding to different input features. This follows the information-theoretic idea of waterfilling: distribute the available rate unevenly instead of assigning every column the same budget. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models report state-of-the-art performance at quantization rates from one to four bits. The theoretical result concerns compression rate relative to output discrepancy, while the experiments establish usefulness in the tested language models. Together, they support feature-dependent rate allocation as both a principled and practically effective quantization strategy.
summary.tldr: WaterSIC allocates different quantization rates across input features and achieves a proven rate gap of at most 0.255 bits from the information-theoretic limit.

title: WaterSIC: Information-Theoretically (Near) Optimal Linear Layer Quantization

abstract: Despite recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs)’ linguistic prowess in medical diagnosis, we find even state-of-the-art MLLMs suffer from a critical perceptual deficit: geometric blindness. This failure to ground outputs in objective geometric constraints leads to plausible yet factually incorrect hallucinations, rooted in training paradigms that prioritize linguistic fluency over geometric fidelity. This paper introduces Med-Scout, a novel framework that "cures" this blindness via Reinforcement Learning (RL) that leverages the intrinsic geometric logic latent within unlabeled medical images. Instead of relying on costly expert annotations, Med-Scout derives verifiable supervision signals through three strategic proxy tasks inspired by the systematic reading and reasoning patterns of clinicians: Hierarchical Scale Localization, Topological Jigsaw Reconstruction, and Anomaly Consistency Detection. To rigorously quantify this deficit, we present Med-Scout-Bench, a new benchmark specifically designed to evaluate geometric perception. Extensive evaluations show that Med-Scout significantly mitigates geometric blindness, outperforming leading proprietary and open-source MLLMs by over 40% on our benchmark. Furthermore, this enhanced geometric perception generalizes to broader medical understanding, achieving superior results on radiological and comprehensive medical VQA tasks. The project page is: https://github.com/HKUSTGZ-ML4Health-Lab/Med-Scout.

Med-Scout targets the perceptual problem through reinforcement learning based on geometric information already present in unlabeled medical images.

Improvements also extend to radiological and broader medical visual question answering. These results indicate that strengthening geometric perception can benefit medical understanding beyond the proxy tasks used during training.
summary.tldr: Med-Scout uses geometry-based reinforcement learning on unlabeled medical images to improve spatial perception and medical question answering.

title: Med-Scout: Curing MLLMs’ Geometric Blindness in Medical Perception via Geometry-Aware RL Post-Training

abstract: Precise prediction of spatiotemporal dynamics over predictive horizons is constrained by the computational cost of high-fidelity solvers and the sparsity, noise, and irregularity of data. We introduce MERLIN, a Koopman-based framework that lifts dynamics to the evolution of learned observation functionals with near-linear progression, enabling full-field reconstruction at arbitrary resolutions. Theoretically, we develop a functional Koopman theory for PDEs and compensate for the loss of finite-dimensional linear invariance via the Mori–Zwanzig formalism, which augments the linear backbone with non-Markovian memory terms to improve predictive accuracy. Practically, MERLIN employs discretization-invariant function encoders that map partial, irregular observations to observables, and resolution-free function decoders that reconstruct states at arbitrary query points. Training under linear constraints yields an interpretable, low-dimensional model that captures principal modes and supports reduced-order modeling, while memory correction further enables stable long-horizon rollouts even in ultra-low-dimensional latent spaces. Our code is available at: https://github.com/RobinLufdu/MERLIN.

Theoretically, we develop a functional Koopman theory for PDEs and compensate for the loss of finite-dimensional linear invariance via the Mori–Zwanzig formalism, which augments the linear backbone with non-Markovian memory terms to improve predictive accuracy. Practically, MERLIN employs discretization-invariant function encoders that map partial, irregular observations to observables, and resolution-free function decoders that reconstruct states at arbitrary query points. paragraphs: Predicting systems that evolve across space and time is difficult when detailed simulation is expensive and measurements are sparse, noisy, or irregular. MERLIN learns observation functionals: compact quantities derived from the system’s spatial state whose evolution is approximately linear. This provides a low-dimensional representation that can expose principal modes of the dynamics.

A finite collection of learned quantities does not generally preserve perfectly closed linear dynamics. The framework addresses that loss using the Mori–Zwanzig formalism, adding memory terms that allow predictions to depend on past behavior. The memory correction complements the linear backbone instead of requiring the reduced state alone to explain every future change.

Function encoders accept partial, irregular observations without depending on a particular discretization. Function decoders reconstruct the spatial state at arbitrary query points and resolutions. Training with linear constraints supports interpretability and reduced-order modeling, while the memory correction enables stable long-horizon rollouts even with very small latent spaces. The approach joins flexible handling of spatial measurements with a compact dynamical model that retains useful historical information.
summary.tldr: MERLIN combines approximately linear learned dynamics with memory corrections to predict spatial systems from irregular observations at arbitrary resolutions.

title: Interpretable Functional Koopman Learning with Non-Markovian Closure for Spatiotemporal Systems

abstract: Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) based on interconnected Lookup Tables (LUTs) have attracted attention for inference in extremely compact models, but achieving competitive accuracy under such tight resource budgets remains challenging. To address these issues, we introduce the Convolutional Learnable-Group Weightless Neural Network (CLGN). CLGN constructs convolutional layers using LUTs and incorporates a learnable GroupSum connection, thereby enhancing the accuracy of WNNs while maintaining low implementation resource consumption. Moreover, we propose a hierarchical training strategy to improve the training efficiency. We evaluate CLGN in two edge computing scenarios: (1) FPGA, where we evaluate accuracy, latency, throughput, power consumption, LUTs usage, and parameter size; and (2) Microprocessor, where we evaluate latency and memory usage. Compared with the state-of-the-art solutions, the proposed CLGN achieves superior accuracy while maintaining lower implementation resource consumption.

paragraphs: Weightless neural networks use interconnected lookup tables to perform inference in very compact models. Their appeal is low resource consumption, but maintaining competitive accuracy within such small budgets is difficult. This paper introduces CLGN, a convolutional weightless network designed to improve that accuracy while retaining economical implementation.

CLGN builds convolutional layers from lookup tables and adds a learnable GroupSum connection. The architecture therefore makes the connections used to combine information part of the learning process. The authors also introduce a hierarchical training strategy to improve training efficiency. Together, these contributions address both the quality of the compact model and the effort needed to train it.

The evaluation covers two edge computing settings. On FPGAs, the authors examine accuracy, latency, throughput, power, lookup-table usage, and parameter size. On microprocessors, they examine latency and memory usage. They report higher accuracy with lower implementation resource consumption than state-of-the-art solutions. The result matters because compact inference is judged by its hardware demands as well as its predictions, and the evaluation explicitly considers both.
summary.tldr: CLGN combines lookup-table convolutions with learned connections to improve compact neural-network accuracy while reducing reported implementation resource demands.

title: Convolutional Learnable-Group Weightless Neural Network

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has become the standard for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its efficacy is bottlenecked by the high cost of acquiring preference data, especially in low-resource and expert domains. To address this, we introduce ActiveUltraFeedback, a modular active learning pipeline that leverages uncertainty estimates to dynamically identify the most informative responses for annotation. Our pipeline facilitates the systematic evaluation of standard response selection methods alongside Double Reverse Thompson Sampling (DRTS) and DeltaUCB, two novel methods prioritizing response pairs with large predicted quality gaps, leveraging recent results showing that such pairs provide good signals for fine-tuning. Our experiments demonstrate that ActiveUltraFeedback yields high-quality datasets that lead to significant improvements in downstream performance, notably achieving comparable or superior results with as little as one-sixth of the annotated data relative to static baselines. Our pipeline is available at https://github.com/lasgroup/ActiveUltraFeedback and our preference datasets at https://huggingface.co/ActiveUltraFeedback.

paragraphs: Preference-based language model training depends on judgments about which responses are better. Collecting these judgments can be expensive, particularly when relevant expertise or resources are scarce. ActiveUltraFeedback addresses that cost by choosing which responses should receive annotation as data collection proceeds.

The pipeline uses uncertainty estimates to identify informative annotation candidates dynamically. Its modular design allows systematic comparisons between standard selection methods and two proposed methods: Double Reverse Thompson Sampling and DeltaUCB. These new methods prioritize response pairs with large predicted quality differences, drawing on findings that such pairs can provide useful signals for fine-tuning.

In the reported experiments, datasets assembled through this pipeline improve downstream performance. Some results match or exceed those of static selection baselines using as little as one-sixth of the annotated data. This finding supports selective annotation as a way to make preference data collection more efficient: the usefulness of a dataset depends on which comparisons it contains, as well as how many judgments were collected.
summary.tldr: ActiveUltraFeedback selects informative preference comparisons, achieving comparable or better downstream results with as little as one-sixth of the annotated data.

title: ActiveUltraFeedback: Efficient Preference Data Generation using Active Learning

abstract: As language models are increasingly deployed for complex autonomous tasks, their ability to reason accurately over longer horizons becomes critical. An essential component of this ability is planning and managing a long, complex chain-of-thought (CoT). We introduce LongCoT, a scalable benchmark of 2,500 expert-designed problems spanning chemistry, mathematics, computer science, chess, and logic to isolate and directly measure the long-horizon CoT reasoning capabilities of frontier models. Problems consist of a short input with a verifiable answer; solving them requires navigating a graph of interdependent steps that span tens to hundreds of thousands of reasoning tokens. Each local step is individually tractable for frontier models, so failures reflect long-horizon reasoning limitations. At release, the best models achieve $<$10% accuracy (GPT 5.2: 9.8%; Gemini 3 Pro: 6.1%) on LongCoT, revealing a substantial gap in current capabilities. Overall, LongCoT provides a rigorous measure of long-horizon reasoning, tracking the ability of frontier models to reason reliably over extended periods.

paragraphs: A model may solve individual reasoning steps successfully yet struggle to manage a long sequence of dependent steps. LongCoT is designed to measure that extended reasoning capability directly. It contains 2,500 expert-designed problems spanning chemistry, mathematics, computer science, chess, and logic, with short inputs and answers that can be verified.

The difficulty comes from navigating a graph of interdependent reasoning steps. Solving the problems requires reasoning traces ranging from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens, even though each local step is individually tractable for frontier models. This design makes long-horizon coordination central to the evaluation rather than relying on a single unusually difficult operation.

At the benchmark’s release, the best reported models remain below 10% accuracy: GPT 5.2 reaches 9.8%, and Gemini 3 Pro reaches 6.1%. These results expose a substantial gap between handling local steps and sustaining reliable reasoning across a much larger dependency structure. The benchmark provides a scalable way to track improvements in planning and managing such extended reasoning processes.
summary.tldr: LongCoT exposes major failures in sustained reasoning through problems whose manageable individual steps form very long dependency chains.

title: LongCoT: Benchmarking Long-Horizon Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

abstract: Model editing aims to correct errors in large, pretrained models without altering their unrelated behaviors. While some recent works have edited vision–language models (VLMs), no existing editors tackle reasoning-heavy tasks, which typically require humans and models to reason about images. We therefore propose ReasonEdit, the first VLM editor to let users explain their reasoning during editing, introducing a new, practical model editing setup. ReasonEdit continuously stores human reasoning in a codebook, and retrieves only relevant facts during inference using a novel topology-balanced multimodal embedding method inspired by network science. Across four VLMs on multiple rationale-based visual question answering datasets, ReasonEdit achieves state-of-the-art editing performance, ultimately showing that using human reasoning during editing greatly improves edit generalization.

paragraphs: Model editing aims to correct a pretrained model’s mistakes while preserving unrelated behavior. For vision–language models, reasoning-heavy questions introduce a further challenge: a correction may depend on an explanation of how to interpret an image. ReasonEdit introduces an editing setup in which users supply that reasoning, giving the editor more information than an answer correction alone.

The system continually stores human reasoning in a codebook. At inference time, it retrieves relevant facts using a topology-balanced multimodal embedding method inspired by network science. This connects the stored explanations to the current visual question, so the model can draw on applicable reasoning when answering. Selective retrieval is central to making accumulated edits useful across different questions.

Experiments evaluate four vision–language models on multiple visual question-answering datasets containing rationales. ReasonEdit achieves leading editing performance, and the results show that incorporating human reasoning substantially improves edit generalization. This suggests that explanations can help corrections apply beyond the particular example that originally prompted an edit.
summary.tldr: ReasonEdit stores and retrieves human explanations to make vision–language model corrections generalize better across reasoning-heavy visual questions.

title: ReasonEdit: Editing Vision–Language Models using Human Reasoning

abstract: While reasoning over long context is crucial for various real-world applications, it remains challenging for large language models (LLMs) as they suffer from performance degradation as the context length grows. Recent work MemAgent has tried to tackle this by processing context chunk-by-chunk in an RNN-like loop and updating a textual memory for final answering. However, this naive recurrent memory update faces two crucial drawbacks: (i) memory can quickly explode because it can update indiscriminately, even on evidence-free chunks; and (ii) the loop lacks an exit mechanism, leading to unnecessary computation after even sufficient evidence is collected. To address these issues, we propose GRU-Mem, which incorporates two text-controlled gates for more stable and efficient long-context reasoning. Specifically, in GRU-Mem, the memory only updates when the update gate is open and the recurrent loop will exit immediately once the exit gate is open. To endow the model with such capabilities, we introduce two reward signals $r^{\text{update}}$ and $r^{\text{exit}}$ within end-to-end RL, rewarding the correct updating and exiting behaviors respectively. Experiments on various long-context reasoning tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of GRU-Mem, which generally outperforms the vanilla MemAgent with up to 400% times inference speed acceleration.

paragraphs: Processing long inputs in chunks lets a language model maintain a textual memory instead of handling everything at once. The paper identifies two weaknesses in MemAgent's recurrent approach: memory can grow through indiscriminate updates on chunks without useful evidence, and processing can continue even after sufficient evidence has been gathered. Both behaviors create unnecessary work.

GRU-Mem adds two text-controlled gates to this loop. An update gate determines whether the current chunk should change memory, while an exit gate determines whether processing should stop immediately. End-to-end reinforcement learning uses separate reward signals for correct updating and correct exiting, teaching the model to control both information retention and the duration of its reading process.

Experiments on multiple long-context reasoning tasks show improved effectiveness and efficiency, generally outperforming vanilla MemAgent and reporting substantial inference acceleration. The contribution is a learned decision about when further reading or memory revision is useful. This links long-context reasoning quality with explicit control over memory growth and computation, rather than updating and continuing at every chunk automatically.
summary.tldr: GRU-Mem learns when to update textual memory and when to stop reading, improving long-context reasoning efficiency and performance.

title: When to Memorize and When to Stop: Gated Recurrent Memory for Long-Context Reasoning

abstract: Object-centric learning (OCL) aims to learn structured scene representations that support compositional generalization and robustness to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. However, OCL models are often not evaluated regarding these goals. Instead, most prior work focuses on evaluating OCL models solely through object discovery and simple reasoning tasks, such as probing the representation via image classification. We identify two limitations in existing benchmarks: (1) They provide limited insights on the representation usefulness of OCL models, and (2) localization and representation usefulness are assessed using disjoint metrics. To address (1), we use instruction-tuned VLMs as evaluators, enabling scalable benchmarking across diverse VQA datasets to measure how well VLMs leverage OCL representations for complex reasoning tasks. To address (2), we introduce a unified evaluation task and metric that jointly assess localization (where) and representation usefulness (what), thereby eliminating inconsistencies introduced by disjoint evaluation. Finally, we include a simple multi-feature reconstruction baseline as a reference point.

paragraphs: Object-centric learning represents scenes in terms of objects, with the aim of supporting compositional generalization and robustness to unfamiliar data. Yet identifying objects does not by itself establish that their representations support useful reasoning. This paper examines an evaluation gap: existing benchmarks often emphasize object discovery or simple classification probes rather than the broader goals of object-centric learning.

The authors propose using instruction-tuned vision-language models as evaluators. Across visual question-answering datasets, these evaluators measure how effectively object-centric representations can support more complex reasoning. This makes representation usefulness a direct focus of evaluation and provides a way to benchmark it across diverse question-answering settings.

A second contribution is a task and metric that assess localization and representation usefulness together. Jointly evaluating where an object is and what its representation supports addresses inconsistencies from measuring those properties separately. The paper also supplies a simple baseline based on reconstructing multiple features. Its central contribution is therefore a broader evaluation framework for assessing what object-centric representations actually enable.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes evaluating object-centric representations through complex visual reasoning and a joint measure of localization and usefulness.

title: Evaluating Object-Centric Models beyond Object Discovery

abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) to diverse human preferences is fundamentally challenging since criteria can often conflict with each other. Inference-time alignment methods have recently gained popularity as they allow LLMs to be aligned to multiple criteria via different alignment algorithms at inference time. However, inference-time alignment is computationally expensive since it often requires multiple forward passes of the base model. In this work, we propose inference-aware meta-alignment (IAMA), a novel approach that enables LLMs to be aligned to multiple criteria with minimal computational overhead at inference time. IAMA trains a base model such that it can be effectively aligned to multiple task optima via different inference-time alignment algorithms. To solve the non-linear optimization problems involved in IAMA, we propose non-linear GRPO, which provably converges to the optimal solution in the space of probability measures.

paragraphs: Different human preferences can demand conflicting behavior from the same language model. Inference-time alignment offers flexibility by adapting a model’s outputs to different criteria when it is used. That flexibility can be computationally expensive, however, because alignment procedures often require multiple forward passes through the base model for each response.

Inference-aware meta-alignment changes how the base model is trained. The aim is to prepare a model that different inference-time alignment algorithms can efficiently move toward multiple task optima. This makes the later alignment procedure part of the training objective and seeks to retain preference flexibility with minimal additional computation during use.

The resulting training problems are nonlinear, motivating the proposed non-linear GRPO algorithm. The authors prove convergence to the optimal solution in the space of probability measures. That mathematical setting specifies the scope of the convergence claim; it is not a blanket guarantee about every neural-network implementation. The contribution connects preparation during training with efficient adaptation to diverse criteria at inference time.
summary.tldr: IAMA trains language models for efficient inference-time alignment and introduces non-linear GRPO with an optimality guarantee in probability-measure space.

title: Inference-Aware Meta-Alignment of LLMs via Non-Linear GRPO

abstract: Exams are a fundamental test of expert-level intelligence and require integrated understanding, reasoning, and generation. Existing exam-style benchmarks mainly focus on understanding and reasoning tasks, and current generation benchmarks emphasize the illustration of world knowledge and visual concepts, neglecting the evaluation of rigorous drawing exams. We introduce GenExam, the first benchmark for multidisciplinary text-to-image exams, featuring 1,000 samples across 10 subjects with exam-style prompts organized under a four-level taxonomy. Each problem is equipped with ground-truth images and fine-grained scoring points to enable a precise evaluation of semantic correctness and visual plausibility. Experiments on 17 text-to-image and unified models demonstrate the great challenge of GenExam and the huge gap where open-source models consistently lag behind the leading closed-source ones. By framing image generation as an exam, GenExam offers a rigorous assessment of models’ ability to integrate understanding, reasoning, and generation, providing insights on the path to intelligent generative models. Our benchmark and evaluation code will be released.

paragraphs: Producing an exam drawing requires a model to understand a question, reason about its requirements, and express the answer visually. GenExam evaluates this combination. The paper identifies a gap between exam benchmarks focused on understanding and reasoning and generation benchmarks focused on depicting knowledge or visual concepts, leaving rigorous drawing examinations comparatively neglected.

The benchmark contains 1,000 examples across 10 subjects, with exam-style prompts organized into a four-level taxonomy. Each problem includes reference images and detailed scoring points. These support evaluation of both semantic correctness and visual plausibility, so the assessment considers whether an image communicates the required answer as well as whether its visual presentation makes sense.

Tests of 17 text-to-image and unified models show that GenExam is challenging. Open-source models consistently trail the leading closed-source systems in these experiments. The benchmark’s contribution is to make integrated understanding, reasoning, and generation the object of assessment, using explicit scoring criteria to examine image generation as a substantive answer to an academic problem.
summary.tldr: GenExam evaluates image generation through 1,000 multidisciplinary exam problems that require integrated understanding, reasoning, and drawing.

title: GenExam: A Multidisciplinary Text-to-Image Exam

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong perception and reasoning capabilities. However, most existing models focus on isolated objects and neglect structured relationships for efficient target navigation, limiting their performance on visually intensive tasks. To address this challenge, we introduce Scene Graph Thinking (SaGe), a novel paradigm that enables fine-grained and structured visual reasoning through explicit scene-graph representations. Specifically, we first introduce an automated data engine that converts flat image–text corpora into structured scene graphs, where hierarchical entities constitute the nodes and diverse visual relations define the edges. Building upon this, we construct 120K high-quality training data by sampling reasoning traces from scene graphs. Then two-stage graph-aligned post-training paradigms are introduced, where supervised fine-tuning internalizes MLLMs with structured reasoning, and subsequent reinforcement fine-tuning proposes node-as-proxy graph rewards to consolidate efficient graph exploration. With curated data and graph-aligned training, our approach achieves significant improvements across eight multimodal benchmarks, demonstrating strong effectiveness on fine-grained perception and reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning often depends on relationships between objects, yet multimodal models can focus on objects in isolation. Scene Graph Thinking, or SaGe, gives models an explicit structure for reasoning about entities and their relationships. The goal is to improve fine-grained perception and make navigation toward relevant visual targets more efficient.

An automated data engine converts image–text examples into scene graphs, with hierarchical entities as nodes and visual relations as edges. The authors sample reasoning traces from these graphs to construct 120,000 training examples. This turns existing flat image–text material into supervision that exposes how visual entities connect.

Training proceeds in two stages: supervised fine-tuning teaches structured reasoning, and reinforcement fine-tuning uses node-as-proxy graph rewards to strengthen efficient graph exploration. The approach produces significant improvements across eight multimodal benchmarks. These findings support coordinating the structure of training data with the reward used for reasoning, so that both stages encourage the model to use relationships when interpreting visually demanding inputs.
summary.tldr: SaGe trains multimodal models with scene-graph reasoning traces and graph-based rewards, improving fine-grained visual reasoning across eight benchmarks.

title: Scene Graph Thinking: Reinforcing Structured Visual Reasoning for Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Multi-fidelity (MF) regression often operates in regimes of extreme data imbalance, where the commonly-used Gaussian-process surrogates struggle with cubic scaling costs and overfit to sparse high-fidelity observations, limiting efficiency and generalization in real-world applications. We introduce FIRE, a training-free MF framework that couples tabular foundation models (TFMs) to perform zero-shot in-context Bayesian inference via a high-fidelity correction model conditioned on the low-fidelity model’s posterior predictive distributions. This cross-fidelity information transfer via distributional summaries captures heteroscedastic errors, enabling robust residual learning without model retraining. Across 31 benchmark problems spanning synthetic functions and real-world tasks (e.g., DrivAerNet, LCBench), FIRE delivers a stronger performance–time trade-off than seven state-of-the-art GP-based or deep learning MF regression methods, ranking highest in accuracy and uncertainty quantification with runtime advantages. Limitations include context window constraints and dependence on the quality of the pre-trained TFMs. Code & data can be found here: https://github.com/rosenyu304/FIRE.

paragraphs: Multi-fidelity regression combines observations of differing quality, often with many low-fidelity examples and very few high-fidelity ones. Common Gaussian-process approaches can become expensive as data grows and can overfit the scarce high-quality observations. FIRE addresses this imbalance using pretrained tabular foundation models without retraining them for the regression task.

The framework connects a low-fidelity predictor to a high-fidelity correction model through predictive distributions. Passing distributional summaries gives the correction model information about uncertainty as well as predicted values. This supports learning residual corrections when error levels vary across inputs. The models perform Bayesian inference through examples supplied in context, making cross-fidelity transfer part of inference itself.

Across 31 synthetic and real-world benchmark problems, FIRE ranks highest in accuracy and uncertainty quantification among the seven compared methods, while offering runtime advantages. The results support its reported performance–time trade-off. Its applicability remains constrained by the models’ context windows and by the quality of the pretrained tabular foundation models, both limitations explicitly identified in the abstract.
summary.tldr: FIRE transfers predictive distributions between tabular foundation models to perform accurate, uncertainty-aware multi-fidelity regression without retraining.

title: FIRE: Multi-Fidelity Regression with Distribution-Conditioned In-Context Learning Using Tabular Foundation Models

abstract: Most federated recommender systems represent each user with a single embedding learned from local interaction data, implicitly assuming that user preferences are fixed and precisely identifiable. In federated settings, however, each client observes only a limited and fragmentary view of user behavior, rendering such point estimates inherently brittle. To address this mismatch, we model user preferences as distributions rather than points, allowing multiple compatible preference representations to coexist. Rather than collapsing evidence into a single embedding, our approach preserves uncertainty and diversity in user representations, providing a richer basis for preference modeling. We instantiate this idea with a diffusion-based generative framework that produces diverse user embeddings and derives recommendation scores by aggregating predictions across them. This distributional formulation yields more stable ranking behavior and improved robustness under ambiguous feedback. Extensive experiments on federated recommendation benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent and significant improvements over baselines. Our code is available.

paragraphs: Federated recommendation must infer preferences from the limited interactions visible to each client. Representing a user with one learned vector compresses that fragmentary evidence into a single estimate. The paper argues that this is brittle because the available observations can be compatible with several different preference representations, rather than identifying one precise profile.

The proposed approach represents preferences as a distribution of possible user embeddings. A diffusion-based generative framework produces diverse vectors that remain compatible with the evidence. Recommendation scores are then formed by aggregating predictions across those vectors. This preserves uncertainty and diversity through the scoring process instead of discarding them when constructing the user representation.

The authors report more stable rankings and better robustness when feedback is ambiguous. Experiments on federated recommendation benchmarks also show consistent, significant improvements over the compared baselines. The central implication is that uncertainty in a user’s observed behavior can be represented explicitly and used in recommendation, rather than treated as something a single embedding has already resolved.
summary.tldr: A diffusion-based recommender models each user with multiple plausible embeddings and aggregates their predictions to improve ranking stability.

title: Beyond Single Embedding: Modeling User Preferences as Distribution in Federated Recommendation

abstract: Knowledge distillation improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by compressing the knowledge of a teacher LLM to train smaller LLMs. On-policy distillation advances this approach by having the student sample its own trajectories while a teacher LLM provides dense token-level supervision, addressing the distribution mismatch between training and inference in off-policy distillation methods. However, on-policy distillation typically requires a separate, often larger, teacher LLM and does not explicitly leverage ground-truth solutions available in reasoning datasets. Inspired by the intuition that a sufficiently capable LLM can rationalize external privileged reasoning traces and teach its weaker self, we introduce On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), a learning algorithm where a single LLM acts as both teacher and student with different contexts. The teacher policy conditions on privileged information while the student policy sees only the question; training minimizes the per-token divergence between these distributions over the student’s own rollouts. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, achieving superior token efficiency compared to reinforcement learning methods and better performance over off-policy distillation methods.

However, on-policy distillation typically requires a separate, often larger, teacher LLM and does not explicitly leverage ground-truth solutions available in reasoning datasets. The teacher policy conditions on privileged information while the student policy sees only the question; training minimizes the per-token divergence between these distributions over the student’s own rollouts. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, achieving superior token efficiency compared to reinforcement learning methods and better performance over off-policy distillation methods.

paragraphs: On-policy distillation trains a student on reasoning trajectories it generates itself, with a teacher supplying guidance at each token. This helps align training with the situations the student encounters during generation. However, conventional versions typically require a separate teacher and do not explicitly exploit ground-truth solutions already available in reasoning datasets.

On-Policy Self-Distillation uses one language model in two contexts. As the teacher, it sees privileged information; as the student, it receives only the question. Training reduces the per-token divergence between their distributions along the student's own rollouts. The teaching advantage therefore comes from additional context rather than a separate, larger model.

The approach is motivated by the idea that a sufficiently capable model can interpret external reasoning traces and use them to guide its less-informed self. Across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, the paper reports better token efficiency than reinforcement-learning methods and better performance than off-policy distillation methods. These findings support combining privileged solution information with feedback on the model's own generated trajectories.
summary.tldr: OPSD lets a model teach itself on its own reasoning rollouts by giving its teacher context privileged solution information.

abstract: We propose machine learning methods for the estimation of deformation fields that transform two given objects into each other, thereby establishing a dense point to point correspondence. The fields are computed using a modified support vector machine containing a penalty enforcing that points of one object will be mapped to “similar” points on the other one. Our system, which contains little engineering or domain knowledge, delivers state of the art performance. We present application results including close to photorealistic morphs of 3D head models.
originalAbstract: We propose machine learning methods for the estimation of deformation fields that transform two given objects into each other, thereby establishing a dense point to point correspondence. The fields are computed using a modified support vector machine containing a penalty enforcing that points of one object will be mapped to “similar” points on the other one. Our system, which contains little engineering or domain knowledge, delivers state of the art performance. We present application results including close to photorealistic morphs of 3D head models.

paragraphs: The paper treats object correspondence as a learning problem: given two objects, estimate how points on one should map to points on the other. It seeks a dense point-to-point correspondence through a deformation field, a description of how the object must change to align with its counterpart across its points.

The authors compute this field using a modified support vector machine. An added penalty encourages points to map to similar points on the other object, giving the learning procedure an explicit correspondence requirement. This puts the matching objective inside the model used to estimate the deformation, with little engineering or domain-specific knowledge in the overall system.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance and demonstrate applications that include nearly photorealistic morphs of three-dimensional head models. These examples show the estimated correspondences supporting visible transformations between objects. The contribution connects a learned deformation field to dense matching, with the similarity penalty supplying the central requirement that makes the transformation meaningful as a correspondence.
summary.tldr: A modified support vector machine learns dense object correspondences through deformation fields, including nearly photorealistic 3D head morphs.

title: Object correspondence as a machine learning problem
Semi-supervised learning for structured output variables

abstract: This paper suggests a method for multiclass learning with many classes by simultaneously learning shared characteristics common to the classes, and predictors for the classes in terms of these characteristics. We cast this as a convex optimization problem, using trace-norm regularization and study gradient-based optimization both for the linear case and the kernelized setting.
originalAbstract: This paper suggests a method for multiclass learning with many classes by simultaneously learning shared characteristics common to the classes, and predictors for the classes in terms of these characteristics. We cast this as a convex optimization problem, using trace-norm regularization and study gradient-based optimization both for the linear case and the kernelized setting.

paragraphs: When a classification problem has many classes, the classes may have characteristics in common. This paper proposes learning those shared characteristics at the same time as the predictors for individual classes. Each predictor is expressed in terms of the learned common structure, making shared representation and class prediction parts of one learning problem.

The authors formulate the joint task as a convex optimization problem using trace-norm regularization. The regularization is the mechanism through which the formulation addresses shared structure across class predictors. Learning both components together allows the common characteristics to be determined in connection with the classification task, rather than requiring them to be specified beforehand.

The paper studies gradient-based optimization in both the linear case and a kernelized setting. These two settings extend the proposed formulation across different forms of classifier representation. The stated contribution is a method for jointly discovering common characteristics and learning multiclass predictors, together with an optimization treatment. It provides a concrete mathematical framework for sharing information across a large collection of classes.
summary.tldr: A convex trace-norm formulation jointly learns shared characteristics and class predictors for multiclass classification.

title: Uncovering shared structures in multiclass classification

abstract: We introduce confidence-weighted linear classifiers, a new class of algorithms that maintain confidence information about classifier parameters. Learning in this framework updates parameters by estimating weights and increasing model confidence. We investigate a new online algorithm that maintains a Gaussian distribution over weight vectors, updating the mean and variance of the model with each instance. Empirical evaluation on a range of NLP tasks show that our algorithm improves over other state of the art online and batch methods, learns faster in the online setting, and lends itself to better classifier combination after parallel training.

paragraphs: The paper introduces linear classifiers that track confidence in their parameters as learning proceeds. Learning therefore involves both estimating useful weights and increasing confidence in those estimates. This adds an explicit account of parameter uncertainty to the classifier's representation of what it has learned from examples.

The authors investigate an online algorithm that maintains a Gaussian distribution over weight vectors. Each new training instance updates the distribution's mean and variance. The mean represents the current weight estimates, while the variance carries confidence information. Updating both quantities lets the model revise its predictions and its certainty about the parameters within the same learning process.

Evaluations on several natural language processing tasks show improvements over the online and batch methods used for comparison. The authors also report faster learning in the online setting and better classifier combination following parallel training. These findings give confidence information two practical roles: supporting learning as examples arrive and helping combine classifiers that were trained separately. The reported advantages are empirical results from the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: An online linear classifier updates a Gaussian distribution over weights to learn predictions and parameter confidence together.

title: Confidence-weighted linear classification

abstract: Recent advances in Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) have positioned it as an attractive tool for tackling many supervised learning tasks. The development of efficient gradient descent based optimization schemes has made it possible to tackle large scale problems. Simultaneously, MKL based algorithms have achieved very good results on challenging real world applications. Yet, despite their successes, MKL approaches are limited in that they focus on learning a linear combination of given base kernels. In this paper, we observe that existing MKL formulations can be extended to learn general kernel combinations subject to general regularization. This can be achieved while retaining all the efficiency of existing large scale optimization algorithms. To highlight the advantages of generalized kernel learning, we tackle feature selection problems on benchmark vision and UCI databases. It is demonstrated that the proposed formulation can lead to better results not only as compared to traditional MKL but also as compared to state-of-the-art wrapper and filter methods for feature selection.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines given base kernels for supervised learning. Efficient gradient-based optimization had made these methods practical for large problems, but the formulations considered here were restricted to linear combinations. This paper asks whether a broader family of combinations can be learned without giving up that computational efficiency.

The authors show how existing formulations can extend to general kernel combinations with general regularization. They state that the extension retains the efficiency of existing large-scale optimization algorithms. This matters because the combination rule and its regularization become more flexible while remaining connected to the optimization machinery that made multiple kernel learning practical.

The proposed formulation is evaluated through feature selection on benchmark vision and UCI datasets. Results show that it can improve on traditional multiple kernel learning and on leading wrapper and filter feature-selection methods. The reported advantage establishes the potential of the broader formulation in these applications, rather than asserting that every generalized kernel combination will outperform a linear one.
summary.tldr: Multiple kernel learning can support more general combinations and regularization while retaining efficient optimization and improving some feature-selection results.

title: More generality in efficient multiple kernel learning

abstract: We consider multiclass classification problems where the set of labels are organized hierarchically as a category tree. We associate each node in the tree with a classifier and classify the examples recursively from the root to the leaves. We propose a hierarchical Support Vector Machine (SVM) that encourages the classifier at each node to be different from the classifiers at its ancestors. More specifically, we introduce regularizations that force the normal vector of the classifying hyperplane at each node to be orthogonal to those at its ancestors as much as possible. We establish conditions under which training such a hierarchical SVM is a convex optimization problem, and develop an efficient dual-averaging method for solving it. We evaluate the method on a number of real-world text categorization tasks and obtain state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Some multiclass classification tasks arrange labels in a category tree. This paper associates a classifier with each node and classifies examples by following decisions from the root toward a leaf. Because several classifiers participate along a path, their relationships become part of the learning problem rather than treating every decision independently.

The proposed hierarchical support vector machine encourages each node's classifier to differ from its ancestors. Specifically, regularization pushes the normal vectors of their separating hyperplanes toward orthogonality as much as possible. In geometric terms, the approach encourages decisions at successive levels to use different directions, making the category hierarchy shape the learned classifiers.

The authors establish conditions under which training this hierarchical SVM is a convex optimization problem and develop an efficient dual-averaging solver. Convexity is thus a conditional result, rather than an unrestricted property of every version of the setup. On several real-world text categorization tasks, the method achieves reported state-of-the-art performance, supporting this form of structured differentiation among classifiers.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical SVM encourages orthogonal decision directions between ancestor and descendant classifiers and achieves strong text categorization results.

title: Hierarchical Classification via Orthogonal Transfer

abstract: We present a comprehensive framework for structured sparse coding and modeling extending the recent ideas of using learnable fast regressors to approximate exact sparse codes. For this purpose, we develop a novel block-coordinate proximal splitting method for the iterative solution of hierarchical sparse coding problems, and show an efficient feed forward architecture derived from its iteration. This architecture faithfully approximates the exact structured sparse codes with a fraction of the complexity of the standard optimization methods. We also show that by using different training objective functions, learnable sparse encoders are no longer restricted to be mere approximants of the exact sparse code for a pre-given dictionary, as in earlier formulations, but can be rather used as full-featured sparse encoders or even modelers. A simple implementation shows several orders of magnitude speedup compared to the state-of-the-art at minimal performance degradation, making the proposed framework suitable for real time and large-scale applications.

paragraphs: Structured sparse coding seeks representations with a constrained pattern of active components, but obtaining those representations through iterative optimization can be expensive. This paper develops a framework for replacing that repeated computation with learned fast encoders. It extends approaches that train regressors to approximate exact sparse codes.

The authors first introduce a block-coordinate proximal splitting method for hierarchical sparse coding. They then derive an efficient feedforward architecture from an iteration of that method. This connects the learned encoder to the underlying optimization procedure. The resulting architecture closely approximates structured sparse codes using a fraction of the complexity of standard optimization methods.

Different training objectives also allow the encoders to act as sparse representation learners or modelers, beyond reproducing codes for a fixed dictionary. A simple implementation achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude over the state of the art with minimal performance degradation. These reported results support the framework's suitability for real-time and large-scale uses where repeatedly solving the original optimization problem would be costly.
summary.tldr: Optimization-derived feedforward encoders produce structured sparse representations with reported orders-of-magnitude speedups and minimal performance loss.

title: Learning Efficient Structured Sparse Models
